course.title: Modern Physics: Relativity and the Quantum
course.description: Special relativity, light as photons, atomic spectra, quantum behaviour and nuclear energy, each taught from the measurements that forced the idea.
course.audience: A capable adult who has finished Discere's two classical physics courses and is comfortable with powers, square roots and a calculator with ln. No calculus is needed. Calculations are a real part of the course, and every lesson also asks for a judgement about a real measurement.

paragraphs: Special relativity, light as photons, atomic spectra, quantum behaviour and nuclear energy, each taught from the measurements that forced the idea.
outcomes: You'll be able to find how much a moving clock lags and how much a moving rod shortens, and say when the effect is too small to matter.
You'll be able to say which of two distant events happens first for observers in relative motion.
You'll be able to convert between mass and energy and judge whether a mass change could be seen.
You'll be able to predict what a photoelectric experiment shows and work out photon energies and photon counts.
You'll be able to compute hydrogen's spectral lines and say where the Bohr model stops working.
You'll be able to predict a double-slit pattern, estimate a momentum spread from the uncertainty principle and compare tunnelling in different barriers.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Physics: Motion and Forces, Physics II: Waves, Electricity and Magnetism, and Heat, Maths Foundations.

modules.title: Special relativity
modules.description: Moving clocks, simultaneity, moving rods and the equivalence of mass and energy, each checked against real measurements.

modules.title: Light as particles
modules.description: The photoelectric effect, photon energy in electron-volts and what a photon count tells you.

modules.title: Atoms and spectra
modules.description: Hydrogen's emission lines from energy-level jumps, and the limits of the Bohr model.

modules.title: Quantum behaviour
modules.description: Wave-particle duality, the uncertainty principle and tunnelling.

modules.title: Nuclear energy and what came after
modules.description: Half-life, binding energy, fission and fusion, then choosing the right physics for a case.

concepts.title: Lorentz factor
concepts.summary: The factor gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) by which a moving clock's tick is stretched, as measured by an observer who sees it move at speed v.

concepts.title: Proper time
concepts.summary: The time between two events as shown by a clock present at both, which every inertial observer agrees on and which is the shortest time between those events.

concepts.title: Relativity of simultaneity
concepts.summary: Two events at different places that are simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally not simultaneous in another, unless the motion is perpendicular to the line joining them.

concepts.title: Reciprocity
concepts.summary: Each of two observers in relative motion measures the other's clock to run slow, with no contradiction, because each compares the other's clock with several of their own.

concepts.title: Proper length
concepts.summary: The length of an object in its own rest frame, which is the greatest length any observer will measure for it.

concepts.title: Length contraction
concepts.summary: An object measured moving along its length is shorter by the factor 1/gamma, L = L0 / gamma, and unchanged across its width.

concepts.title: Rest energy
concepts.summary: A body at rest has energy E = m c^2, and any change in its energy changes its mass by that energy divided by c^2.

concepts.title: Closed and open systems
concepts.summary: Mass is lost only when the released energy leaves the system; in a sealed, insulated container the total mass stays the same.

concepts.title: Threshold frequency and work function
concepts.summary: Each metal has a minimum frequency below which no electrons are emitted, whatever the intensity, and the energy h times that frequency is the work function W, the least energy needed to free an electron.

concepts.title: Photon
concepts.summary: Light is absorbed in packets of energy hf, and an electron takes all of one packet's energy or none of it, so K_max = hf - W.

concepts.title: Photon energy
concepts.summary: A photon of frequency f has energy E = hf = hc / wavelength, and hc is 1239.84 eV nm.

concepts.title: Photon rate
concepts.summary: A beam's power is the number of photons per second times the energy of each, so beams of equal power carry more photons per second at longer wavelengths.

concepts.title: Spectral series
concepts.summary: Hydrogen's lines fall in families named by the level they end on: Lyman on n = 1, Balmer on n = 2 and Paschen on n = 3.

concepts.title: Energy-level jump
concepts.summary: A line's photon energy is the difference between two level energies, so 1/wavelength = R(1/nf^2 - 1/ni^2), with R about 1.0974e7 per metre.

concepts.title: Domain of the Bohr model
concepts.summary: It gives almost exact results where two charged points orbit at speeds far below c: hydrogen, singly ionised helium, doubly ionised lithium, positronium. It fails for neutral helium and for most other features of spectra.

concepts.title: Standing-wave quantisation
concepts.summary: De Broglie's wavelength h/mv fitted a whole number of times around the orbit, n wavelength = 2 pi r, gives m v r = n h-bar.

concepts.title: Wave-particle duality
concepts.summary: Photons and electrons show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others; one electron at a time lands at a single point, and the points build up a wave pattern.

concepts.title: De Broglie wavelength
concepts.summary: A particle of mass m and speed v has wavelength h / (m v).

concepts.title: Uncertainty relation
concepts.summary: The spreads in position and momentum of a quantum state obey sigma_x sigma_p >= h-bar / 2, with h-bar = h / 2 pi.

concepts.title: Origin in waves
concepts.summary: A narrow wave packet needs many wavelengths added together, so a sharp position means a wide spread of momentum; this belongs to every wave and is not a limit of instruments.

concepts.title: Tunnelling
concepts.summary: A particle can cross a barrier it does not have the energy to climb, because its wave extends into and through the barrier.

concepts.title: Dependence on the barrier
concepts.summary: The probability of tunnelling falls exponentially as the barrier gets wider, higher or the particle heavier, so it is large only for light particles and very thin barriers.

concepts.title: Half-life
concepts.summary: The time for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay, fixed for each nuclide, so the number remaining is N = N0 x 2^(-t / half-life).

concepts.title: Decay without memory
concepts.summary: An atom's chance of decaying in a given time does not depend on its age, so one atom's decay time cannot be predicted while a large sample decays predictably.

concepts.title: Mass defect and binding energy
concepts.summary: A nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons, and the missing mass times c^2 is the binding energy that would be needed to take it apart.

concepts.title: Binding energy curve
concepts.summary: Binding energy per nucleon rises through the light nuclei, peaks at nickel-62 and iron, and falls slowly for heavier nuclei, so fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both release energy.

concepts.title: Size of the correction
concepts.summary: Relativity matters when v/c is not small (0.5% at one tenth of c), and quantum effects matter when the scales of position, momentum or energy approach h-bar; below that, classical physics is accurate.

concepts.title: What came after the old quantum theory
concepts.summary: In 1925 and 1926 matrix mechanics and wave mechanics replaced Bohr's orbits with probability waves, and general relativity adds a gravitational effect on clocks that works against the speed effect.

lessons.title: Time dilation

lead.text: Any clock ticks by repeating something at a steady rate, so the simplest clock to reason about is a **light clock**: a pulse of light bouncing between two mirrors a distance $L$ apart, with one tick each time the pulse returns to the lower mirror. The pulse covers a path of length $2L$ at speed $c$, so an observer at rest beside the clock measures the time between ticks to be

Now let the clock move past you at a steady speed $v$, with the mirrors one above the other and the motion sideways. While the pulse climbs to the upper mirror, the mirror moves on, so you see the pulse follow a slanted line that is longer than $L$. Light has the same speed $c$ for you as for the observer beside the clock, so a longer path takes longer, and the time between ticks that you measure, written $\Delta t'$, is greater than $\Delta t$.

afterFigure.text: In half a tick the pulse rises through $L$ while the clock moves sideways through $v\,\Delta t'/2$, so the slanted path of length $c\,\Delta t'/2$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with those two sides. Pythagoras gives
and putting $L = c\,\Delta t/2$ and solving for $\Delta t'$ leaves

The factor $\gamma$ is called the **Lorentz factor**. It is never less than 1, so the moving clock's ticks are always further apart than the same clock's ticks at rest, which is what it means to say that a moving clock *runs slow*. At 0.6 c the sides of the triangle in the figure are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5, so each tick takes 5/4 = 1.25 times as long.

Moving sideways, the pulse follows a slanted path, the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides L and v t′ over 2, and the slanted path is longer the faster the clock moves.
diagram.caption: The same clock drawn at rest and at two speeds, with the upper mirror shown where it is when the pulse arrives. The faster the clock moves, the longer the slanted path and the longer each tick. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: The figure shows the triangle for 0.6 c and 0.9 c. The same triangle, with sides $L$, $v\,\Delta t'/2$ and $c\,\Delta t'/2$, applies at every speed.

reveal.text: At 0.8 c the triangle has sides 0.6, 0.8 and 1 in units of $c\,\Delta t'/2$, which is why the answer comes out as the reciprocal of 0.6.

lead.text: Putting numbers into $\gamma$ shows how it behaves. At $v = 0.1c$ the quantity $v^2/c^2$ is 0.01, so $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{0.99} = 1.005$. At $0.6c$ the square root is $\sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$, so $\gamma = 1.25$, at $0.8c$ it is $\sqrt{0.36} = 0.6$, so $\gamma = 1.667$, and at $0.98c$ it is $\sqrt{0.0396} = 0.199$, so $\gamma = 5.025$.

The curve stays close to 1 over most of its range and then climbs steeply as $v$ approaches $c$, which is why moving clocks look ordinary at everyday speeds and the effect becomes dramatic only near the speed of light.

afterFigure.text: The second view gives a rule of thumb. At 0.1 c, about 30,000 km/s, a tick lasts only 0.5% longer, and below that speed the effect is smaller still. A change of 0.5% can be ignored in a rough estimate and has to be allowed for in a careful one, so one tenth of the speed of light marks roughly where time dilation starts to matter.

diagram.alt: Two graphs of the Lorentz factor gamma against speed as a fraction of the speed of light. The first runs to 0.98 c and shows gamma staying near 1 for a long way and then climbing steeply, with marked points at 0.1, 0.6, 0.8 and 0.98 c. The second enlarges the range below 0.2 c and marks the 0.5 percent point at 0.1 c.
diagram.caption: The curve hugs 1 until the speed is a sizeable fraction of c and then climbs steeply. The second view enlarges the low speeds, where the lengthening of a tick reaches 0.5% at about one tenth of c.

lead.text: The fraction $\gamma - 1$ is how much longer a tick lasts than it would at rest, so it gives a quick test of whether a correction is needed.

reveal.text: The three slow cases are all far below 0.1 c, and the three fast ones are all far above it, so none of them needs a close call.

lead.text: Return to the muon. Its lifetime of 2.197 microseconds is read from a clock that travels with it, and that clock is present at both events, the muon's creation and its decay. The time between two events as shown by a clock present at both is called the **proper time**, and every observer, whatever their own motion, agrees on what that clock shows.

An observer on the ground has no single clock at both events. They record the creation with one clock at one place and the decay with another clock at a different place, and the interval between those two readings is longer than the proper time by the factor $\gamma$. The proper time is therefore the shortest time that any observer measures between the two events, and the two are related by
where $\Delta\tau$ is the proper time and $\Delta t$ is the interval the ground observer measures.
Three clocks record the muon's life. One rides with the muon, and two sit at rest on the ground, set to agree, one beside the place where the muon is created and one beside the place where it decays.

reveal.text: The ground clocks give a longer interval, and that is the one the next example works out.

steps.headline: A muon lasts 2.197 microseconds at rest. Find how long it lasts, and how far it travels, as measured on the ground when it moves at 0.98 c.

workedSteps.text: The muon's own clock reads the proper time, which is its lifetime at rest.
The ground measures a longer time, longer by the factor $\gamma$. Work out $\gamma$ for $v = 0.98c$.
Multiply the proper time by $\gamma$ to get the ground's interval.
In that time the muon moves at 0.98 c as measured on the ground, so the distance is the speed times the time.
Without time dilation the muon would cover only the distance it manages in one lifetime at rest, about a fifth of that.

lead.text: At everyday speeds $\gamma$ is so close to 1 that a calculator shows it as exactly 1, and the interesting quantity is the small excess $\gamma - 1$. For $v$ much smaller than $c$, the first terms of the expansion of $\gamma$ are

so that $\gamma - 1 \approx \tfrac12 (v/c)^2$, and each later term is far smaller than the one before. At $v = 0.1c$ the first term gives 0.005, the 0.5% of the rule of thumb, and the second adds only 0.00004.

The expansion keeps what a ten-digit calculator loses. An astronaut on the International Space Station, orbiting at about 7,700 m/s, is reported to be about 5 milliseconds behind a person on Earth after six months on board, and the next example reproduces that figure from the expansion.

steps.headline: Find how far behind a clock on the International Space Station falls in six months, at 7,700 m/s.

workedSteps.text: Write the speed as a fraction of $c$.
Use the expansion to find the excess $\gamma - 1$.
Six months is half of a year of 365.25 days of 86,400 seconds.
The clock falls behind by the fraction $\gamma - 1$ of the time elapsed.
This counts the effect of speed alone. Being higher above Earth makes a clock run slightly faster, which partly offsets it, a second effect that a later lesson treats.

lead.text: The light clock is a device for deriving $\gamma$, and nothing in the result depends on light. A mechanical watch, an atomic clock and a heartbeat all repeat at steady rates, and any clock that keeps step with the light clock at rest should keep step with it when moving, so every kind of clock is slowed by the same factor. Measurements bear this out. In 1971 Hafele and Keating flew caesium atomic clocks round the world in airliners and compared them with a clock that stayed at the U.S. Naval Observatory, and their results agreed with the predictions of relativity. In 2010 optical atomic clocks joined by 75 metres of optical fibre showed time dilation at speeds below 10 metres per second.

Time dilation is a relation between clock readings, so it cannot be seen by looking at the moving clock. What you see includes the delay as light travels from the clock to your eye, together with a Doppler shift, and those can make a moving clock look fast. The slowing appears when readings from separate, synchronised clocks are compared. For a train passing at 0.86 c, where $\gamma = 1.96$, two experimenters along the track find about 2 seconds elapse on their clocks while the engineer's clock records 1 second.
The Station's 5 milliseconds raises an obvious doubt about what kind of clock is affected.

reveal.text: That is why the Global Positioning System corrects the clocks it carries in orbit for time dilation, so that, seen from Earth's surface, they keep the same rate as clocks on the ground.

lessons.orientation: Use the Lorentz factor to find how much a moving clock lags, and judge from real measurements when the effect is large enough to matter.
lessons.nextAction: Say which of two separated events comes first for observers in relative motion, find the size of the gap, and explain why each observer can say the other's clock runs slow.

blocks.text: A muon lasts only 2.197 microseconds at rest before it decays, and in that time even light would cover just 659 metres. Cosmic rays make muons high in the atmosphere, and measured from the ground the atmosphere is too thick for a muon to cross in that time, even at the speed of light, yet muons do reach the surface.

The explanation is that a moving clock runs slow. Muons moving at 98% of the speed of light are found to last about five times longer than muons at rest, and this stretching of time is called **time dilation**. How large it is follows from a short argument about a clock made of light, and the same argument shows when the effect can safely be ignored.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find how much a moving clock lags with the Lorentz factor, and say from real measurements whether the effect matters.
intro.whyItMatters: It tells you when a clock in motion needs a correction and when the correction is too small to bother with.

recap.keyIdea: A clock moving at speed v is measured to tick γ = 1 ÷ √(1 − v²/c²) times more slowly than at rest, and the effect reaches 0.5% only near one tenth of the speed of light.

blocks.text: A pulse of light bouncing between two mirrors ticks more slowly when the clock moves, because the pulse takes a longer, slanted path at the same speed, and the stretching factor is the Lorentz factor $\gamma$. The proper time between two events, read from a clock present at both, is the shortest interval any observer measures, so the muon's 2.197 microseconds becomes 11.04 microseconds on the ground at 0.98 c.

For small speeds $\gamma - 1$ is about $\tfrac12 (v/c)^2$, a few parts in $10^{10}$ on the Station and 0.5% at about 0.1 c. The slowing applies to every kind of clock, and it is found by comparing readings, not by watching the moving clock.

recap.nextHook: Time dilation depends on observers disagreeing about when things happen, and the next lesson shows how that disagreement arises for events in different places.

lessons.title: Relativity of simultaneity

lead.text: To say when something happens at a distant place, an observer needs a clock there that agrees with their own, and agreeing is a procedure that has to be carried out. Einstein proposed one that uses light. Clock 1 sends a signal at time $\tau_1$, clock 2 reflects it at once, and the signal arrives back at clock 1 at time $\tau_2$. Clock 2 is then set so that it read the midpoint time when the signal reached it:

The rule treats the outward and return journeys as equal, so it assumes that light has the same speed in both directions, and no measurement made at one place can test that. Synchronisation is therefore a convention, adopted because it fits how the world behaves. An observer who sets all their clocks this way, with every clock at rest relative to the others and to the observer, works in what is called a **frame of reference**.

The times that a frame assigns to distant events already allow for the travel of light. When a passenger works out when a bolt struck, the delay between the strike and the flash reaching the eye has been taken out, so a difference that remains between two observers cannot be blamed on that delay.
Clock 2 is set to the halfway time of the round trip, and the rule rests on an assumption.

reveal.text: This is why two observers who each use the rule on their own clocks can end up with different times, as the next screens show.

lead.text: Einstein's train sets the problem. An observer stands on a platform while a train passes at a steady speed $v$, with a passenger sitting at the middle of one carriage. At the instant the two are level, lightning strikes the two ends of the carriage. The platform observer is level with the middle, so the two flashes arrive together after covering equal distances at the same speed, and the observer assigns the two strikes the same time.

The passenger is moving toward the flash from the front and away from the flash from the back, so the front flash arrives first. The passenger also knows that the two ends are equal distances away, since the carriage is at rest for the passenger, and that light has the same speed in both directions. Allowing for the travel time, which is the same for both flashes, the passenger concludes that the front bolt struck before the back bolt.

This is one case of a general rule. If two events are simultaneous in one frame and lie along the direction in which a second frame moves, *the event ahead of the motion happens earlier* in the second frame. Both observers have allowed for the travel of light, and they still assign different times.
The rule about events ahead of the motion depends on which way the train goes.

reveal.text: Neither passenger is making a mistake, since each has assigned times with their own synchronised clocks.

lead.text: The same result follows from a flash given off at the middle of the carriage as the passenger and the platform observer pass each other. For the passenger, the front and back of the carriage stay at equal distances from the flash, and light has the same speed in every direction, so the light reaches the two ends together, as the first view shows.

For the platform observer the carriage is moving. Its rear is moving up to meet the light that went backward, and its front is moving away from the light that went forward, and light has speed $c$ in both directions for this observer too, so the rear is struck first, as the later views show.

afterFigure.text: Both accounts are correct. Each observer assigns times with their own synchronised clocks, and the two frames disagree about which separated events count as simultaneous. That disagreement is called the **relativity of simultaneity**: whether two events at different places happen at the same time depends on the frame, and no frame has a better claim than another. It is the idea from which time dilation and length contraction both follow.

lead.text: The rule concerns events spread along the direction of motion.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the formula, which shows why this case differs.

lead.text: The Lorentz transformation gives the time that an observer moving at velocity $v$ along $x$ assigns to an event that the first observer places at time $t$ and position $x$, with $\gamma$ the [[Lorentz factor|The factor 1 ÷ √(1 − v²/c²) that stretches a moving clock's ticks. Met in 'Time dilation'.]] from the first lesson:
Two events that are simultaneous for the first observer have the same $t$ and different positions, so the moving observer assigns them times that differ by

afterFigure.text: where $\Delta x$ is the distance between the events along the direction of motion, positive when the event we are comparing lies ahead. The term $vx/c^2$ is the one that breaks absolute simultaneity. It vanishes when $\Delta x = 0$, which is the case of the two flashes across the track, and its minus sign gives the earlier time to the event with the larger $x$, which is the one ahead of the motion, matching the rule from the train.
The gap grows with the separation $\Delta x$ and with the speed, and it is tiny for ordinary trains: at 30 m/s, with the strikes 1 km apart, it is under $10^{-12}$ seconds.

steps.headline: Strikes 150 m apart along the track are simultaneous on the platform. For a train at 0.6 c, find the gap between them and which comes first.

workedSteps.text: The platform gives both strikes the same $t$, so only the second term contributes, and $\Delta x = 150$ m.
Find $\gamma$ for $v = 0.6c$.
Write $v = 0.6c$, so that one factor of $c$ cancels, and substitute.
The size of the gap is 375 nanoseconds. The negative sign gives the earlier time to the strike with the larger $x$, so the front strike comes first in the train's frame.

steps.headline: Strikes 200 m apart along the track are simultaneous on the platform. For a train at 0.5 c, find the gap between them and which comes first.

workedSteps.text: The strikes are simultaneous on the platform, so again $\Delta t' = -\gamma v\,\Delta x/c^2$, here with $\Delta x = 200$ m.
Find $\gamma$ for $v = 0.5c$.
Substitute the values to find the size of the gap.
The sign of $\Delta t'$ decides the order.

steps.headline: Each observer sees the other's clock slow

lead.text: Two observers who move relative to each other at a steady speed each measure the other's clock to run slow. This looks contradictory, since each says the other's clock lags, but a familiar case has the same form: two people far apart each look small to the other, and nobody concludes that one of them is really smaller. Relative motion is symmetric in the same way, and the symmetry is called **reciprocity**.

The two statements do not collide because each observer compares the other's single clock with two of their own, at different places, and the two observers disagree about whether those two clocks were set to the same time. The relativity of simultaneity means that the comparison one observer makes is not the comparison the other would make.

The twin puzzle adds a journey with a turn. One twin leaves Earth and returns, and is younger on arrival, although each twin measured the other's clock to be slow while the motion was steady. The situation is not symmetric: the twin who stays at home is in one frame throughout, while the traveller is in one frame going out and in another coming back, and the change of frame at the turn breaks the symmetry.
Steady motion is symmetric, so each crew's measurement has to be as good as the other's.

reveal.text: Disagreeing about simultaneity is what lets two correct measurements disagree about the clocks.

lead.text: The twin case turns up in any setting where one of two observers changes direction.

reveal.text: The proper time of a path depends on the route taken between the two meetings, and a route with a turn in it records the shorter time.

lessons.orientation: Say which of two separated events comes first for observers in relative motion, find the size of the gap, and explain why each observer can say the other's clock runs slow.
lessons.nextAction: Find the length of a moving object along its line of motion, and change frames to explain one event in two ways that agree.

blocks.text: Suppose two lightning bolts strike the two ends of a railway carriage at exactly the same moment, as judged by an observer on the platform who is level with the middle of the carriage. A passenger sitting at the middle of the carriage, travelling at a steady speed, passes that observer at the instant the bolts strike. Everyday experience says the passenger must agree that the bolts struck together, since the time of an event seems to be a fact about the event itself, the same for everyone.

Special relativity says otherwise. For events at different places, whether they happen at the same time depends on the motion of the observer who is judging, and the passenger finds that one bolt struck before the other. The size of that disagreement can be calculated, and the same idea explains how two observers can each find the other's clock running slow without either of them being mistaken.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which of two events comes first for observers in relative motion, find the gap between them, and explain how each observer can say the other's clock runs slow.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows why time dilation and the twin puzzle do not contradict themselves.

recap.keyIdea: Events that are simultaneous in one frame and separated along the line of motion get different times in a frame moving along that line, by γvΔx/c², with the event ahead of the motion earlier.

blocks.text: A clock at a distance is set by a rule that assumes light travels equally fast both ways, so each frame has its own idea of which separated events are simultaneous. For strikes 150 m apart and a train at 0.6 c, the train's frame finds a gap of 375 nanoseconds with the front strike first, and across the track there is no gap at all.

Each of two observers in steady relative motion can measure the other's clock to be slow, because each compares one clock with two of their own that the other would call out of step. The twin who turns round changes frames, and that is what leaves the traveller younger.

recap.nextHook: With simultaneity now relative, the length of a moving object, which depends on marking both ends at the same time, turns out to depend on the observer as well.

lessons.title: Length contraction

lead.text: A rod at rest is measured by laying a ruler along it, and the result is the rod's **proper length**, its length in its own rest frame. A rod that is moving cannot be measured that way, since its ends keep moving while the ruler is laid against it. One method is to set a row of synchronised clocks along the track, let the rod pass, and have each clock record the time at which an end goes by. The observer then finds the clock that recorded the front end at some time and the clock that recorded the back end at the *same* time, and the distance between those two clocks is the length of the moving rod.

Everything in that method depends on the word *same*. The observers who move with the rod say that the two ends were not marked at the same time, since simultaneity depends on the frame, so they arrive at a different length. The [[relativity of simultaneity|Two events at different places that are simultaneous in one frame are generally not simultaneous in another. Met in 'Relativity of simultaneity'.]] is what allows the length of a moving rod to differ from its proper length.
A station marks the two ends of a passing ship at the same moment by the station's clocks, and reads the distance between the marks.

reveal.text: The next screen finds the size of the difference with a clock that travels along the ship.

lead.text: A single clock that travels along the rod gives a second way to measure it. Let the rod have proper length $L_0$, and let the clock move along it at speed $v$ from one end to the other. In the rod's frame the trip takes $T = L_0/v$. The clock is moving, so it records the [[proper time|The time between two events shown by a clock present at both. Met in 'Time dilation'.]] $T_0 = T/\gamma$ between passing the two ends. In the clock's own frame the rod rushes past at speed $v$ for that time, so the length measured there is

A moving object is therefore found to be shorter than its proper length by the factor $1/\gamma$, an effect called **length contraction**, and the proper length is the greatest length that any observer measures. The shortening acts only along the direction of motion, and widths across the motion are unchanged.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows what a station measures for a ship 100 m long at rest. At 0.0447 c, about 13,400 km/s, the length is still 99.9% of the proper length, and at 0.141 c it is 99%, so at everyday speeds, and at speeds far beyond them, the contraction is too small to measure. It becomes large only as $v$ approaches $c$: the ship measures 60 m at 0.8 c and about 20 m at 0.98 c.

steps.headline: A ship is 100 m long at rest. Find the length a station measures as the ship passes at 0.8 c.

workedSteps.text: The ship's proper length is its length in its own rest frame.
Work out $\gamma$ for $v = 0.8c$.
The station measures a shorter length, the proper length divided by $\gamma$.
The ship's own crew measure the ship to be 100 m, and the station's 60 m is a measurement of the same ship made by observers for whom it moves.

reveal.text: The width across the motion keeps its rest value, which is why the square becomes a rectangle and not a smaller square.

lead.text: The principle of relativity says that the laws of nature are the same in every frame moving at a steady speed, and it requires length contraction to be symmetric. A rod at rest in a frame S has its proper length in S and is contracted in a frame S′ that moves past it, and a rod at rest in S′ has its proper length there and is contracted in S. Each observer finds the other's rods shorter, just as each finds the other's clocks slower.

Nobody sees any change in the rods that move with them, so contraction is measured only by an observer for whom the rod moves. That also explains why the effect is hard to test directly: the only objects moving fast enough are atomic particles, which are too small for their lengths to be measured, and objects large enough to measure cannot be accelerated to such speeds.

reveal.text: Each observer finds the other's rods shorter by the same factor, just as each finds the other's clocks slow.

lead.text: Return to the muon, with a layer of air that measures 3.0 km thick in the ground frame. The thickness is a made-up round figure, chosen to be a little less than the muon's range. In the ground frame the muon's lifetime is dilated to 11.04 microseconds, and at 0.98 c it covers 3.24 km in that time, which is enough to cross the layer.

In the muon's frame there is no dilation, and its clock reads the ordinary 2.197 microseconds. The layer rushes past at 0.98 c and is contracted to $3.0\ \text{km}/5.025 = 0.597$ km. Crossing that distance at 0.98 c takes $0.597\ \text{km}/(0.98c) = 2.03$ microseconds, which is less than 2.197 microseconds, so in this frame the muon also arrives.

afterFigure.text: The two frames give different reasons and the same result. The ground says that time is stretched, the muon says that the distance is shortened, and both agree on every event that either can check, here the muon's arrival before it decays. Using both effects in one frame would count the same physics twice.

diagram.alt: The same muon trip drawn in two frames at one scale. In the ground frame the layer of air is 3.0 kilometres thick and the muon's dilated lifetime gives a range of 3.24 kilometres. In the muon's frame the layer is contracted to 0.597 kilometres and the ground passes 0.645 kilometres in one ordinary lifetime. In both frames the range exceeds the layer.
diagram.caption: Both views use the same scale, with 3.0 km for the layer in the ground frame (a made-up thickness). The two accounts give different reasons and the same result: the muon arrives.

lead.text: Take the muon's frame for a thicker layer and a faster muon.

reveal.text: In the ground frame the same muon lives 15.57 microseconds and covers 4.62 km, which is also more than the 4.0 km layer, so both frames agree that it arrives.

lead.text: Length contraction refers to the positions of the ends of an object at one moment in a given frame. A photograph is a different kind of measurement: it is taken from a distance, and the light that reaches the camera together left different parts of the object at different times. Roger Penrose and James Terrell showed in 1959 that moving objects generally do not look contracted in a photograph, and that a moving sphere of small angular size stays circular and looks rotated.

Contraction is not seen directly, but it accounts for measurable effects. In the frame of the moving electrons in a current-carrying wire, the wire's positive charges are packed more closely, and the resulting imbalance explains the magnetic attraction between parallel wires with currents in the same direction. Results from collisions of heavy ions can be explained only when the contraction of the colliding nuclei is taken into account.

reveal.text: The same care is needed with the ladder paradox, which arises from applying the contraction formula carelessly and is resolved by the relativity of simultaneity.

lessons.orientation: Find the length of a moving object along its line of motion, and change frames to explain one event in two ways that agree.
lessons.nextAction: Convert between a released energy and the mass a system loses, and judge whether a given mass change is large, small, or hidden in a closed system.

blocks.text: In its own frame a muon lasts 2.197 microseconds, and the ground approaches it at 98% of the speed of light, so only a short stretch of ground and air goes past in one lifetime. Measured from the ground, the atmosphere is thicker than that stretch, yet muons reach the surface. The ground's account is that the muon's clock runs slow, which stretches its lifetime, and the muon's account has to reach the same outcome without any such stretching.

For both accounts to agree, the distance to be crossed must be different in the two frames: a length measured along the direction of motion is shorter than the same length at rest. How much shorter follows from what has already been found about moving clocks and about simultaneity.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the length of a moving object along its motion, and explain one event in two frames so that both accounts agree.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you check an account from one frame against an account from another, which is how many relativity puzzles are settled.

recap.keyIdea: An object moving along its length is measured to be shorter by the factor 1/γ, so L = L₀ ÷ γ, while widths across the motion are unchanged, and every frame finds the other's rods shorter.

blocks.text: A moving length is found by marking both ends at the same time in the observer's frame, so it depends on the relativity of simultaneity. A clock travelling along a rod gives $L = L_0/\gamma$, with the proper length the greatest any observer measures, and a 100 m ship measures 60 m at 0.8 c.

The muon's arrival is explained in the ground frame by time dilation and in the muon's frame by a contracted layer of air, and the two accounts agree. A photograph is a different measurement from a length, and a passing sphere looks rotated and not flattened.

recap.nextHook: Time and length are not the only quantities that depend on the observer, and the next lesson shows that energy has a mass, so that a change of energy changes mass.

lessons.title: Mass and energy

lead.text: A body at rest has energy simply because it has mass. The relation is $E = mc^2$, where $m$ is the body's mass and $E$ is its **rest energy**, the energy it has in a frame in which it is at rest. The mass is the rest mass, which is the same for every observer, and since $c$ is large and enters squared, a small mass corresponds to a very large energy.

One kilogram therefore corresponds to about $9.0\times10^{16}$ J, which is 25 billion kilowatt-hours, or the energy released by 21.5 megatons of TNT. The relation also works in the other direction: when energy is added to a system its mass rises by that energy divided by $c^2$, and when energy is removed its mass falls by the same amount.

afterFigure.text: Each row of the figure is a thousand times smaller than the one above it. A gram still corresponds to 21.5 kilotons of TNT, and 1.5 picograms, which is the change in mass when a 1 kg metal standard is warmed by one degree Celsius, corresponds to only 135 J.

One gram corresponds to 9.0 times 10 to the 13 joules or 21.5 kilotons. One milligram corresponds to 21.5 tons of TNT, and 1.5 picograms to 135 joules.

steps.headline: Find the energy that corresponds to a mass of 1 g, and compare it with a familiar scale.

workedSteps.text: The relation $E = mc^2$ gives joules when the mass is in kilograms.
Square the speed of light.
Multiply the mass by $c^2$.
One kilogram corresponds to 21.5 megatons of TNT, so one gram corresponds to a thousandth of that.

lead.text: The same relation gives the mass lost when a known energy is released:

The plutonium bombs used at Trinity and Nagasaki had a yield equivalent to 21 kilotons of TNT, about $9\times10^{13}$ J. Dividing by $c^2$ gives $9\times10^{13}/(9.0\times10^{16}) = 10^{-3}$ kg, one gram. About 1 kg of the roughly 6.15 kg of plutonium in each bomb fissioned. Once the lighter elements it produced had cooled they weighed almost exactly one gram less than that kilogram, and the radiation and the kinetic energy of the explosion had carried the gram away.
One gram out of the kilogram that fissioned is 0.1%, which is the order of the loss when uranium fissions, where the products weigh about 0.1% less than the original atom.
A stick of dynamite explodes inside a hermetically sealed, insulated steel chamber that stands on a balance.

reveal.text: Mass is lost only when the released energy leaves the system, which the next screen follows through.

lead.text: The balance follows the mass of everything inside the chamber, and the energy released stays inside, so the mass cannot change. A system that exchanges no energy with its surroundings is a **closed system**, and its mass stays the same however violent the process inside it. A system from which energy can escape is an **open system**, and its mass falls by the escaping energy divided by $c^2$.

Suppose that a window which passes only light and X-rays is opened in the chamber after the explosion, and the radiation escapes. When the chamber has cooled to room temperature it weighs less than before by the energy that left divided by $c^2$: for a charge that releases the energy of 21.5 kilotons of TNT, that is one gram. Whatever absorbs the radiation gains that gram, so the mass has moved from the chamber to its surroundings and has not been destroyed.

diagram.alt: A balance carrying a chamber in which a charge has exploded. In the first view the chamber is sealed, so the heat, sound and light stay inside and the balance reading is unchanged. In the second view a window lets radiation escape, and the reading falls by the escaped energy divided by c squared.

lead.text: Because any energy has mass, every change of energy changes mass, and not only nuclear ones. A water molecule is slightly lighter than the two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom it is made from, by the heat given off when it formed divided by $c^2$. Adding energy raises mass: a spring is heavier when it is compressed or stretched, a metal block is heavier when it is warmed, and a ball is heavier when it spins. The former primary mass standard for the kilogram, a cylinder of platinum and iridium, gains 1.5 picograms for each degree Celsius that its temperature rises, and the Earth is more massive than it would be without its rotation, by over $10^{7}$ kg.
In each case the change is the energy divided by $c^2$, which is minute for chemical and thermal changes, and whether a balance could see it depends on whether the energy stays in the system.
The sign of the change depends on whether energy enters the system or leaves it.

reveal.text: In the water and the fission cases the system has released energy, so it is the lighter one afterwards.

lead.text: Rest energy is the first term of a longer expression. For a body moving at speed $v$ the energy is $E = \gamma mc^2$, and the expansion of the [[Lorentz factor|The factor 1 ÷ √(1 − v²/c²) that stretches a moving clock's ticks. Met in 'Time dilation'.]] $\gamma$ from the first lesson gives

For speeds much less than $c$ every term after the second can be dropped, leaving $E \approx mc^2 + \tfrac12 mv^2$. The first term is the rest energy, which classical mechanics leaves out because only changes of energy can be measured, and the second is the kinetic energy of classical mechanics, so Newton's expression is the low-speed limit of the relativistic one.

How good is the limit? The next term multiplies the kinetic energy by $1 + 3v^2/4c^2$, so the relative error of the classical expression is $3v^2/4c^2$. For a probe moving at 30 km/s, a made-up speed, that is $0.75 \times (3.0\times10^{4}/c)^2 = 7.5\times10^{-9}$, which is a few parts in a thousand million.
A real probe gives a case where the relativistic correction can be set against other uncertainties.

reveal.text: The same reasoning shows why the Newtonian expression is good enough for a spacecraft, while particles moving near the speed of light need the relativistic one.

lead.text: Nuclear changes follow the same relation as chemical ones and differ only in size. When uranium fissions, the products weigh about 0.1% less than the original atom, and soon after the discovery of radioactivity in 1897 it was noticed that the energy involved is about a million times greater than in any known molecular change. A chemical change therefore alters mass by roughly a part in a billion, which is far too little for a balance to show, while a nuclear change can alter it by a thousandth.

The equation converts a mass difference into the energy released. It does not explain where the energy comes from. The energy of fission was measured directly, at about 200 MeV per fission, and the physicist Robert Serber noted that the theory of fission is non-relativistic, because relativistic effects are too small to change its dynamics. The equation itself was tested in 1933 with the reaction of lithium-7 and a proton, which gives two alpha particles, and it held to within 0.5%.
A battery stores energy in chemical form, and storing energy adds mass.

reveal.text: Chemical energy changes are far below what a balance can resolve, and the nuclear changes of the previous screen, about a thousandth of the mass, are not.

lessons.orientation: Convert between a released energy and the mass a system loses, and judge whether a given mass change is large, small, or hidden in a closed system.
lessons.nextAction: Predict what happens to the emitted electrons when the frequency or the intensity of the light changes, and find their maximum kinetic energy from the work function.

blocks.text: The relation $E = mc^2$ is often read as saying that matter vanishes into energy. It says that energy itself has mass: whenever the energy of a system changes, the mass of the system changes by that energy divided by $c^2$, and the equation applies in the same way to a flame, a compressed spring and a fission reaction.

Two questions decide how the equation applies to a real case. One is how large the change in mass is, which is nearly always tiny. The other is whether the energy has left the system, since a balance registers a change in mass only when it has.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert between a released energy and the mass a system loses, and judge whether a mass change is large, small or hidden in a closed system.
intro.whyItMatters: It tells you when a mass change from an energy change could ever be seen, and when it can be ignored.

recap.keyIdea: A body at rest has energy E = mc², so a system's mass changes by ΔE ÷ c² whenever energy enters or leaves it, and a balance shows the change only if the energy crosses the system's boundary.

blocks.text: One kilogram corresponds to about $9.0\times10^{16}$ J and one gram to $9.0\times10^{13}$ J, which is 21.5 kilotons of TNT. A bomb with that yield lost about a gram, carried off by the radiation and the kinetic energy of the explosion, and any energy change gives $\Delta m = \Delta E/c^2$, up when energy is added and down when it leaves.

In a sealed chamber the mass stays the same, and an open system loses the mass of the energy that escapes. For ordinary speeds $\tfrac12 mv^2$ is the low-speed limit of $\gamma mc^2$, and the relativistic correction to it for a fast probe is smaller than the uncertainty in $G$.

recap.nextHook: Light carries energy too, and the next lesson shows that the way light delivers it to a metal surface cannot be explained if light is only a wave.

lessons.title: The photoelectric effect

lead.text: In the standard arrangement, light falls on a clean metal plate, the emitter, inside an evacuated tube, and the electrons it frees travel to a second electrode, the collector, whose voltage can be set. The tube is evacuated so that gas does not scatter the electrons, and the metal is clean because an oxide layer on its surface raises the energy barrier to leaving. The freed electrons are called **photoelectrons**.

afterFigure.text: Making the collector more and more negative turns back all but the fastest photoelectrons, and the voltage at which the current just drops to zero is the **stopping potential** $V_0$. At that voltage even the most energetic electrons are stopped, and the work done against them by the retarding voltage equals their kinetic energy, so

where $e$ is the electron's charge and $K_{\max}$ is the greatest kinetic energy. Measuring the stopping potential therefore measures the fastest electrons directly: a stopping potential of 1.5 V means a greatest kinetic energy of 1.5 [[electron-volts|The energy an electron gains crossing one volt, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Met in 'Fields and voltage'.]].

With no retarding voltage the electrons cross to the collector and a current flows. At the stopping potential the collector is negative enough that even the fastest electrons turn back and the current is zero.

lead.text: The [[wave picture|Light as an electromagnetic wave, with energy carried continuously. Met in 'Light as an electromagnetic wave'.]] of light, in which energy arrives continuously, makes definite predictions about this experiment. A brighter beam delivers more energy to each electron every second, so the electrons should leave faster. A very dim beam should free electrons only after the energy has had time to accumulate. And light of any frequency should do so, given a bright enough beam or a long enough exposure.

afterFigure.text: The results differ in all three respects. For each metal there is a **threshold frequency**, and below it no electrons are emitted whatever the intensity or the length of the exposure. Above it, a higher frequency gives a higher greatest kinetic energy, and so a higher stopping potential. Raising the intensity of light of a given frequency increases the number of electrons leaving each second, which is the photoelectric current, and leaves their kinetic energy and the stopping potential unchanged. And the delay between the light arriving and an electron leaving is under a nanosecond.

One view lists what the wave picture predicts: faster electrons, a delay while energy builds up, and emission after a long enough exposure. The other lists what is observed: more electrons with the same energy, no delay, and no electrons below a threshold however bright or long.

lead.text: In 1905 Einstein proposed that light comes in small packets of energy, now called **photons**, each carrying an energy proportional to the frequency of the light:

where $h$ is the **Planck constant**, $4.136\times10^{-15}$ eV s. Planck had suggested around 1900, in work on black-body radiation, that electromagnetic energy is released only in packets, and Einstein applied the idea to light itself. An electron takes the whole energy of one photon or none of it. Part of that energy frees the electron from the metal and the rest becomes its kinetic energy. The least energy that can free an electron is a property of the surface called the **work function** $W$, a few electron-volts for typical metals, and the most energetic photoelectrons are those that lose nothing on the way out:

No electron is freed when $hf < W$, which gives the threshold frequency $f_0 = W/h$, and above it $K_{\max} = h(f - f_0)$. Each of the three observations now follows. Intensity sets the number of photons arriving each second, and so the number of electrons, but not the energy of any one photon. A photon gives its energy in one step, so no delay can build up. And below the threshold every photon falls short, so extra brightness or a longer exposure changes nothing.

reveal.text: The red lamp delivers more energy each second than the dim ultraviolet one, and still frees no electrons, which is the observation that the wave picture could not give.

steps.headline: A made-up metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. Find its threshold wavelength and what 400 nm and 700 nm light do to it.

workedSteps.text: A photon's energy is $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, and $hc = 1239.84$ eV nm, so the energy in electron-volts is 1239.84 divided by the wavelength in nanometres.
The threshold is where the photon energy just equals the work function.
At 400 nm each photon carries more than the work function, so electrons are freed.
The greatest kinetic energy is the photon energy less the work function, and the stopping potential in volts has the same number.
At 700 nm each photon carries less than the work function, so no electrons are freed at any intensity.

lead.text: The first view plots the greatest kinetic energy against frequency for the 2.3 eV metal. There are no electrons below the threshold frequency, $5.56\times10^{14}$ Hz, and above it the points fall on a straight line of slope $h$. A metal with a different work function gives a parallel line that starts at a different threshold. The 400 nm light, at $7.49\times10^{14}$ Hz, gives 0.80 eV, and the 700 nm light, at $4.28\times10^{14}$ Hz, lies below the threshold.

afterFigure.text: The second view shows what intensity changes. Doubling the intensity of light of one frequency doubles the number of photons arriving each second, so it doubles the number of electrons and the current, as Lenard found in 1902 for the number of electrons emitted. Each electron still has the same greatest energy, so the current stops at the same stopping voltage in both curves. This holds when the intensity is not too high.

The second plots current against collector voltage at two intensities: doubling the intensity doubles the current and leaves the stopping voltage unchanged.

steps.headline: A made-up metal has a work function of 2.0 eV. Find the greatest kinetic energy of electrons freed by 500 nm light.

workedSteps.text: A photon's energy in electron-volts is 1239.84 divided by the wavelength in nanometres.
Work out the energy of one 500 nm photon.
This is above the work function of 2.0 eV, so electrons are freed, and the surplus becomes kinetic energy.
Subtract the work function from the photon energy.

steps.headline: A line with slope h over e

lead.text: Because $V_0 = (h/e)(f - f_0)$, a graph of the stopping potential against frequency is a straight line whose slope is $h/e$ for every metal, with a different threshold for each. Before Einstein's paper it was already known that higher frequencies gave faster electrons and that brightness made no difference to their speed, but how the speed rose had not been measured, and his equation predicted a straight line.

Robert Millikan showed in 1914 that the prediction was correct, and his accurate measurements of the Planck constant supported Einstein's model, although Millikan himself found a particle theory of light unthinkable at the time. The idea had been strongly resisted, since it contradicted the wave theory that follows from Maxwell's equations. The word photon is later still: Gilbert Lewis introduced it in a letter to the journal *Nature* in 1926.

A photomultiplier is a vacuum tube whose photocathode is made of materials such as caesium, rubidium and antimony, chosen for a low work function so that even very low levels of light release electrons. A series of electrodes at rising voltages then multiplies the electrons into a current that is easy to detect, and photomultipliers are still used wherever very little light must be measured.

The effect also charges spacecraft: parts of a spacecraft in sunlight lose electrons and become positive, while parts in shadow can charge negatively from nearby plasma, and the imbalance can discharge through delicate electronics. The charge is self-limiting, because a more positive surface gives up electrons less easily. And in photoelectron spectroscopy, light of a known energy is shone on a sample and the electrons' kinetic energies are measured, so that the binding energy of each electron follows from the photon energy minus the kinetic energy.
The condition for emission decides which materials a detector can be built from.

reveal.text: A low work function is what lets a photomultiplier respond to the weakest light, since each photon only has to carry more than that small energy.

lessons.orientation: Predict what happens to the emitted electrons when the frequency or the intensity of the light changes, and find their maximum kinetic energy from the work function.
lessons.nextAction: Convert between wavelength, frequency and photon energy in electron-volts, and compare beams by photons per second as well as by power.

blocks.text: Shine ultraviolet light on a clean metal plate in a vacuum, and electrons leave the plate. Shine light of lower frequency, even from a very bright lamp, and for a typical metal none do, however long the plate is left in the beam. Suppose light is a wave that carries energy continuously, as the wave theory says. Then a brighter beam should deliver more energy to each electron every second, a dim beam should free electrons only after the energy has had time to build up, and light of any colour should work if you wait long enough.

None of that is what happens. Electrons leave only when the frequency of the light is above a certain value, whatever the intensity and however long the exposure, and understanding why took a new idea about light, which Einstein proposed in 1905.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict what happens to the freed electrons when the frequency or the intensity of the light changes, and find their greatest kinetic energy from the work function.
intro.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case where treating light as a wave gives the wrong answer, and it shows how a single photon's energy is used.

recap.keyIdea: Light is absorbed in packets of energy hf, so the greatest kinetic energy of the freed electrons is K_max = hf − W, nothing is emitted below the threshold frequency, and intensity changes the number of electrons only.

blocks.text: The wave picture predicted faster electrons from brighter light, a delay for dim light and emission at any frequency, and the experiments showed a threshold frequency, no change in electron energy with intensity, and no delay. Einstein's photons explain all three: an electron takes the energy $hf$ of one photon or none, and pays the work function $W$ to leave.
A metal with $W = 2.3$ eV gives 0.80 eV at 400 nm and nothing at 700 nm, and a plot of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line of slope $h/e$.

recap.nextHook: A photon's energy depends on its colour, and the next lesson turns wavelengths into electron-volts and compares two beams by the number of photons they send each second.

lessons.title: Photon energy and photon counts

reveal.text: The red lamp sends more. Its photons carry less energy, so it takes more of them each second to deliver the same 2.0 mW. The next screens give the photon energies and counts.

lead.text: A photon of frequency $f$ carries the energy $E = hf$, where $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s is the Planck constant. Green light of wavelength 550 nm has a frequency of $5.45 \times 10^{14}$ Hz, so each of its photons carries $3.61 \times 10^{-19}$ J. The number is correct but inconvenient, because the joule is far too large a unit for a single photon.

Atomic physics uses the [[electron-volt|The energy one electron gains in crossing a voltage of one volt, 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Met in “Fields and voltage”.]] instead, and in that unit the green photon carries $3.61 \times 10^{-19} / 1.602 \times 10^{-19} = 2.25$ eV. Despite the volt in its name, the electron-volt is a unit of *energy*, and a few electron-volts is the size of a step between an atom's energy levels.

A spectrometer reports the wavelength of light and not its frequency, and the relation $c = f\lambda$ lets one stand in for the other, so $E = hf$ becomes $E = hc/\lambda$. The product $hc$ is a single fixed number, and with energies in electron-volts and wavelengths in nanometres it equals 1239.84 eV nm. A photon's energy in electron-volts is therefore 1239.84 divided by its wavelength in nanometres.

At 550 nm this gives $1239.84 / 550 = 2.25$ eV, which agrees with the value found from the frequency. Because the wavelength is in the denominator, **a longer wavelength means a smaller photon energy**, and halving the wavelength doubles the energy.

afterFigure.text: Visible light runs from about 400 nm to about 700 nm, which is 3.10 eV down to 1.77 eV. A photon at 800 nm, in the infrared, carries only 1.55 eV, and a photon of any longer wavelength carries less still.

lead.text: These energies explain which light can free electrons from a metal. A typical metal needs a few electron-volts for each electron, and that corresponds to short-wavelength visible light or ultraviolet, so a photon with less energy than the metal's [[work function|The least energy needed to remove an electron from the metal's surface. Met in “The photoelectric effect”.]] frees nothing, however many such photons arrive.

A wavelength can therefore be read as a verdict. For a metal with a work function of 4.0 eV (a made-up value), a photon has just enough energy at $1239.84 / 4.0 = 310$ nm, so shorter wavelengths can eject electrons from it and longer ones cannot.

Power is the energy delivered each second, and a beam delivers it in photons, so a beam's power is the number of photons arriving each second multiplied by the energy of one photon, $P = NE$. The number arriving each second is called the **photon rate**, and it is $N = P/E$.

The energy has to be in joules, because a watt is a joule each second, so a photon energy found in electron-volts is first multiplied by $1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ J per electron-volt. The table gives the results for a beam of 1.0 mW at three wavelengths.

afterFigure.text: Each step to a longer wavelength lowers the energy of one photon and raises the number a beam of the same power needs. The photon rate is proportional to the wavelength, so a beam at 800 nm sends twice as many photons each second as a beam of equal power at 400 nm.

steps.headline: A beam of 1.0 mW has a wavelength of 550 nm. Find the number of photons it sends each second.

workedSteps.text: The power is the photon rate times the energy of one photon, so the rate is the power divided by that energy.
Find the energy of one photon in electron-volts from the wavelength.
Convert it to joules, since a watt is a joule each second.
Divide the power by the energy of one photon.

steps.headline: A beam of 1.0 mW has a wavelength of 1000 nm. Find the number of photons it sends each second.

workedSteps.text: The energy of one photon is the constant divided by the wavelength.
Before calculating, decide which way the answer should differ from the 550 nm beam.
In joules the photon energy is the following.
Divide the power by the energy of one photon.

lead.text: A beam that sends $10^{15}$ photons each second looks like a steady glow, although every photon arrives as a separate event. In a photomultiplier, light falling on a coated surface releases electrons, and a series of electrodes multiplies them into a current that can be detected. Such tubes are still used wherever very low levels of light must be measured, and at those levels the photons arrive one at a time.

A photon also carries momentum. Arthur Compton's experiments from 1922 to 1924 demonstrated it, and it is why sunlight can push a solar sail and why light can slow atoms down to cool them. The photon picture sits beside the wave picture of light, and each is needed to describe some experiment. The lesson on waves and particles shows how particles that arrive one at a time can still build up a wave pattern.
Counting also works in reverse. A measured power and a measured photon rate fix the energy of one photon, and that fixes the wavelength.

reveal.text: The beam is infrared. Its photons carry about 1.25 eV each, almost the same as those at 1000 nm.

lessons.orientation: Convert between wavelength, frequency and photon energy in electron-volts, and compare beams by photons per second as well as by power.
lessons.nextAction: Read hydrogen's spectral lines as jumps between energy levels and calculate their wavelengths.

blocks.text: A photon of green light, at a wavelength of 550 nm, carries an energy of about $3.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J. That is so small that physicists quote photon energies in electron-volts instead, and in those units the same photon carries 2.25 eV, close to the few electron-volts needed to free an electron from a metal.

A beam of light is a stream of such photons, so a second way of comparing two beams is to ask how many photons each one sends every second. Two lamps of equal power do not necessarily send equal numbers of photons, and which of them sends more depends on the energy each photon carries.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find a photon's energy in electron-volts from its wavelength and work out how many photons a beam of known power sends each second.
intro.whyItMatters: The energy of a photon decides what light can do to an atom, and the number of photons decides how often it does it.

recap.keyIdea: A photon's energy is $E = hc/\lambda$, which is 1239.84 eV nm divided by the wavelength, and a beam's power is its photon rate times that energy, so at equal power the longer wavelength sends more photons.

blocks.text: The energy of one photon falls as the wavelength rises, from 3.10 eV at 400 nm to 1.24 eV at 1000 nm, and an electron can be freed from a metal only if one photon carries more than the work function. Dividing a beam's power by the energy of one photon, in joules, gives the number of photons arriving each second.
A brighter beam of the same colour sends more photons of the same energy, while a beam of a longer wavelength needs more photons than a shorter one to carry the same power.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson applies these energies to hydrogen, whose light arrives at a few sharp wavelengths, each of them the energy of one photon.

lessons.title: Hydrogen's spectral lines

reveal.text: The lamp shows sharp lines instead of a smooth band, so a hydrogen atom can lose only certain amounts of energy. Each line is a photon of one definite energy, and the Rydberg formula gives their wavelengths.

lead.text: Balmer's formula for the visible lines was generalised by Rydberg into a rule that covers every line that hydrogen gives out. Written for wavelength, the Rydberg formula is $1/\lambda = R\left(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2\right)$, where $n_f$ and $n_i$ are whole numbers with $n_i$ the larger, and the Rydberg constant $R$ is about $1.0974 \times 10^7$ per metre.

Take an electron that falls from $n_i = 3$ to $n_f = 2$. Then $1/\lambda = 1.0974 \times 10^7 \times (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.524 \times 10^6$ per metre, so the wavelength is 656.1 nm. In the same way 4 to 2 gives 486.0 nm, 5 to 2 gives 433.9 nm and 6 to 2 gives 410.1 nm.

afterFigure.text: Each result agrees with the measured wavelength to about 0.03 per cent, which is close for a rule with one constant and two whole numbers. The formula began as a fit to the measurements. Bohr's model went further by giving a reason for its structure and for the fundamental constants that make up $R$.

lead.text: The lines fall into families, each defined by the level on which the electron lands. The jumps that end on $n = 2$ form the **Balmer series**, those that end on $n = 1$ the **Lyman series**, and those that end on $n = 3$ the **Paschen series**, and Bohr's formula agreed with the observed lines of all three.

Where a series lies follows from its lower level. The longest Lyman wavelength, for 2 to 1, is 121.5 nm, far below the 400 nm of violet light, so the whole series is ultraviolet. The Balmer lines from 3 to 2 down to 6 to 2 run from 656 nm to 410 nm, which is the visible range, and the Paschen series begins at 1875 nm, longer than red light, so it is infrared.

Within a series the lines crowd together towards a limit. As $n_i$ grows the term $1/n_i^2$ shrinks towards zero, so the shortest Balmer wavelength is $4/R = 364.5$ nm, and no Balmer line lies below it.

Multiplying the [[Rydberg formula|1/λ = R(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²), met earlier in this lesson.]] by $hc$ turns the wavelength into a [[photon energy|The energy hc/λ of one photon. Met in “Photon energy and photon counts”.]], because $E = hc/\lambda$, and the constant $hcR$ is 13.606 eV. The photon energy is therefore $E = 13.606 \times \left(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2\right)$ eV, a difference between two terms of the same form.

That suggests the atom has a set of allowed energies, called its **energy levels**, given by $E_n = -13.606/n^2$ eV, and that a line is the photon given out when the atom drops from one level to a lower one. Bohr read the combination principle of Rydberg and Ritz in this way, recognising its terms as the levels divided by Planck's constant. The levels are $-13.61$ eV for $n = 1$, $-3.40$ eV for $n = 2$, $-1.51$ eV for $n = 3$ and $-0.85$ eV for $n = 4$, and they close up as $n$ grows.

afterFigure.text: The photon's energy is the *difference* between the two levels. For the jump from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$ it is $-1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89$ eV, and $1239.84 / 1.89 = 656$ nm, the red line of the Balmer series. The closing up of the levels is the reason that the lines of a series crowd together.

lead.text: Bohr's model of 1913 states in a few rules what the levels mean. The electron moves in certain allowed orbits and does not radiate while it stays in one, although classical electromagnetism suggests that a circling charge would. It gives out or takes in light only when it jumps between two allowed orbits, and the photon's energy $hf$ equals the difference between the levels. The smallest orbit has a radius of 52.9 pm, and the electron cannot come any nearer to the nucleus than that.

The rules answer the question that the lamp posed at the start. An atom cannot give out light of every wavelength, because it can only jump between its levels, and each line is one jump. The lines of a series share their lower level, and a hydrogen lamp shows many lines together because it contains very many atoms making different jumps.

steps.headline: A hydrogen line is measured at 388.9 nm, and it ends on $n = 2$. From which level does the electron fall?

workedSteps.text: Invert the wavelength to find $1/\lambda$ in per metre.
Divide by the Rydberg constant, which gives the bracket of the formula.
The bracket is $1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2$, so subtract it from $1/n_f^2 = 1/4$ to leave $1/n_i^2$.
Take the reciprocal and then the square root.

steps.headline: NIST lists a hydrogen line at 1281.8 nm that ends on $n = 3$. From which level does the electron fall?

workedSteps.text: Invert the wavelength to find $1/\lambda$, then divide by $R$.
Subtract the bracket from $1/n_f^2 = 1/9$ to find $1/n_i^2$.
Take the reciprocal and then the square root to find the level.

lead.text: Photon energies add along a route, because each jump gives out the energy difference between its two levels.

reveal.text: The straight drop from $n = 3$ to $n = 1$ is itself a Lyman line, and it is the sum of the energies of the two steps.

lessons.orientation: Calculate the wavelengths of hydrogen's emission lines from the Rydberg formula and read a measured line as a jump between two energy levels.
lessons.nextAction: See where Bohr's model works, where it fails, and how de Broglie's waves explain its rule.

blocks.text: A hydrogen lamp, with its light spread out by a prism, does not give a continuous rainbow. It gives a few sharp lines, four of them in the visible range, at wavelengths that the NIST Atomic Spectra Database lists as 656.279, 486.135, 434.047 and 410.173 nm. In 1885 Johann Balmer found a formula that reproduces them.

Nobody knew why the formula worked until February 1913, when Niels Bohr was told of it by his friend Hans Hansen. Bohr said that everything then became clear to him. His answer was that each line is a photon carrying the energy that an atom gives up in one jump between two of its allowed energies.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to calculate the wavelength of a hydrogen line from the two levels involved, and read a measured line as a jump between two levels.
intro.whyItMatters: Every element has its own set of levels, so reading a spectrum as jumps between levels tells you which atoms made the light.

recap.keyIdea: Hydrogen's lines follow $1/\lambda = R(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2)$, and each one is the photon given out when an atom drops between two energy levels, with an energy equal to the difference between them.

blocks.text: The lines that end on $n = 1$ are the Lyman series, in the ultraviolet, those that end on $n = 2$ are the Balmer series, in the visible range, and those that end on $n = 3$ are the Paschen series, in the infrared. Given a wavelength and the level a line ends on, the formula can be turned round to find the level it starts from.
Energies add along a route of several jumps, so the wavelengths do not, and the energy of a photon is always a difference between two levels and never the energy of one level alone.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks where Bohr's model stops working, since it fits hydrogen's lines closely and gives no levels for neutral helium.

lessons.title: Limits of the Bohr model

reveal.text: Neutral helium has no energy levels in the model, because the model is built for two charged points. Where it applies, it is almost exact, and the next screens say where that is.

lead.text: Bohr's model combines a classical picture with one quantum rule. The picture is that the electron moves on a circle round the nucleus, held there by the electric attraction between them. The rule is that only certain orbits are allowed, those in which the electron's **angular momentum**, the product $mvr$ of its mass, speed and orbit radius, is a whole number $n$ of the quantity $\hbar = h/2\pi$.

Written out, the rule is $mvr = n\hbar$ with $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, and the smallest orbit, for $n = 1$, has a radius of 52.9 pm. The energies of the allowed orbits are the levels that the last lesson used, and they reproduce the Rydberg formula. The rule also fixes the electron's speed in each orbit, since $v = n\hbar/mr$.

The model is accurate only for a system of two charged points that circle each other far more slowly than light travels. That covers hydrogen and the other systems with one electron, such as singly ionised helium and doubly ionised lithium, and it covers a **Rydberg state**, in which one electron of any atom is far away from everything else.

Outside that domain it fails. Multi-electron atoms have no energy levels predicted by the model, and it does not work for neutral helium. It cannot give the relative brightness of spectral lines, although a few simple cases came out reasonably, and it cannot account for the Zeeman effect, the change in spectral lines caused by an external magnetic field. It also gives no reason why some energy levels lie very close together, which shows up as close pairs of lines in the spectra of some atoms.
