reveal.text: The contradicted part is the angular momentum, which is zero in the true ground state. The spectral lines test the energies, and those agree with the model.

lead.text: The model gives the ground state an angular momentum of $\hbar$, since $mvr = n\hbar$ with $n = 1$, and experiment shows that the true ground state has none. An electron circling the nucleus like a planet is therefore the wrong picture. Modern quantum mechanics replaces the orbit with a spherical cloud of probability around the nucleus, thickest close to it.

The energies are another matter, because the spectral lines test them and the model's values agree. The full quantum treatment of hydrogen gives the same energy levels, so the levels survive in the later theory while the picture of the orbit does not.

Bohr stated the rule $mvr = n\hbar$ as an assumption. In 1924 de Broglie reinterpreted it as a condition on a **standing wave**. The electron has a wave, and the wave has to close on itself around the orbit, so that exactly $n$ wavelengths make up the circumference, $n\lambda = 2\pi r$. The wavelength of an electron is $\lambda = h/mv$, so the condition reads $nh/mv = 2\pi r$, which rearranges to $mvr = nh/2\pi = n\hbar$, the rule that Bohr had assumed.

afterFigure.text: A wave that travels once round the orbit has to meet itself on its return, as a standing wave on a string has to fit its ends. With three wavelengths it does, and with two and a half it does not, so the orbits are those with $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ and nothing in between. The rule is no longer arbitrary, because it follows from requiring the electron's wave to close up.

diagram.alt: A circular orbit around a nucleus with a wave drawn along it. For two, three and four whole wavelengths the wave closes on itself. For two and a half wavelengths the wave ends at a different height from where it began, leaving a gap.
diagram.caption: A de Broglie wave on a circular orbit. Only whole numbers of wavelengths close up. Use the buttons to change the number.

steps.headline: Check that exactly one de Broglie wavelength fits around the $n = 1$ orbit, whose radius is 52.9 pm.

workedSteps.text: The rule $mvr = \hbar$ fixes the speed in this orbit, which the earlier calculation found.
The de Broglie wavelength of an electron at that speed follows from $\lambda = h/mv$.
Count how many wavelengths go round the circumference of the orbit, which is $2\pi r$.

lead.text: In 1925 Heisenberg proposed a new kind of mechanics, which he developed with Max Born and Pascual Jordan into matrix mechanics, and Schrödinger arrived by a different route at a second version, wave mechanics, which builds on de Broglie's matter waves. These replaced Bohr's orbits with atomic orbitals, the clouds of probability described above.

Bohr's model remains in use as a simple one. It is obsolete as a theory, but it gives correct results for the systems inside its domain and is still the easiest way into energy-level diagrams, so it is worth knowing both what it explains and where it stops.
The standing-wave condition can be used as a test of any proposed orbit.

reveal.text: A wave of 1.9 wavelengths would be out of step with itself after one turn, so this orbit is not one of Bohr's allowed orbits.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether the Bohr model can be trusted for a given atom or spectral feature, and say how de Broglie's waves explain its quantisation rule.
lessons.nextAction: Fire electrons at two slits one at a time and predict the pattern that builds up on the screen.

blocks.text: Bohr's model predicts the wavelengths of hydrogen's lines to within a few hundredths of a per cent, and the same two rules applied to neutral helium predict nothing useful, since the model gives helium no energy levels at all. A model that works so well for one atom and so badly for the next has a domain, a set of systems and measurements for which it can be trusted, and the edge of that domain matters as much as the model.
The model's rule for the allowed orbits also needs a reason. Bohr stated it as an assumption that fitted the lines, and in 1924 de Broglie reinterpreted it as a condition on the electron's wave.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether Bohr's model can be trusted for a given atom or spectral feature, and show how de Broglie's waves lead to its rule for the allowed orbits.
intro.whyItMatters: Every model in physics has a domain, and a skilled physicist asks where it lies before relying on a result.

recap.keyIdea: Bohr's model is almost exact for two charged points orbiting slowly, as in hydrogen and other one-electron systems, and it fails for neutral helium and for brightness and fine detail in spectra, while de Broglie's standing waves explain its rule $mvr = n\hbar$.

blocks.text: The model's picture of an electron circling the nucleus is wrong, since the true ground state has no orbital angular momentum, but its energy levels for hydrogen agree with the lines and survive in the later theory. It is therefore reliable inside its domain and silent or wrong outside it.

De Broglie's wave of wavelength $h/mv$ has to close up after one turn around the orbit, so a whole number $n$ of wavelengths fits, $n\lambda = 2\pi r$, and that gives $mvr = n\hbar$ without any further assumption.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes de Broglie's idea on its own, with electrons fired at two slits one at a time, and asks what pattern builds up on the screen.

lessons.title: Waves and particles

reveal.text: The dots look random at first, and bands appear only as they add up. The wave does not need many electrons: each electron on its own is governed by it.

lead.text: The puzzle came first with light. In the late seventeenth century Newton favoured a stream of particles and Huygens a wave, and Thomas Young's interference experiments of 1801 supported the wave. Around 1900 Planck's law for black-body radiation, and Einstein's account of the photoelectric effect in 1905 in terms of photons, pointed to particles, and the photon theory remained controversial until Arthur Compton's experiments from 1922 to 1924 demonstrated the momentum of light.

For electrons the evidence arrived in the opposite order. J. J. Thomson's measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio in 1897 was among the experiments that showed free electrons to be particles, and in 1924 de Broglie proposed that electrons, and all matter, can be treated as waves. In 1927 two experiments confirmed it: Davisson and Germer at Bell Labs scattered electrons from nickel, and G. P. Thomson and Alexander Reid at Cambridge sent them through thin nickel films and saw rings of diffraction.

In the electron double-slit experiment the source can be turned down until only one or two electrons are detected each second, and each appears on the detector as a single dot. The first dots seem to fall at random. After some time a pattern emerges, and it settles into bright and dark bands, as the figure shows for the same run stopped after 10, 100 and 700 electrons.

afterFigure.text: The bands therefore do not need electrons to interfere with one another, because each electron arrives alone. It lands at one point, at random, and the pattern is a statistical one: the wave decides where an electron is likely to land, and many arrivals map that out. The same build-up has been found with atoms and with large molecules.

diagram.alt: A rectangular detecting screen shown face on, with dots where single electrons have landed after 10, 100 and 700 electrons have arrived. With 10 the dots look random, with 100 a pattern begins to show, and with 700 there are clear vertical bands of many and few dots.
diagram.caption: The same run, stopped at three moments. Electrons arrive one at a time, and the bands appear only as the dots add up. Use the buttons to change the number of electrons.

reveal.text: The bands vanish. The next screen says what that tells us about the electrons.

lead.text: When detectors are placed at the slits to find which slit each electron went through, the interference pattern disappears. Many such experiments have been proposed and many carried out, and in each of them the interference vanishes once the paths are recorded.

What the experiment shows therefore depends on how it is set up. With nothing recording the path, the electrons build up the bands of a wave, and with a record of the path they behave as particles that each went through one slit. The idea of wave-particle **duality** does not mean that an electron switches between the two as it likes. It means that no single picture, wave or particle, covers every experiment, and that each picture is needed for some of them.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares the screen's record for three set-ups. The bands in the first are the pattern of a wave, and the smooth hump in the second is what a record of the path leaves behind.

diagram.alt: Three graphs of the number of electrons detected across the screen. With two slits and no detectors the graph has regular peaks and dips under a broad hump. With a detector at each slit the peaks and dips are gone and a smooth hump remains. With one slit alone there is a single smooth hump, lower than the other two.
diagram.caption: What the screen records for three set-ups. Marking which slit each electron used removes the bands. Use the buttons to change the set-up.

lead.text: If electrons behave as waves, they should have a wavelength, and the last lesson used it: $\lambda = h/mv$, where $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s is the Planck constant. De Broglie proposed in 1924 that it applies to any particle of mass $m$ and speed $v$, and the product $mv$ is the particle's momentum, so a particle with more momentum has a shorter wavelength.

Whether the wave shows depends on its wavelength compared with the sizes in the experiment. Double-slit fringes are [[spaced by λL/d|The spacing of double-slit fringes for wavelength λ, slit separation d and screen distance L. Met in “When waves add”.]], so a shorter wavelength gives finer fringes, and when the wavelength is far smaller than anything in the apparatus the pattern is too fine to notice. The worked example puts numbers on this for an electron, and the next one for a ball.

steps.headline: An electron moves at $1.0 \times 10^6$ m/s. Find its de Broglie wavelength.

workedSteps.text: Write the wavelength in terms of the momentum $mv$.
Find the electron's momentum, with $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg.
Divide the Planck constant by the momentum.

steps.headline: A ball of mass 0.145 kg (a made-up value) is thrown at 40 m/s. Find its de Broglie wavelength.

workedSteps.text: The ball's momentum is the product of its mass and speed.
Before dividing, decide how the ball's wavelength compares with the electron's.
Divide the Planck constant by the momentum.

lead.text: The relation can be run backwards. Choose the wavelength that an experiment needs, and the speed follows.

reveal.text: Electrons at about $7 \times 10^6$ m/s have wavelengths of atomic size, so they can be diffracted by structures as small as atoms, as the nickel experiments of 1927 showed.

lessons.orientation: Predict the pattern that electrons or photons make in a double-slit experiment, with and without detectors at the slits, and compute a de Broglie wavelength.
lessons.nextAction: Use the position and momentum of a wave to find the limit on knowing both.

blocks.text: Suppose we fire a beam of electrons at a screen with two narrow slits in it, and record where they land on a detector behind it. They do not pile up in two stripes behind the slits, as pellets would. They land in alternating bands of many and few, which is the pattern that waves make when they pass through two slits, so in this experiment a beam of electrons behaves as a wave.

Yet each electron is detected at a single point, with all of its charge and mass. So what happens if we turn the source down until only one electron at a time crosses the apparatus? A wave might seem to need many electrons to interfere with one another, and a particle ought to go through one slit or the other, and the experiment decides between the two.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict the pattern that electrons make at a double slit, with and without detectors at the slits, and calculate a de Broglie wavelength.
intro.whyItMatters: The same particle needs a wave description in one experiment and a particle description in another, and the wavelength says which one will show.

recap.keyIdea: Electrons and photons build wave patterns from single arrivals and lose the pattern when the path is detected, and a particle of momentum $mv$ has the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/mv$.

blocks.text: Electrons arriving one at a time land at single points, and the dots gradually form the bands of a wave, which shows that each electron is governed by a wave and that the pattern needs no interference between electrons. When detectors record which slit each electron used, the bands disappear, so what an experiment shows depends on how it is set up.

The wavelength $h/mv$ is tiny for anything with a large momentum, $1.1 \times 10^{-34}$ m for a thrown ball. The wave therefore shows only when the wavelength is comparable to the sizes in the experiment, as it is for electrons at a few million metres per second.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to what a wave implies for position and momentum: a narrow wave needs many wavelengths added together, and that sets a limit on how well both can be known.

lessons.title: The uncertainty principle

reveal.text: A short sound needs many frequencies added together. A particle that is confined to a small region likewise needs many momenta, and the next screens give the rule and its size.

lead.text: A wave of a single wavelength has the same size everywhere, so it says nothing about where a particle is. To describe a particle that is more or less in one place, waves of many wavelengths are added so that they reinforce one another in one region and cancel elsewhere, and the result is a **wave packet**. The more waves are added, the more narrowly the packet can be confined.

Each added wave brings a different momentum, because a particle's wavelength is $\lambda = h/p$, so narrowing the packet in position widens it in momentum. The figure shows the same kind of packet described in two ways, by position and by momentum: a wide packet contains a narrow range of momenta, and a narrow packet contains a wide range. The two plots are mathematical partners, each the Fourier transform of the other.

afterFigure.text: The width of each plot can be measured by its [[standard deviation|A measure of how widely values are spread about their average.]], written $\sigma_x$ for position and $\sigma_p$ for momentum, and the trade-off between them takes the form of a single inequality.

diagram.alt: Two pairs of graphs. On the left, a wave packet in position: the wave is large near the middle and fades away on both sides. On the right, the spread of momenta it contains. A wide packet in position has a narrow hump in momentum, and a narrow packet in position has a wide hump in momentum.
diagram.caption: The same wave described by position and by momentum. Squeezing the packet in position widens it in momentum. Use the buttons to change the packet.

lead.text: Werner Heisenberg first introduced the idea in 1927, and Earle Kennard derived the modern inequality later that year, with Hermann Weyl following in 1928. The statement is that $\sigma_x \sigma_p \ge \hbar/2$, where $\hbar = h/2\pi = 1.0546 \times 10^{-34}$ J s, and it is the **uncertainty principle**. It applies to certain pairs of properties, of which position and momentum are one, and for such a pair the more sharply one is known, the less sharply the other can be.

The relation sets a floor, so the product of the spreads can be larger than $\hbar/2$ but never smaller. For a particle of mass $m$ the momentum spread is $m$ times the speed spread. Taking the width $\Delta x$ of the region that holds the particle as its position spread then gives an estimate of the least spread in speed, $\Delta v \ge \hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$.

steps.headline: An electron is confined to a region 0.20 nm wide. Find the least possible spread in its speed.

workedSteps.text: Write the relation for the speed spread.
Find the denominator, with $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg and $\Delta x = 2.0 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
Divide $\hbar$ by it.

steps.headline: The electron in a hydrogen atom is confined to about the size of its smallest orbit, a radius of 52.9 pm. Find the least spread in its speed.

workedSteps.text: Take the size of the region as the position spread.
Use $\Delta v \ge \hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$ to find the least spread in speed.
Compare it with the speed that Bohr's model gave for this orbit.

reveal.text: The limit follows from the wave nature of the particle. The next screen shows where the kick picture came from, and why it was given up.

lead.text: Heisenberg first explained the limit with an imagined microscope. Light of short wavelength gives a sharp image of an electron, but each photon carries a large momentum and knocks the electron by a large and random amount. Light of long wavelength disturbs the electron less and shows its position only vaguely. Whatever wavelength is chosen, the product of the two uncertainties is never smaller than about $h$, up to a small numerical factor.

The picture is easy to remember and it is misleading, since it makes the limit sound like a flaw of the method that a better instrument could remove. The limit belongs to the particle itself. Every quantum object has a matter wave, a narrow packet needs many wavelengths, and so the spread of momentum would be there whether anyone measured it or not. It is a fundamental property of quantum systems, and it would be the same with perfect instruments.

Every object has a matter wave, so the relation applies to all of them, and what changes from one object to the next is the size of the effect. The least speed spread $\hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$ falls in inverse proportion to both the mass and the size of the region. For the electron in hydrogen's smallest orbit it is $1.1 \times 10^6$ m/s, and the figure compares it with two made-up objects: a dust grain of mass 1.0 microgram located to 1 micrometre, and a baseball of mass 0.145 kg located to 1 millimetre.

afterFigure.text: The effect is significant only for the motion of microscopic objects. For the dust grain and the baseball it is present and far too small for any instrument to detect. It does matter for the most precise measurements that have been made: the mirrors of a gravitational-wave interferometer are watched so closely that a mirror of 100 kg observed for 2 ms is limited in accuracy to about $6 \times 10^{-20}$ m by quantum uncertainty.

The second view adds the least spread in speed, which is about a million metres per second for the electron and many powers of ten smaller for the other two.

lead.text: A similar limit joins the energy of a state to how long it lasts. A state has a definite energy only if its frequency is defined accurately, and that takes many cycles, so a state that exists only briefly cannot have a definite energy. An excited atom lasts a short time before it emits a photon, so its energy is slightly uncertain, and the photons from many such atoms carry slightly different energies. They cluster around the energy of the state, and their spread is the **natural linewidth** of the spectral line.

Fast-decaying states have broad lines and slow-decaying states have narrow ones, because the product of the lifetime and the energy width is fixed up to a small numerical factor. A state that lasts a thousand times longer therefore gives a line about a thousand times narrower.
Two excited states are compared by the lines they emit, with the same photon energy and different lifetimes.

reveal.text: The width of a line tells how long its state lives, which is how lifetimes of states are measured from spectra.

lessons.orientation: Use the position-momentum inequality to find the least spread in speed for a confined particle, and decide whether the limit matters in a given case.
lessons.nextAction: Judge how the chance of tunnelling changes with barrier width, barrier height and particle mass.

blocks.text: A pure musical tone is a wave of a single frequency, and a wave of that kind goes on for ever. A click, which lasts only a few milliseconds, cannot be made in that way. It is built by adding together waves of many different frequencies, which cancel one another everywhere except in the short moment that the click lasts, and the shorter the sound, the wider the range of frequencies that it needs.

Quantum mechanics describes a particle by a wave, and the same trade-off then governs where the particle is and how fast it is moving. A wave narrow enough to say where the particle is needs many wavelengths, and many wavelengths mean a spread of momentum. The uncertainty principle puts a floor under the product of the two spreads, and it is useful because it shows when the quantum effect is large enough to matter and when it can be ignored.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the least spread in speed of a confined particle and decide whether the uncertainty limit matters in a given case.
intro.whyItMatters: The limit sets the width of spectral lines, and it tells you when a quantum effect is large enough to matter and when it can safely be ignored.

recap.keyIdea: The spreads in position and momentum obey $\sigma_x \sigma_p \ge \hbar/2$ because a narrow wave needs many wavelengths, so the limit belongs to every wave-like object and is large only for microscopic ones.

blocks.text: For a confined particle the least spread in speed is $\hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$, which is about $10^5$ to $10^6$ m/s for an electron held to the size of an atom and about $10^{-31}$ m/s for a baseball held to a millimetre. Better instruments cannot lower the limit, since it follows from the particle's wave nature and not from the kick of a measurement.

The same relation between a wave's extent and its spread of frequencies joins energy to lifetime: a state that exists only briefly cannot have a definite energy, so fast-decaying states give broad spectral lines.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows a wave into a barrier that a classical particle could not enter, and asks how the chance of getting through changes with the barrier and the particle.

lessons.title: Quantum tunnelling

reveal.text: Some of them are found beyond the barrier. A particle with too little energy to climb a barrier is described by a wave, and a wave does not end at the barrier's edge, which is the idea the next screen develops.

lead.text: A ball without the energy to climb a hill rolls part of the way up and comes back, and classical mechanics treats a particle that meets a [[potential energy barrier|A region that a particle could enter only with more energy than it has.]] in the same way. Quantum mechanics treats an electron as a wave, as the lesson on [[waves and particles|Matter shows both wave and particle behaviour. Met in 'Waves and particles'.]] showed, and the square of the wave's size at a point gives the probability of finding the particle there. In the figure a **wave packet**, a short pulse of that wave, approaches a barrier that the particle has too little energy to surmount.

Most of the packet is reflected and some of it is transmitted, so afterwards the packet lies on both sides of the barrier with a lower peak than before. The total probability stays equal to one, since the particle is still somewhere, and the chance of finding it on the far side is called the **tunnelling probability**.

afterFigure.text: The particle is not divided into a large piece and a small one. A detector beyond the barrier finds the whole particle or finds nothing, and the transmitted part of the packet says how often each of those outcomes happens.

diagram.alt: A wave packet approaches a barrier, reaches into it, and afterwards a large reflected packet moves back while a small transmitted packet continues beyond the barrier.
diagram.caption: A wave packet meeting a barrier that the particle cannot climb. Use the buttons to follow it from the approach to the aftermath.

lead.text: Three things set the tunnelling probability, and each acts in the same way. The probability of transmission decreases exponentially with the height of the barrier, with its width and with the mass of the tunnelling particle, so a wider barrier, a higher barrier or a heavier particle all make crossing less likely.

An exponential fall means that **each equal step in width multiplies the probability by the same factor**, where a straight-line fall would subtract the same amount each time. Suppose, with invented numbers meant only to show the pattern, that one extra step of width cut the chance to a tenth: a second step would cut it to a hundredth and a third to a thousandth, and the chance would shrink very fast without ever reaching exactly zero.

afterFigure.text: Mass enters in the same way, so the particles that tunnel most readily are light ones, and electrons crossing barriers only a few atoms wide are the clearest case, although protons and even whole atoms have been seen to tunnel as well. There is no thickness below which every particle tunnels and above which none does: the probability falls smoothly and steeply.

diagram.alt: The same wave packet meets three barriers: a narrow low one, a wider one of the same height, and a higher one of the same width. The transmitted packet beyond each is much smaller for the wider and the higher barrier.
diagram.caption: The transmitted part gets smaller as the barrier widens or rises. The drawing is qualitative and carries no numbers.

reveal.text: The thicker barrier lets through far less than half as many electrons, though not none, because each extra step of width multiplies the probability by the same factor.

The first experiment is better on both width and mass, so it wins without any number. The sources give no figure for how much a heavier particle loses, so a comparison like this has to stay qualitative.

lead.text: You have met an optical version of this effect. Light inside a prism at an angle just above the [[critical angle|The angle of incidence beyond which light in glass is totally reflected at the surface. Met in 'Why light bends'.]] is reflected, and none of it seems to leave. If a second prism is brought up close to the first, to within a few wavelengths of the light, some of it tunnels across the gap, and the effect is called **frustrated total internal reflection**.

The gap plays the part of the barrier, and the light that crosses it plays the part of the transmitted packet. The effect can be calculated with tunnelling theory and measured by counting single photons.

The scanning tunnelling microscope, invented by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer in 1981, uses the steep dependence of tunnelling on the width of the gap. A conducting needle is brought close to a surface that has a voltage across it, and electrons tunnel between the needle and the surface, so that the current they make reveals how far the needle is from the surface.

To form an image the tip is scanned across the surface while piezoelectric rods, which change length when a voltage is applied, adjust its height so as to keep the tunnelling current constant. The voltages applied to the rods are recorded, and because they follow the height of the surface they can be used to draw it. The instrument is accurate to 0.001 nm, about 1% of the diameter of an atom.

afterFigure.text: Holding the current constant holds the gap constant, which is why the tip's height follows the bumps of the surface atom by atom, with nothing touching it.

diagram.alt: A needle tip above a row of atoms. With the tip far away a thin dashed line marks a tiny current, with the tip close a thick line marks a large current, and in a scan the tip rises over an extra atom to keep the gap constant.
diagram.caption: A scanning tunnelling microscope. The current depends steeply on the gap, and holding it constant makes the tip follow the surface.

reveal.text: The same steepness that makes the current a precise ruler for the gap also makes 0.001 nm measurable. Binnig and Rohrer shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for the instrument.

lead.text: A strong electric field can also make a barrier thin. When the field at the surface of a metal is strong enough, the barrier that holds the electrons in thins until they can tunnel out, which is called **cold emission**, and the current rises roughly exponentially with the field. It resembles **thermionic emission**, in which electrons leave a hot metal because collisions happen to give some of them more energy than the barrier needs, but those electrons climb over the barrier and tunnelling electrons go through it.

In electronics the barrier is often a thin insulating layer. Electrons tunnel readily through insulating layers thinner than about 1 nm, so transistors that thin leak current, which drains power and heats the device, and this leakage sets a lower limit on how small microelectronic devices can be made. Tunnel junctions, two conductors separated by a very thin insulator, show tunnelling that is readily detected when the layer is about 3 nm or thinner, and flash memory uses tunnelling to program its floating gates.

reveal.text: The two kinds of emission differ in what the electron does at the barrier: thermionic electrons climb over it, and tunnelling electrons go through it.

lead.text: Tunnelling was first put to work on the nucleus. In 1928 George Gamow, and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon, showed that alpha decay is tunnelling. Gurney and Condon used the Schrödinger equation with a model of the nuclear potential to relate the half-life of an alpha particle to its emission energy, and the relationship rests directly on the probability of tunnelling. It was a great success of the theory, and the next lesson takes up half-lives.

Stars depend on it as well. Atomic nuclei repel one another because they are positively charged, and that repulsion is called the Coulomb barrier. The temperature in a stellar core is generally insufficient to let nuclei overcome the barrier, and tunnelling increases the probability of getting through it. The probability is still low for any one pair of nuclei, but the extremely large number of nuclei in a core is enough to sustain a steady fusion reaction.
The claim comes from experiments on how long tunnelling takes, and other physicists, among them Herbert Winful, have disputed it.

reveal.text: Winful argued that those experiments were misinterpreted, because the group velocity of a wave packet is not its speed, and the theorems rule out faster-than-light tunnelling. A probability spread over both sides of a barrier does not make the crossing instantaneous.

lessons.orientation: Judge how the chance of tunnelling changes with barrier width, barrier height and particle mass, and recognise where it operates in devices, stars and nuclei.
lessons.nextAction: Use a half-life to predict how much of a radioactive sample remains and to date a sample from its measured activity.

blocks.text: A ball that rolls towards a hill with too little energy to reach the top comes back down, and classical mechanics says the same of an electron that meets an energy barrier it cannot climb. The scanning tunnelling microscope shows that electrons do not always turn back: the needle of the instrument is held a small gap above the surface it scans, yet a current of electrons flows across the gap, and the current is so sensitive to the width of the gap that the instrument is accurate to 0.001 nm, about 1% of the diameter of an atom.

The chance that a particle crosses a barrier it should not be able to cross changes steeply with the width and height of the barrier and with the mass of the particle, and that steepness explains why the effect that lets a microscope see single atoms also limits how small a transistor can be made and makes fusion possible in the Sun.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to judge how the chance of tunnelling changes with a barrier's width, its height and the particle's mass, and say where tunnelling operates in devices, nuclei and stars.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why chips leak current, how a microscope can image single atoms, and why a star can fuse hydrogen at the temperatures it has.

recap.keyIdea: A particle's wave reaches through a barrier that the particle has too little energy to climb, and the chance of crossing falls exponentially as the barrier gets wider or higher or the particle heavier.

blocks.text: When a wave packet meets a barrier, most of it is reflected and a small part is transmitted, and the part beyond the barrier gives the probability of finding the particle there. That probability decreases exponentially with the barrier's width and height and with the particle's mass, so it is large enough to matter only for light particles and very thin barriers, and it never reaches an exact cut-off.

The steep dependence on width lets a scanning tunnelling microscope trace a surface by holding its current constant, it makes insulating layers thinner than about 1 nm leak, and in nuclei and stars it drives alpha decay and lets fusion run at core temperatures. Claims of tunnelling faster than light are disputed, and relativistic theory forbids them.

recap.nextHook: An alpha particle leaves its nucleus at a moment that nothing can predict, yet a large sample of such nuclei decays on a steady schedule, and the next lesson turns that schedule into the half-life.

lessons.title: Radioactive decay and half-life

lead.text: The activity of a sample is the number of its atoms that decay each second, and it is measured in becquerels (Bq), where one becquerel is one decay per second.

reveal.text: The activity halves again, to 200 Bq. The time for the activity to halve belongs to the isotope, and the next screens show why it stays the same as the sample thins out.

lead.text: Radioactive decay happens when an unstable nucleus gives up energy as radiation, and for a single atom the moment it happens is random: quantum theory offers no way to say when a given atom will go, however old it is. A large collection of identical atoms behaves differently, since its overall rate of decay settles to a steady value that one number, the half-life, can describe. The half-lives of the isotopes we know range from almost no time at all to many times the age of the universe.

The rate at which a sample decays is its **activity**, the number of decays per second. The SI unit is the **becquerel**, named after Henri Becquerel, who discovered radioactivity in 1896, and one becquerel is one decay per second.

afterFigure.text: The pattern is one of unpredictable events with a predictable total. Each atom has a fixed chance of decaying in a given time, which leaves the moment of any one atom's decay unknowable and the number of decays in a large sample predictable, and the next screens turn that chance into a formula.

lead.text: The **half-life** $T$ of an isotope is the time taken for half of the atoms in a sample to decay. After one half-life half the atoms remain, after two half-lives a quarter and after three an eighth, and after any time $t$ the number left is $N = N_0 \times 2^{-t/T}$, where $N_0$ is the number at the start. The exponent $t/T$ counts half-lives, so it does not have to be a whole number.

Every atom that remains has the same chance of decaying, so the activity of a sample is proportional to the number of atoms left, and it follows the same law. The first case in the figure plots the fraction left against time in half-lives. The second shows an invented source of 1,200 Bq with a half-life of 6.0 hours, whose activity is 600 Bq after 6.0 hours, 300 Bq after 12 hours and 150 Bq after 18 hours.

afterFigure.text: The curve never reaches zero, because half of any number of atoms is still some atoms, and every equal stretch of time takes the same proportion of the atoms that are left. Highly radioactive substances have short half-lives and are quickly spent, while weakly radioactive ones endure, and the known half-lives run from 8.6 × 10⁻²³ s for hydrogen-5 to more than 2.25 × 10²⁴ years for tellurium-128, almost 54 orders of magnitude, with the same law covering all of them.

diagram.alt: Two graphs of exponential decay. The first plots the fraction of atoms left against time in half-lives, passing through 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 at 0 to 4 half-lives. The second plots the activity of an invented source of 1,200 becquerels with a half-life of 6.0 hours, passing through 600, 300, 150 and 75 becquerels at 6, 12, 18 and 24 hours.
diagram.caption: The fraction left halves in every half-life. Use the buttons to compare the fraction with the activity of a made-up source.

steps.headline: A source's activity falls from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 9.0 hours. Find its half-life.

workedSteps.text: Halve the activity until you reach 100 Bq, and count the halvings.
That is three halvings, so the 9.0 hours is three half-lives.
Divide the time by the number of half-lives.

steps.headline: A source with a half-life of 3.0 hours has an activity of 800 Bq. Find its activity after 7.5 hours.

workedSteps.text: Find how many half-lives 7.5 hours is.
The activity follows the same halving law as the number of atoms, with the power counting half-lives. The power does not have to be a whole number.
Work out the power, and check the result against the whole-number cases: two half-lives would give 200 Bq and three would give 100 Bq.

lead.text: An atom does not wear out. The mathematics of radioactive decay rests on one assumption, that a nucleus **has no memory**: it has no way of turning its history into its present behaviour, so the probability that it breaks down stays constant for as long as the nucleus exists. A car or a person is different, because ageing objects have a chance of breaking down per unit of time that grows from the moment they begin to exist.

A constant chance is what makes the halving exact. Whichever atoms remain after one half-life, each of them has the same 50% chance of decaying during the next one, whether it is newly formed or has lasted a long time, so half of the remainder decays and the sample halves again. The figure shows one simulated run of 100 atoms, each with a 50% chance of decaying in every half-life.

afterFigure.text: The counts in this run wander a little from the expected 50, 25 and 12.5, because each atom's decay is a matter of chance. A larger sample follows the smooth curve more closely, which is why a half-life describes a large sample well and says little with certainty about a handful of atoms.

diagram.alt: A ten by ten grid of 100 atoms, shown at the start and after one, two and three half-lives. Filled circles have not decayed. In this simulated run 54, 24 and 11 atoms are left, against expected values of 50, 25 and 12.5.
diagram.caption: One simulated run of 100 atoms that each have a 50% chance of decaying in every half-life. Use the buttons to step through the half-lives.

lead.text: Early experiments found that electric and magnetic fields split radioactive emissions into three beams, and Ernest Rutherford named them alpha, beta and gamma in order of how far they penetrate matter, from least to most. The way the fields bent each beam showed that alpha particles are positive, beta particles negative and gamma rays neutral, and further work showed that alpha particles are helium nuclei, beta particles are fast electrons and gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation, which an excited nucleus gives out after an alpha or beta decay.

A decay does not make the atom vanish. The decaying nucleus, the parent, becomes at least one **daughter nuclide**, and when the number of protons changes the daughter is a different element. The daughter may be radioactive too, and a sequence of decays, called a **decay chain**, continues until a stable nuclide is made. Some nuclides have more than one route: 35.94% of bismuth-212 decays by alpha emission to thallium-208 and 64.06% by beta emission to polonium-212, and both of those decay directly to stable lead-208.

afterFigure.text: The two percentages are probabilities for each atom, in the way that 50% is the probability in a half-life, and in a large sample they set how many atoms take each route: of 10,000 bismuth-212 atoms about 3,594 decay by alpha emission.

diagram.alt: A branching diagram. Bismuth-212 decays 35.94% of the time by alpha emission to thallium-208 and 64.06% of the time by beta emission to polonium-212, and both of those decay on to stable lead-208.
diagram.caption: Each bismuth-212 atom takes one of two routes, with fixed probabilities, and both routes end at the same stable nuclide.

reveal.text: About 64 atoms in every 100 take the beta route, whatever the size of the sample, and each single atom takes one route or the other at random.

lead.text: Dating a sample turns the halving law around. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5700 years, known to within 30 years, and natural carbon gives 14 decays per minute per gram. Because activity is proportional to the number of atoms left, the ratio of a sample's activity to 14 is the fraction of its carbon-14 that has survived, and the age follows from solving $2^{-t/T} = N/N_0$ for $t$. The unknown sits in the exponent, so the solution needs a logarithm: $t = T \times \ln(N_0/N) \div \ln 2$.

The factor $\ln 2$ is the natural logarithm of 2, 0.6931, which converts the base 2 of the halving form into the base $e$ in which many books write the law, as $N = N_0 e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = T/\ln 2$. The two forms are the same law. The method assumes that the carbon started with the activity of living material and has only decayed since.

afterFigure.text: The result is only as good as its inputs. The half-life of carbon-14 is known to 30 years in 5700, about 0.5%, so an age of about 10,000 years carries an uncertainty of about 50 years from that source alone.

steps.headline: An artefact's carbon gives 4 decays per minute per gram, and living carbon gives 14. Taking the half-life of carbon-14 as 5700 years, find the artefact's age.

workedSteps.text: Find the fraction of the carbon-14 that is left, using the ratio of the activities.
Estimate the answer first. Halving 14 gives 7 and halving again gives 3.5, so an activity of 4 comes a little before two half-lives, and the age is a little under 11,400 years.
Now turn the halving law around with logarithms, using N₀/N = 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5.
Work out the number of half-lives.
Multiply by the half-life. The result, a little under 11,400 years, agrees with the estimate.

reveal.text: An age of about 10,300 years is as much as the inputs justify, and the activity of 4 is quoted to a single figure, which would widen the uncertainty further.
The short-lived sample decays faster and is soon spent, while the long-lived one decays slowly and endures, so for the same number of atoms a shorter half-life means a higher activity.

lessons.orientation: Use a half-life to predict how much of a sample remains and to date a sample from its measured activity.
lessons.nextAction: Use mass defect and the binding energy curve to decide whether a nuclear change releases energy, and estimate the energy per kilogram of fuel.

blocks.text: A single radioactive atom decays at a random moment, and according to quantum theory nothing can tell you when, however long that atom has already existed. Yet a gram of carbon from living material gives 14 decays per minute, and a gram of carbon from an artefact that gives only 4 per minute can be given an age of about ten thousand years from those two counts and one more number, the half-life.
Both statements hold together because a large number of identical atoms behaves predictably although each atom does not, and the half-life is the number that describes that behaviour.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use a half-life to predict how much of a sample remains, and to work out a sample's age from its measured activity.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you plan around a source that decays at a known rate and read an age from a count of decays.

recap.keyIdea: A half-life is the time for half of a sample's atoms to decay, and because an atom has no memory of its age, the number left falls by the same factor in every equal stretch of time, which lets a measured activity give a sample's age.

blocks.text: Decay is random for a single atom and steady for a large sample. Each remaining atom has the same chance of decaying in any interval, so the number of atoms and the activity halve in every half-life, following $N = N_0 \times 2^{-t/T}$, and an atom that has survived for a long time is no likelier to decay than a new one.

A decay turns the atom into a daughter nuclide that may decay again in a chain, and some nuclides, such as bismuth-212, branch with fixed probabilities. Turning the law around with logarithms gives the age of a sample from the ratio of its activity to that of living material, 14 decays per minute per gram for carbon, so that an activity of 4 gives about 10,300 years, with an uncertainty of about 50 years from the half-life of 5700(30) years alone.

recap.nextHook: A decay releases energy, and the next lesson asks where that energy comes from, and why splitting heavy nuclei and joining light ones can both release it.

lessons.title: Binding energy, fission and fusion

reveal.text: The helium atom has about 0.8% less mass than the four hydrogen atoms. That difference in mass is the subject of the next screen.

lead.text: A nucleus weighs less than the protons and neutrons it is made of would weigh apart. The shortfall is called the **mass defect**, and making it destroys no nucleon: all the particles are still there, and the missing mass left as energy when the nucleus formed. A helium atom, for example, is about 0.8% lighter than four hydrogen atoms put together.

Einstein's relation $E = mc^2$ turns the mass defect into energy, and the energy has a second meaning. It is the **binding energy**, the minimum energy needed to take the nucleus apart into its separate protons and neutrons, so it measures how tightly the nucleus is held. The nuclear force that holds the nucleons acts over a very short range, and the binding energies it produces are about a million times larger than the energies that bind an electron to a light atom such as hydrogen.

afterFigure.text: The same reckoning applies to any nuclear change. If the products have less mass than the reactants, the difference multiplied by $c^2$ leaves as energy, and one kilogram of mass is equivalent to 8.99 × 10¹⁶ J.

steps.headline: Hydrogen fusing into helium loses about 0.8% of its mass. Find the energy released by 1.0 kg of hydrogen.

workedSteps.text: Find the mass that is lost.
Each kilogram of mass is equivalent to $c^2$ joules.
Multiply the lost mass by $c^2$.
That energy comes from 8 g of lost mass, which is a small part of the kilogram of hydrogen that fused.

steps.headline: Splitting uranium loses about 0.1% of the starting mass of each atom. Find the energy released by 1.0 kg of uranium.

workedSteps.text: Find the mass that is lost.
Multiply by $c^2$, as in the hydrogen case, and give the result in units of 10¹³ J.

lead.text: Plotting the binding energy per nucleon against the number of nucleons in the nucleus gives the **curve of binding energy**. From hydrogen up to about sodium it rises, because each added nucleon is attracted by more neighbours, with helium-4 and oxygen-16 as especially stable exceptions. From about mass 30 to about mass 90 it is nearly flat, and beyond that it falls gradually. The peak is at nickel-62, followed by iron-58 and iron-56, and the first view in the figure shows the seven nuclides whose values the sources give.

The shape comes from two forces that differ in range. The nuclear force pulls close neighbours together but acts over a very short distance, while the electric repulsion between protons dies away more slowly, so in a large nucleus every proton repels all the others and the repulsion outweighs what each added nucleon gains. An iron nucleus has 26 protons, and each of them repels the other 25, while the nuclear force reaches only the nearest neighbours.

afterFigure.text: The curve gives the direction of any nuclear change. A change that moves nuclei towards the peak raises their **binding energy per nucleon**, and the difference leaves as energy: light nuclei fuse to climb the left side, and heavy nuclei split to climb the right. A change that moves away from the peak absorbs energy, which is why splitting iron and fusing two similar nuclei heavier than iron both need energy put in. When several nuclei are involved the comparison uses the average, weighted by the number of nucleons in each.

diagram.alt: A graph of binding energy per nucleon against the number of nucleons. The first view plots the seven measured values, from deuterium at 1.11 MeV to nickel-62 at 8.79 MeV. The other two sketch the whole curve, which rises, is nearly flat from about mass 30 to 90 and falls slowly, and mark that fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both move towards the peak.

reveal.text: The two halves lie near the top of the curve, so splitting a nucleus of this size climbs it. This is the reasoning behind fission, which the next screen describes.

lead.text: **Fission** is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter ones, or occasionally three, with some free neutrons left over. It releases about 200 MeV for each fission, and the mass lost is about 0.1% of the mass of a uranium atom. The energy leaves as radiation and as the kinetic energy of the fragments, which in a nuclear reactor is captured as heat and used to make electricity.

**Fusion** joins light nuclei into a heavier one. In the Sun four protons combine into a helium nucleus, and two of them are converted to neutrons on the way. The nuclei repel one another, so the process needs a very hot gas in which they move fast enough to come within range of the nuclear force, and [[tunnelling|A particle crossing a barrier it lacks the energy to climb. Met in 'Quantum tunnelling'.]] helps them through the repulsion in a star's core. The Sun's own weight compresses and confines its core, which nothing on Earth can match, so physicists who work on fusion for power confine the hot gas with strong magnetic fields and use heavy forms of hydrogen as fuel.

afterFigure.text: In both processes the number of nucleons stays the same, and the energy comes from the small drop in mass.

lead.text: The energies of nuclear changes are large because the binding energy of a nucleus is large. The electron in a hydrogen atom has a binding energy of 13.6 eV, while the deuteron, the nucleus of one proton and one neutron, has a binding energy of 2.22452 MeV, about 160,000 times as large. Soon after the discovery of radioactivity it was noticed that radioactive energies are about a million times greater than those of any known molecular change, and in 1903 Rutherford and Soddy proposed that atoms hold a huge store of latent energy.

The same difference shows in the energy from each kilogram of fuel. Hydrogen fusing into helium loses about 0.8% of its mass, which releases 7.2 × 10¹⁴ J from each kilogram, and uranium fissioning loses about 0.1%, which releases 9.0 × 10¹³ J, so a kilogram of fusing hydrogen gives about eight times as much energy as a kilogram of fissioning uranium. Converting all of a kilogram of mass would release 8.99 × 10¹⁶ J.

lessons.orientation: Use mass defect and the shape of the binding energy curve to decide whether a nuclear change releases energy, and estimate the energy per kilogram of fuel.
lessons.nextAction: Decide for a given case whether classical physics is enough or whether relativity or quantum theory is needed, and judge a measurement against its prediction.

blocks.text: A helium atom is about 0.8% lighter than the four hydrogen atoms that could make it, and the missing mass, multiplied by c², is the energy that leaves when helium forms. A kilogram of hydrogen that becomes helium therefore loses 0.008 kg, which at 8.99 × 10¹⁶ joules for each kilogram of mass is about 7.2 × 10¹⁴ J, and the same reckoning applied to a heavy nucleus such as uranium gives a loss of about 0.1% of the atom's mass.

The bookkeeping also shows which changes cost energy: the binding energy of each nucleon peaks at nickel-62 and iron, so splitting iron or fusing two similar nuclei heavier than iron absorbs energy, where fusing light nuclei or splitting heavy ones releases it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a nuclear change releases or absorbs energy, and estimate the energy that a kilogram of fuel gives.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains where the energy of the Sun and of nuclear reactors comes from, and why it is about a million times larger than the energy of a chemical change.

recap.keyIdea: A nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons, the missing mass times c² is its binding energy, and any change that moves nuclei towards the peak of the curve at nickel-62 and iron releases energy.

blocks.text: The mass defect times $c^2$ is the binding energy, and the curve of binding energy per nucleon rises through the light nuclei, peaks at nickel-62 and iron and falls slowly beyond, so fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both climb towards the peak and release energy, while splitting iron or fusing two similar nuclei heavier than iron absorbs it. No nucleon is destroyed in any of these changes, and the energy comes from the small drop in mass.

Hydrogen fusing into helium loses about 0.8% of its mass and releases 7.2 × 10¹⁴ J from each kilogram, while uranium fission loses about 0.1% and releases 9.0 × 10¹³ J, so fusion gives about eight times as much per kilogram. Nuclear binding energies are about a million times those of atoms, which is why a nuclear change releases so much more energy than a chemical one.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson gathers the course's measurements and asks, for any given case, which physics it needs and how large the correction would be.

lessons.title: Choosing the right physics

reveal.text: The correction is about 560 times smaller than the uncertainty in the gravitational constant, so it could never show up in the result. The rest of the lesson uses the same comparison for relativity and for quantum effects.

lead.text: Relativity does not make classical physics wrong. The classical results are what relativity gives at low speed, and the two differ by an amount that grows with the square of the speed as a fraction of the speed of light. For kinetic energy the relativistic expression exceeds the classical one by a fraction of about $3v^2/4c^2$, and a moving clock is slowed by a fraction of about $\tfrac{1}{2}(v/c)^2$ of the elapsed time. At 68,600 m/s the first is 3.9 × 10⁻⁸, and at one tenth of the speed of light the second is 0.5%, the threshold at which time dilation may become important.

Whether a correction matters depends on what you need to know. A fractional correction of 3.9 × 10⁻⁸ is invisible beside an uncertainty of 2.2 × 10⁻⁵, a correction of 0.5% would be easily seen in a measurement good to 0.1%, and at 98% of the speed of light the lifetime of a muon changes by a factor of about five. The figure puts the first three of these sizes on one scale.

afterFigure.text: Classical physics therefore remains the right choice wherever the correction is smaller than the precision you need, and the rule has no fixed speed attached to it.

diagram.alt: A scale in powers of ten of the fraction by which classical physics is off. The Parker Solar Probe's kinetic energy correction, 3.9 × 10⁻⁸, lies far to the left, the uncertainty of the gravitational constant, 2.2 × 10⁻⁵, lies in the middle, and time dilation at one tenth of the speed of light, 5 × 10⁻³ or 0.5%, lies to the right.

lead.text: Quantum effects have a yardstick of their own in the uncertainty principle, which says that the spreads in an object's position and momentum satisfy $\Delta x \, \Delta p \geq \hbar/2$. An object confined to a region of size $\Delta x$ must therefore have a spread in speed of at least $\hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$. For an electron confined to 0.20 nm, about the size of an atom, that is 2.9 × 10⁵ m/s, roughly 0.1% of the speed of light, so quantum effects shape how an electron in an atom moves. For a baseball of mass 0.145 kg, an invented case, confined to 1 mm it is 3.6 × 10⁻³¹ m/s, far too small to measure.

The uncertainty principle applies to every object, and it is negligible at the scales of everyday life, so it becomes significant for microscopic objects or for instruments that measure so precisely that they reach the limit. A mirror of 100 kg observed for 2 ms in a gravitational wave detector cannot be located to better than about 6 × 10⁻²⁰ m. Tunnelling supplies a second yardstick in size, since electrons tunnel readily through insulating layers thinner than about 1 nm, and hydrogen's spectral lines are a third, since their explanation needed quantum theory.

lead.text: Speed is not the only thing that changes the rate of a clock. Gravity does too, and in **gravitational time dilation** a clock in weaker gravity runs faster, so that in theory a climber's clock at the top of a mountain runs slightly faster than a clock at sea level. For a clock in orbit the two effects pull in opposite directions, because the speed slows it and the weaker gravity at its height speeds it up, to a lesser degree.

The Global Positioning System depends on getting both right, and it can be seen as a continuously operating experiment in special and general relativity: the satellite clocks are adjusted for the two effects together, so that to an observer on the ground they keep the same time as ground clocks do. In 1971 Hafele and Keating tested the two effects together by flying caesium atomic clocks eastward and westward around the Earth in commercial airliners and comparing them with a clock that stayed at the U.S. Naval Observatory. The figure shows the predicted and measured change in the flying clocks' reading for each flight, with the uncertainty of each as a bar.

afterFigure.text: In both flights the bar of the prediction and the bar of the measurement overlap, but overlap alone is not the test, and the next two screens set out a better one.

diagram.alt: Two number lines showing the change in the flying clocks' reading in nanoseconds. For the eastward flight the prediction is a loss of 40 plus or minus 23 and the measurement is a loss of 59 plus or minus 10. For the westward flight the prediction is a gain of 275 plus or minus 21 and the measurement is a gain of 273 plus or minus 7.
diagram.caption: Hafele and Keating's predictions and measurements, each with its uncertainty as a bar. The bars on the measurements are standard deviations.

steps.headline: On the eastward flight the theory predicted a loss of 40 ± 23 ns, and the flying clocks lost 59 ± 10 ns. Do the measurement and the prediction agree?

workedSteps.text: Find the gap between the two values.
Two independent uncertainties combine by adding their squares and taking the square root.
Set the gap beside the combined uncertainty.
The gap is smaller than the combined uncertainty, so the measurement is consistent with the prediction. A gap of 19 ns looks like a discrepancy until it is set beside uncertainties of this size.

steps.headline: On the westward flight the theory predicted a gain of 275 ± 21 ns, and the flying clocks gained 273 ± 7 ns. Do the measurement and the prediction agree?

workedSteps.text: Find the gap between the two values.
Combine the two uncertainties by adding their squares and taking the square root.

The gap of 2 ns is far inside the combined uncertainty, so the westward result agrees with the prediction too. In 2005 the National Physical Laboratory repeated the experiment on a shorter trip with more accurate clocks, and its results agreed with relativity to within 4%, which was inside the uncertainty of its measurements.

lead.text: The Bohr model reproduced hydrogen's spectral lines and gave way to a better theory in the 1920s. In 1925 Werner Heisenberg proposed a new kind of mechanics in a paper that Max Born and Pascual Jordan extended into matrix mechanics, and Wolfgang Pauli used it that year to solve the hydrogen atom. In 1926 Erwin Schrödinger, working independently and from de Broglie's matter waves, developed wave mechanics, whose atomic orbitals are the current picture of the atom. In that picture the electron in hydrogen forms a spherical cloud of probability, densest close to the nucleus, in place of an orbit.

The Bohr model still gives almost exact results for systems of just two charged bodies circling one another far more slowly than light, such as hydrogen, singly ionised helium and doubly ionised lithium, and it fails for neutral helium and for atoms with several electrons. The sources used for this course go no further than this, and the relativistic quantum theories that the tunnelling article names, the Dirac equation and quantum field theory, lie outside it.

reveal.text: Weaker gravity makes a clock run faster, so the mountain clock gains slightly. The effect for a mountain is tiny, and it is the same one that GPS clocks have to be corrected for.

lessons.orientation: Decide for a given case whether classical physics is enough or whether relativity or quantum theory is needed, using the size of the correction, and say what replaced the Bohr model.
lessons.nextAction: You can now say which physics a case needs from the size of its correction, and judge a measurement against its prediction.

blocks.text: The Parker Solar Probe reached 68,600 m/s in 2018, faster than any spacecraft before it, and the correction that relativity makes to its kinetic energy is about 3.9 × 10⁻⁸, four parts in a hundred million. That is far smaller than the relative uncertainty of 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ with which the gravitational constant is known, so for the probe's energy the classical formula is as accurate as the other numbers in the calculation allow.

A cosmic-ray muon is in the opposite position when it moves at 98% of the speed of light, since its lifetime is then about five times the 2.197 μs of a muon at rest, a result that classical physics does not predict at all. Choosing the right physics for a case comes down to estimating how large the correction would be and setting it against the precision you need.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which physics a case needs from the size of its correction, and judge whether a measurement agrees with its prediction.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you decide when the simple formula is good enough and when a case needs relativity or quantum theory.

recap.keyIdea: Classical physics stays accurate wherever the relativistic or quantum correction is smaller than the precision you need, and a measurement agrees with a prediction when their gap is smaller than their combined uncertainty.

blocks.text: The corrections can be sized: about 0.5% for time dilation at one tenth of the speed of light, 3.9 × 10⁻⁸ for the Parker Solar Probe's kinetic energy, and a spread in speed of about 3 × 10⁵ m/s for an electron confined to 0.20 nm. A case needs the new physics when its correction exceeds the precision that matters, which is why the probe's energy can be found classically while muon lifetimes, GPS clocks, hydrogen's spectral lines, leakage through a 1 nm layer and a 100 kg mirror at its limit cannot.

Speed and gravity change a clock's rate in opposite directions, and GPS clocks are corrected for both. Hafele and Keating's flights agree with theory because each gap, 19 ns and 2 ns, is smaller than its combined uncertainty, 25 ns and 22 ns. In 1925 and 1926 matrix mechanics and wave mechanics replaced the Bohr model with a picture in which the electron is a cloud of probability.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. Any new case can be treated in the same way, by estimating how large the correction would be and setting it against the precision of the measurement.

questions.prompt: A muon lives 2.197 microseconds at rest. Using ordinary physics, roughly how far does a muon travel in one lifetime when it moves at 98% of $c$, where $c = 299{,}792{,}458$ m/s?
hints: Convert the lifetime to seconds first: a microsecond is a millionth of a second.
Distance is speed times time, and 98% of the speed of light is a little under $3\times10^{8}$ m/s.

acceptedIdeas: About 650 metres

questions.onCorrect: The distance is $0.98 \times 299{,}792{,}458 \times 2.197\times10^{-6}$, about 645 m. Even light would cover only 659 m in that time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ten times too small. A microsecond is a millionth of a second, and $0.98 \times 3\times10^{8}$ m/s over $2.2\times10^{-6}$ s comes to several hundred metres.
That is ten times too large. Check the power of ten in the lifetime: 2.197 microseconds is $2.197\times10^{-6}$ s, not $10^{-5}$ s.

questions.prompt: A light clock moves past you at 0.8 c. By what factor is each of its ticks longer than when the clock was at rest? Give the factor to two decimal places.
hints: Work out $v^2/c^2$ for $v = 0.8c$.
Take that away from 1 and take the square root.
A moving clock's tick is longer than the tick at rest, so the factor you want is greater than 1.
questions.onCorrect: The triangle's sides are in the ratio 0.8 : 0.6 : 1, so $L$ is 0.6 of the slanted path and a tick lasts $1/0.6 = 1.67$ times as long.

misconceptions.feedback: That is $\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$, the number you divide by. A moving clock's tick is longer, so the factor is its reciprocal.
That is only $v/c$. The factor comes from $1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$.
Adding $v/c$ to 1 is not what the triangle gives. Work out $1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$.

items.explanation: The factor $\gamma$ is 1.021, so a tick lasts 2.1% longer.

questions.onCorrect: A tick is lengthened by the fraction $\gamma - 1$, and that passes 0.5% at about 0.1 c. The first three cases are far below that speed.

questions.prompt: Which reading is the proper time between the muon's creation and its decay?
hints: Proper time needs a single clock that is at the creation and also at the decay.
Which of the three clocks travels from one event to the other?

acceptedIdeas: The reading of the clock riding with the muon, because it is present at both events
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reading of the clock riding with the muon, because it is present at both events

choices.label: The difference between the two ground clocks, because clocks at rest are the reliable ones
None of them, because observers disagree and the interval has no agreed value
The reading of the clock riding with the muon, because it is present at both events

questions.onCorrect: The clock that travels with the muon is present at both events, so every observer agrees on its reading, and the ground's longer interval is $\gamma$ times that.

misconceptions.feedback: The two ground clocks are at different places, so neither is present at both events. Their difference is the time the ground measures, which is $\gamma$ times the proper time.
The clock present at both events gives a reading that every observer agrees on, and that is what proper time means. What observers disagree about is the time measured with separate clocks.

questions.prompt: Why is the proper time multiplied by $\gamma$ here, and not divided by it?
hints: Is the muon's clock measured by the ground to run fast or slow?
A slow clock needs more ground time to show the same reading.

acceptedIdeas: The ground measures the muon's clock to run slow, so its interval comes out longer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ground measures the muon's clock to run slow, so its interval comes out longer

choices.label: The ground measures the muon's clock to run slow, so its interval comes out longer
The muon gains energy at high speed, and the extra energy makes it live longer
A moving clock ticks faster, so more proper time passes on the ground per tick

questions.onCorrect: A moving clock is measured to run slow, so the ground's interval between the same two events is longer than the proper time by $\gamma$.

misconceptions.feedback: The muon at 0.98 c is the same particle, and its own clock still reads 2.197 microseconds. The lengthening is how a moving clock is measured by an observer who sees it go past.
A moving clock is measured to tick more slowly, not faster. Fewer of its ticks fit into each ground second, so the same number of ticks takes longer on the ground.

questions.prompt: With $v/c = 2.568\times10^{-5}$, use $\gamma - 1 \approx \tfrac12 (v/c)^2$ to find $\gamma - 1$. Give it as a number in scientific notation, such as 4.1e-9.
hints: Square $2.568\times10^{-5}$: multiply 2.568 by itself and double the power of ten.
Halve the result.
The answer is a few parts in ten thousand million, so its power of ten is $-10$.
questions.onCorrect: The excess is $3.30\times10^{-10}$, which is why a calculator would show $\gamma$ as exactly 1 here.

misconceptions.feedback: That is $v/c$ itself. The excess is half its square.

questions.prompt: The clock falls behind by the fraction $\gamma - 1 = 3.30\times10^{-10}$ of the time elapsed. How far behind is it after $1.58\times10^{7}$ seconds, in milliseconds?
hints: Multiply the fraction by the time elapsed, in seconds.
The product comes out in seconds.
A millisecond is a thousandth of a second, so there are a thousand milliseconds in each second.
questions.onCorrect: A lag of 5.2 milliseconds agrees with the figure of about 5 milliseconds reported for six months on the Station.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the lag in seconds. The question asks for milliseconds.

questions.prompt: A reader says time dilation applies only to light clocks, so the Station astronaut's wristwatch and body would keep Earth time. Which reply fits the evidence?
hints: Ask what a light clock and an atomic clock have in common at rest.
Which of the three replies points to a measurement made with a clock that is not a light clock?

acceptedIdeas: Clocks that agree at rest agree in motion, and flown atomic clocks showed it, so all slow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Clocks that agree at rest agree in motion, and flown atomic clocks showed it, so all slow

choices.label: The watch could differ from a light clock, but a body cannot, so only the body slows
Clocks that agree at rest agree in motion, and flown atomic clocks showed it, so all slow
Only light clocks slow, since the derivation uses light, so the 5 ms is an instrument effect

questions.onCorrect: Any clock that keeps step with a light clock at rest keeps step with it in motion, and atomic clocks flown in aircraft confirmed it, so every kind of clock slows.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the argument separates a watch from a body. If clocks that agree at rest could disagree in motion, the argument would fail for the watch as well.
The light clock is a device for the derivation. The atomic clocks that Hafele and Keating flew in 1971 were not light clocks, and they showed the effect too.

questions.prompt: Muons made in an accelerator move at 0.995 c in the laboratory (a made-up setup). A muon at rest lasts 2.197 microseconds. How long does one last as measured in the laboratory, in microseconds?
hints: Find $\gamma$ for 0.995 c first, starting from $1 - 0.995^2$.
Take the square root of that and then its reciprocal.
The laboratory measures the longer time, so multiply the lifetime at rest by $\gamma$.
questions.onCorrect: The laboratory measures $\gamma \times 2.197 = 22.0$ microseconds, about ten times the lifetime at rest.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing by $\gamma$ would give a time shorter than the lifetime at rest. A moving clock's interval is longer.
That is $\gamma$ itself. Multiply it by the lifetime at rest.

questions.prompt: At rest these muons last 2.197 microseconds, so time dilation predicts $29.327 \times 2.197 = 64.43$ microseconds, which is 0.05 microseconds more than the measured lifetime. What does the comparison show?
hints: Work out the gap as a fraction of the predicted lifetime.
The lifetime was stretched about thirtyfold. Is a gap of that size large or small next to the stretching?

acceptedIdeas: They agree to within one part in a thousand, so the data support time dilation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They agree to within one part in a thousand, so the data support time dilation

extracts.text: For instance, in the muon storage ring at CERN the lifetime of muons circulating with γ = 29.327 was found to be dilated to 64.378 μs, confirming time dilation to an accuracy of 0.9 ± 0.4 parts per thousand.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia summary of a muon storage-ring measurement at CERN

choices.label: They agree to within one part in a thousand, so the data support time dilation
The 0.05 microsecond gap shows that time dilation holds only roughly, not exactly
The lengthening comes from the ring's magnetic field and not from the muons' speed

questions.onCorrect: The gap is 0.053 of 64.4 microseconds, about 0.8 parts per thousand, which is the accuracy of 0.9 plus or minus 0.4 parts per thousand that the experiment reports.

misconceptions.feedback: The gap is 0.8 parts in a thousand of a lifetime that was stretched about thirtyfold, which is the accuracy the extract quotes. Any measurement has some gap, and it has to be compared with the size of the effect and the stated accuracy.
Muons moving at 98% of c in the atmosphere, with no ring involved, last about five times longer too. The stretching follows the speed.

questions.prompt: A clock is measured to run 0.5% slow, so that $\gamma = 1.005$. What fraction of the speed of light is it moving at, to two decimal places?
hints: Rearrange $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$ to give $v^2/c^2 = 1 - 1/\gamma^2$.
Work out $1/\gamma^2$ for $\gamma = 1.005$ and take it from 1.
The expansion $\gamma - 1 \approx \tfrac12 (v/c)^2$ gives the same answer more quickly.
questions.onCorrect: The clock moves at about 0.10 c, 30,000 km/s, which is where the rule of thumb puts the threshold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the excess of $\gamma$ over 1, not the speed. The excess is half of $(v/c)^2$.

questions.prompt: A passenger sits at the middle of a carriage and sees the flash from the bolt at the front before the flash from the bolt at the back. In the passenger's own frame the two ends are equal distances away, and light has the same speed in both directions. What must the passenger conclude about the bolts?
hints: How long does each flash take to reach the passenger, if the distances are equal and the speed is the same?
If the journeys take equal times, what does the order of arrival say about the order of the strikes?

acceptedIdeas: The front bolt struck first, since both flashes crossed the same distance at the same speed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The front bolt struck first, since both flashes crossed the same distance at the same speed

choices.label: The bolts struck together, because motion toward the front shortens the journey of that flash
The front bolt struck first, since both flashes crossed the same distance at the same speed
No conclusion is possible, because the arrival times depend on where the passenger sits

questions.onCorrect: Equal journeys make the arrival order the strike order, so the passenger finds the front bolt first, while the platform observer finds the two bolts simultaneous.

misconceptions.feedback: The passenger is at the middle of a carriage that is at rest for them, so both flashes have the same distance to cover at the same speed. Their journeys take equal times, and a head start from motion has nothing to act on.
Both ends are equal distances away and light has one speed, so the travel times are equal and can be allowed for. That leaves the arrival order as the order of the strikes.

questions.prompt: What does the midpoint rule assume about the signal?
hints: The rule sets clock 2 to the halfway time of the round trip. When is that the right time?
Which assumption makes the outward trip exactly half of the round trip?

acceptedIdeas: That it takes as long out as back, so light has the same speed both ways
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That it takes as long out as back, so light has the same speed both ways

choices.label: That it takes as long out as back, so light has the same speed both ways
That clock 2 already runs at the same rate as clock 1, so its reading can be copied
That the signal arrives instantly, so no allowance for its journey is needed

questions.onCorrect: Halfway is right only if the outward and return journeys take equal times, which no measurement at one place can check, so it is adopted as a convention.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal running rates are needed for any comparison of clocks, but the midpoint rule is about the signal: it sets clock 2 to the halfway time of the round trip.
The rule allows for the journey by using half of the round-trip time. If the signal were instant, there would be nothing to allow for.

questions.prompt: One train moves east and its passenger finds the east bolt struck first. A second train moves west at the same speed, and the same two bolts, simultaneous on the platform, strike the ends of its carriage. Which bolt does a passenger at the middle of the second carriage find first?
hints: Which of the two bolts lies ahead of the second train's motion?
An observer moving along the line joining two simultaneous events finds the one ahead of the motion earlier.

acceptedIdeas: The west bolt, since it lies ahead of this train's motion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The west bolt, since it lies ahead of this train's motion

choices.label: The east bolt, because it struck first for the other train
Neither, because the platform found them simultaneous
The west bolt, since it lies ahead of this train's motion

questions.onCorrect: Events ahead of the motion are found earlier, so reversing the train's direction reverses the order the passenger finds.

misconceptions.feedback: Which bolt comes first depends on the observer's motion. The second train moves the other way, so the order reverses.
Simultaneity on the platform does not carry over to a train moving along the line between the bolts.

questions.prompt: Two flashes go off at the same instant on the platform, on opposite sides of the track and directly across from each other. A train passes along the track at a steady speed. What do the passengers find?
hints: Along the track, how far apart are the two flashes?
Which separation decides how a moving observer's times for two events differ?

acceptedIdeas: They are simultaneous for the passengers too, since the motion is across the line joining them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are simultaneous for the passengers too, since the motion is across the line joining them

choices.label: They are simultaneous for the passengers too, since the motion is across the line joining them
One flash comes first, since motion always breaks simultaneity for events at different places
They are simultaneous only if the train is slow, since the effect grows with the train's speed

questions.onCorrect: Only separation along the direction of motion shifts the times, and these flashes have none, so they stay simultaneous for the passengers at every speed.
