misconceptions.feedback: Only separation along the direction of motion shifts the times. These two flashes have no separation along the track, so nothing shifts one relative to the other.
With no separation along the motion, there is nothing for the speed to act on, so the flashes stay simultaneous at every speed.

questions.prompt: Why does the calculation use only the term with $v\,\Delta x/c^2$, and leave out any time difference on the platform?
hints: What does the platform say about the times of the two strikes?
Which part of $t' = \gamma(t - vx/c^2)$ is the same for both strikes?

acceptedIdeas: The strikes are simultaneous on the platform, so only the $vx/c^2$ term shifts their times
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The strikes are simultaneous on the platform, so only the $vx/c^2$ term shifts their times

choices.label: The platform's clocks are stopped, so they contribute no time difference
The strikes are simultaneous on the platform, so only the $vx/c^2$ term shifts their times
The train's clocks are the ones that find the strikes simultaneous, so the platform has no gap

questions.onCorrect: Equal platform times make the first term of the difference zero, which leaves the term in $vx/c^2$ to carry the whole gap.

misconceptions.feedback: The platform clocks run normally. They show equal readings at the two strikes because the strikes are simultaneous in the platform's frame.
It is the platform that finds the strikes simultaneous. The train's clocks are the ones that show a gap.

questions.prompt: Put $v = 0.5c$, $\gamma = 1.155$ and $\Delta x = 200$ m into $\gamma v\,\Delta x/c^2$. What is the size of the gap, in nanoseconds?
hints: Write $v = 0.5c$, so that $v/c^2$ becomes $0.5/c$.
Multiply $1.155 \times 0.5 \times 200$ to get a length in metres.
Divide that length by the speed of light for a time in seconds, and convert to nanoseconds.
questions.onCorrect: The gap is 385 nanoseconds. Light would need 667 nanoseconds to cross the 200 metres between the strikes.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the factor $\gamma$. The time term of the Lorentz transformation carries it.

questions.prompt: In the train's frame, which strike is found first?
hints: Which strike has the larger value of $x$, in the direction the train moves?
A negative $\Delta t'$ means the event with the larger $x$ has the smaller time.

acceptedIdeas: The front strike, as it lies ahead of the train's motion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The front strike, as it lies ahead of the train's motion

choices.label: The back strike, because it lies behind the train's motion
The front strike, as it lies ahead of the train's motion
Neither, because the strikes stay simultaneous

questions.onCorrect: The front strike has the larger $x$ and so the earlier time, the same ordering as for the carriage bolts.

misconceptions.feedback: The minus sign in $-\gamma v\,\Delta x/c^2$ gives the earlier time to the event with the larger $x$, which is the one ahead of the motion.
The calculation gave a gap of 385 nanoseconds, so the strikes are not simultaneous in the train's frame.

questions.prompt: Two spaceships pass each other at a steady speed, and each crew measures the other's clock to run slow by the same factor. Which statement is correct?
hints: Each crew uses its own synchronised clocks to measure the other's clock. Do the two crews agree about which of those clocks are in step?
Relative motion is symmetric, and so is the measurement each crew makes of the other.

acceptedIdeas: Both are right: each compares the other's clock with two of their own that the other calls out of step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both are right: each compares the other's clock with two of their own that the other calls out of step

choices.label: One crew must be wrong, and a comparison of clocks when the ships meet again would show which one
Both are right: each compares the other's clock with two of their own that the other calls out of step
Neither is right, because the delay of light distorts what each crew sees of the other's clock

questions.onCorrect: Each crew's measurement is correct in its own frame, because the two crews disagree about which of their separated clocks read the same time.

misconceptions.feedback: Ships passing at a steady speed meet only once, so no comparison can show which crew was wrong. If one ship turns round, the situation changes, as in the twin case.
Each crew assigns times after allowing for the delay of light, so the delay is not the cause of the slowing each measures.

questions.prompt: Ship A coasts at a steady speed throughout. Ship B passes A, travels on at a steady speed for a while, then turns round and returns to meet A again. Each ship carries a clock that was set to zero when they first passed. Which clock shows less elapsed time when they meet?
hints: Which ship stays in one frame for the whole trip?
The symmetry between two observers holds while both move at steady speeds.

acceptedIdeas: The clock on B, because B changes frames to turn round and A does not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The clock on B, because B changes frames to turn round and A does not

choices.label: The clock on A, because B measures A's clock to run slow on the way back
The two show the same, because each ship measured the other's clock to run slow
The clock on B, because B changes frames to turn round and A does not

questions.onCorrect: The ship that turns round changes frames, which breaks the symmetry, so its clock shows the shorter time.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses only B's measurements, as though B stayed in one frame. B changes frame at the turn, so its measurements on the way out and on the way back do not combine into a single account.
The symmetry holds only for steady motion. Here B turns round, so the two ships are not in the same situation.

questions.prompt: Two lightning strikes are simultaneous on the platform and 90 m apart along the track. A train passes at 0.8 c. How many nanoseconds separate the strikes in the train's frame?
hints: Find $\gamma$ for 0.8 c first.
Multiply $\gamma \times 0.8 \times 90$ to get a length in metres.
Divide by the speed of light to get seconds, then convert to nanoseconds.
questions.onCorrect: The strikes are 400 nanoseconds apart in the train's frame, and the one ahead of the train's motion comes first.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the factor $\gamma$. At 0.8 c it is not close to 1.

questions.prompt: Sort each quantity by whether every observer agrees on it or whether it depends on the observer's frame.
hints: A quantity every observer agrees on cannot change when the observer's motion changes.
Ask whether a single clock present at both events is enough, or whether the measurement needs separated clocks.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Same for every observer: the speed of light and a clock's own reading between two events it is present at. Depends on the frame: simultaneity, the time between the carriage bolts, a passing clock's apparent rate and the time between separated clocks.

items.label: The speed of light in vacuum
items.explanation: Light has the same speed for every observer, which is what the whole argument rests on.

items.label: Whether two flashes at different places on the track are simultaneous
items.explanation: Observers in relative motion along the track assign them different times.

items.label: A clock's own reading between two events at both of which it is present
items.explanation: This is the proper time, and every observer agrees on what that clock shows.

items.label: The time between two bolts that strike the ends of a carriage
items.explanation: The platform finds no gap and the train finds a gap of hundreds of nanoseconds.

items.label: How slowly a passing clock appears to tick
items.explanation: It depends on the relative speed, and each of two observers measures the other's clock slow.

items.label: The time between two events measured with two separate synchronised clocks
items.explanation: Each frame uses its own synchronised clocks, and different frames assign different times.

questions.onCorrect: Only the speed of light and a single clock's own reading are agreed by all. Anything that needs separated clocks to be set to agree depends on the frame.

questions.prompt: Two flares go off at the same instant in the Sun's frame, one near Earth and one near Mars, on the line joining them. A ship passes from Mars toward Earth at 0.8 c along that line. In the ship's frame, which flare goes off first?
hints: Which flare lies ahead of the ship's motion?
For events that are simultaneous in one frame, the moving observer finds the one ahead of the motion earlier.

acceptedIdeas: The flare near Earth, because it lies ahead of the ship's motion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The flare near Earth, because it lies ahead of the ship's motion

choices.label: The flare near Mars, because the ship is leaving it behind
Neither, because the two flares went off together in the Sun's frame
The flare near Earth, because it lies ahead of the ship's motion

questions.onCorrect: The ship moves toward Earth, so the Earth flare lies ahead of its motion and is found earlier, with a gap of $\gamma v\,\Delta x/c^2$.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the rule. The flare ahead of the ship's motion is found earlier, and the ship moves toward Earth.
Simultaneity in the Sun's frame does not carry over to a ship moving along the line between the flares.

questions.prompt: In the muon's own frame the muon lasts 2.197 microseconds, while the ground approaches at 0.98 c. Using ordinary physics, how far does the ground move past the muon in that time, in metres?
hints: Distance is speed times time, and the speed here is 0.98 of the speed of light.
A microsecond is a millionth of a second, so convert the lifetime to seconds first.
Multiply 0.98 by 299,792,458 m/s and then by the lifetime in seconds.
questions.onCorrect: The ground moves about 645 m, so by ordinary reasoning the muon could meet at most a 645 m layer of air in its own frame.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full speed of light. The ground approaches at 0.98 of it.
That is the distance in kilometres. The question asks for metres.

questions.prompt: The ship's crew say that the station's length measurement must be wrong, because its two marks on the ship were not made at the same time. Which reply is best?
hints: Which observers say that the two marks were made at the same time, and which do not?
Does either frame have a better claim to say what 'at the same time' means for two separated marks?

acceptedIdeas: Both are correct in their own frames, because the frames disagree about which marks were simultaneous
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both are correct in their own frames, because the frames disagree about which marks were simultaneous

choices.label: The crew are right, because a ship's own length is the only real one and the station's value is an illusion
Both are correct in their own frames, because the frames disagree about which marks were simultaneous
The station is right, because light from the far end reaches the crew late and misleads them

questions.onCorrect: The station marks both ends at one time by its own clocks, the crew disagree about that, and each measurement is right in its own frame.

misconceptions.feedback: The station's number is a genuine measurement, made with its own synchronised clocks. It differs from the crew's because the two frames measure different things.
Both frames allow for the travel of light when they assign times and positions. The disagreement is about simultaneity itself, not about delay.

questions.prompt: Why is the proper length divided by $\gamma$ here?
hints: Which observer measures the greatest length: the crew moving with the ship or the station?
Is the station's value larger or smaller than the proper length?

acceptedIdeas: The proper length is the greatest any observer measures, so any moving observer's value is smaller
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The proper length is the greatest any observer measures, so any moving observer's value is smaller

choices.label: The proper length is the greatest any observer measures, so any moving observer's value is smaller
A ship loses some of its material when it moves at high speed, so less of it is left to measure
Times are stretched by $\gamma$, so every length and every other quantity is stretched by it too

questions.onCorrect: Every other observer measures a smaller value, and the factor that gives it is $1/\gamma$.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing is lost from the ship, and its crew still measure 100 m. The shortening is how a different frame measures the same ship.
Times along the motion stretch, but lengths along the motion shrink. The clock argument gave $L = vT_0$ with $T_0 = T/\gamma$, so $\gamma$ divides.

questions.prompt: A square plate 1.00 m on each side at rest moves at 0.8 c along the direction of one of its edges. What shape does a station measure?
hints: Which of the plate's two directions lies along the motion?
Only a length along the motion is multiplied by $1/\gamma$, which is 0.6 at 0.8 c.

acceptedIdeas: A rectangle 0.60 m along the motion and 1.00 m across it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A rectangle 0.60 m along the motion and 1.00 m across it

choices.label: A square of side 0.60 m, shortened in both directions
A rectangle 1.00 m along the motion and 0.60 m across it
A rectangle 0.60 m along the motion and 1.00 m across it

questions.onCorrect: Only the dimension along the motion shortens, so the station measures a rectangle 0.60 m by 1.00 m.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the direction of the motion is shortened. The width across the motion is unchanged.
That reverses the directions. The shortening acts along the motion and leaves the width alone.

questions.prompt: Observer S′ moves past a rod at rest in frame S and measures it as 0.8 of its rest length. A second rod of the same rest length lies at rest in S′. What does an observer in S measure for it?
hints: Is the frame S at rest in any absolute sense, so that it is special?
Apply the same formula with the roles of S and S′ swapped.

acceptedIdeas: 0.8 of its rest length, because the effect is symmetric
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0.8 of its rest length, because the effect is symmetric

choices.label: 0.8 of its rest length, because the effect is symmetric
1.25 times its rest length, to balance the first result
Its full rest length, because only one frame can see contraction

questions.onCorrect: Each frame measures the other's rods contracted by the same factor, so S finds the second rod 0.8 of its rest length.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the formula lengthens a moving rod. Each frame finds the other's rods shorter, and the two results do not need to balance.
No frame is privileged. The principle of relativity requires the contraction to be the same in both directions of comparison.

questions.prompt: In the ground frame a layer of air is 4.0 km thick (a made-up thickness), and a muon moves through it at 0.99 c. In the muon's own frame, how long does the layer take to pass, in microseconds?
hints: In the muon's frame the layer is contracted. Find $\gamma$ for 0.99 c first.
Divide the 4.0 km by $\gamma$ to get the contracted thickness.
The layer passes at 0.99 c, so divide the contracted thickness by that speed.
questions.onCorrect: The muon's frame finds the layer 564 m thick and crossed in 1.90 microseconds, which is less than the 2.197 microseconds the muon lasts, so it arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by $\gamma$ instead of dividing. In the muon's frame the layer is shorter, not longer.
That uses the uncontracted 4.0 km. In the muon's frame the layer is contracted.

questions.prompt: A student photographs a sphere passing at 0.9 c with a very short exposure, and expects an ellipse flattened along the direction of motion. What will the photograph show?
hints: A photograph records light that arrives together. Did that light leave every part of the sphere at the same moment?
Contraction concerns where the ends are at one moment. Is a photograph a measurement of that?

acceptedIdeas: A circular outline that looks rotated, since light from different parts left at different times
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A circular outline that looks rotated, since light from different parts left at different times

choices.label: A flattened ellipse, because the sphere is contracted along its direction of motion in the station's frame
An unchanged circle, because fast-moving objects look the same as stationary ones in a photograph
A circular outline that looks rotated, since light from different parts left at different times

questions.onCorrect: A passing sphere keeps a circular outline and looks rotated, a result known as Penrose-Terrell rotation.

misconceptions.feedback: The contraction is a statement about the simultaneous positions of the ends. A photograph records light that left different parts at different times, which is a different measurement.
There is a visible effect: because the light left different parts at different times, the sphere appears rotated.

questions.prompt: A rocket is 80.0 m long at rest. A station measures it as it passes at 0.90 c. What length does the station measure, in metres?
hints: Find $\gamma$ for 0.90 c first.
The station measures a shorter length, so divide the proper length by $\gamma$.
Check that your result is smaller than 80.0 m.
questions.onCorrect: The station measures 34.9 m, a little under half the rest length, since $1/\gamma = 0.436$ at 0.9 c.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by $\gamma$. A moving length is shorter than the proper length.
That multiplies by $v/c$. The factor is $1/\gamma = \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$.

questions.prompt: In 1911 Einstein was asked whether length contraction is real. According to his answer, who can find it?
hints: Read the two halves of the sentence: for which observer does the contraction not exist, and for which can it be shown?
Is 'demonstrated by physical means' the language of an artefact or of a measurement?

acceptedIdeas: An observer who moves relative to the object, not one who moves with it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An observer who moves relative to the object, not one who moves with it

extracts.text: It doesn't "really" exist, in so far as it doesn't exist for a comoving observer; though it "really" exists, i.e. in such a way that it could be demonstrated in principle by physical means by a non-comoving observer.
extracts.who: Albert Einstein, replying to Vladimir Varićak, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Length contraction' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: A published reply on whether length contraction is real

choices.label: Every observer, including the crew who move along with the object itself
An observer who moves relative to the object, not one who moves with it
No one, because it is only an artefact of the way the clocks are set

questions.onCorrect: Contraction is found by an observer for whom the object moves, and the object's own frame finds none, which matches the symmetry of the effect.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage says it does not exist for an observer moving with the object, so the crew of the object find nothing.
The passage says it could be demonstrated by physical means by an observer who is not moving with the object, so it is more than a convention.

questions.prompt: A student notes that the ground frame explains the muon's arrival by time dilation and the muon's frame explains it by contraction of the atmosphere, and concludes that only one account can be right. Which reply is best?
hints: Do the two frames reach different conclusions about whether the muon arrives?
Is either of the two frames privileged over the other?

acceptedIdeas: Both accounts are correct, each in its own frame, and they agree that the muon arrives
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both accounts are correct, each in its own frame, and they agree that the muon arrives

choices.label: Both effects act in each frame, so the muon's survival is the product of the two
The ground frame is the right one, because the muon's frame is moving and so does not count
Both accounts are correct, each in its own frame, and they agree that the muon arrives

questions.onCorrect: Each frame gives its own reason, time dilation or contraction, and the two reasons give the same outcome for every event both can check.

misconceptions.feedback: In each frame only one of the effects does the work. Using both in one frame counts the same physics twice and gives a wrong answer.
Both frames move at steady speeds relative to each other, and neither has a claim to be the valid one.

questions.prompt: In $E = mc^2$, with $c$ about $3\times10^{8}$ m/s, roughly how much energy corresponds to 1 kg of mass?
hints: The energy is the mass times $c^2$, so square the speed first.
Square $3\times10^{8}$ by squaring 3 and doubling the power of ten.

acceptedIdeas: About 9 × 10¹⁶ J
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 9 × 10¹⁶ J

choices.label: About 3 × 10⁸ J
About 9 × 10¹⁶ J
About 4.5 × 10¹⁶ J

questions.onCorrect: The rest energy of a kilogram is $c^2$ times 1 kg, about $9\times10^{16}$ J, which is more than 21 megatons of TNT.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the square. The factor is $c^2$, which is about $9\times10^{16}$ in joules per kilogram, not $c$ itself.
That is $\tfrac12 mc^2$, the shape of a kinetic energy. The rest energy is the whole of $mc^2$.

questions.prompt: Why does a mass of only 1 g correspond to so much energy?
hints: Compare the number $c^2$, in m²/s², with the number 1, which is what a conversion between mass and energy would be without relativity.
Does the gram need to be moving for its rest energy to exist?

acceptedIdeas: Because $c^2$ is so large that each kilogram corresponds to about $9\times10^{16}$ J
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because $c^2$ is so large that each kilogram corresponds to about $9\times10^{16}$ J

choices.label: Because $c^2$ is so large that each kilogram corresponds to about $9\times10^{16}$ J
Because the gram has been accelerated to a speed near $c$, which multiplies its energy
Because energy and mass are measured in different units, so the numbers cannot be compared

questions.onCorrect: The conversion factor $c^2$ is about $9\times10^{16}$ J per kilogram, so even a gram corresponds to $9\times10^{13}$ J.

misconceptions.feedback: Rest energy belongs to a body at rest. The gram does not need to move at all for $mc^2$ to apply.
Multiplying a mass in kilograms by $c^2$ in m²/s² gives joules directly, so the two can be compared exactly.

questions.prompt: How does the balance reading change from before the explosion to after it?
hints: Has any energy crossed the walls of the chamber?
Does a balance respond to the energy inside the system or only to the energy that crosses its boundary?

acceptedIdeas: It does not change, because the heat and light stay in the chamber and keep their mass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It does not change, because the heat and light stay in the chamber and keep their mass

choices.label: It falls by the energy released divided by c², since the dynamite gives that energy up
It rises, because the hot gas and light are heavier than the solid dynamite was
It does not change, because the heat and light stay in the chamber and keep their mass

questions.onCorrect: The heat, sound and light stay in the chamber and keep their mass, so the total mass on the balance is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: The energy released stays inside the sealed, insulated chamber, so nothing has left the system. A balance sees only what is on it.
Nothing has been added to the chamber, so there is no extra mass to find. The energy that was stored in the dynamite changes form and stays where it was.

questions.prompt: Sort each change by whether the system's mass increases or decreases, once any energy that is released has left the system.
hints: Energy added to a system adds mass to it.
Energy that leaves the system takes its mass with it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mass increases: the compressed spring, the warmed standard and the spinning ball. Mass decreases: water forming with its heat leaving, and the fissioning device with its energy leaving.

items.label: A spring is compressed
items.explanation: The stored energy adds mass, so the spring is heavier while it is compressed.

items.label: Water forms from hydrogen and oxygen, and the heat leaves
items.explanation: The heat that is given off takes its mass with it, so the molecule is slightly lighter than the atoms it is made from.

items.label: A metal mass standard is warmed by 1 degree Celsius
items.explanation: The added thermal energy adds mass, 1.5 picograms for a 1 kg standard.

items.label: A plutonium device fissions, and the energy leaves
items.explanation: The radiation and kinetic energy that leave carry away about a gram for a yield of 21 kilotons.

items.label: A ball is set spinning
items.explanation: The energy of rotation adds mass, so a spinning ball is a little heavier than the same ball at rest.

questions.onCorrect: Mass follows the energy: it rises when energy is put in and falls when energy is released and leaves the system.

questions.prompt: A mission planner finds the kinetic energy of the Parker Solar Probe, moving at 68,600 m/s, with $\tfrac12 mv^2$. The relativistic correction is about 4 parts in a hundred million, and the gravitational constant is known to about 2 parts in a hundred thousand. What follows?
hints: Compare 4 parts in a hundred million with 2 parts in a hundred thousand. Which is the larger?
A correction much smaller than the uncertainty already in a calculation cannot change its result.

acceptedIdeas: The correction is far below the other uncertainties, so the Newtonian form is adequate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The correction is far below the other uncertainties, so the Newtonian form is adequate

choices.label: Any speed above a few kilometres per second needs the relativistic expression in practice
The correction is far below the other uncertainties, so the Newtonian form is adequate
The correction adds up over every orbit until it can no longer be ignored

questions.onCorrect: The correction, $3.9\times10^{-8}$, is about 560 times smaller than the uncertainty in $G$, so it does not change the planner's result.

misconceptions.feedback: The correction grows as $v^2/c^2$, so there is no sharp threshold at a few kilometres per second. For this probe it is tiny.
The correction is a fractional difference in the energy at a given speed. It does not accumulate from orbit to orbit.

questions.prompt: A phone battery stores 40 watt-hours of energy when it is full (a made-up value), and a balance reads to 0.001 g (also made up). Would the balance show the gain in the battery's mass when it is charged?
hints: Convert the 40 Wh into joules: one watt-hour is 3,600 J.
Divide the energy in joules by $c^2$ to get the mass in kilograms, then convert to grams.
Compare that mass with the balance's smallest division, 0.001 g.

acceptedIdeas: No: the gain is about a millionth of the smallest change that the balance can show
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: the gain is about a millionth of the smallest change that the balance can show

choices.label: No: the gain is about a millionth of the smallest change that the balance can show
No: charging stores the energy chemically, and only nuclear changes alter mass
Yes: the gain is about the size of the balance's smallest division

questions.onCorrect: The battery gains about $1.6\times10^{-9}$ g, roughly 1.6 millionths of the balance's smallest division, so the balance cannot see it.

misconceptions.feedback: Every change in energy alters mass, chemical ones included. The change here is tiny, but it is not zero.
The gain is 144,000 J divided by $c^2$, about $1.6\times10^{-12}$ kg or $1.6\times10^{-9}$ g, which is a millionth of 0.001 g.

questions.prompt: A fission device loses 3.0 g of mass (a made-up value) once its energy has left it. How much energy does that correspond to, in joules?
hints: Express the mass in kilograms first.
Square the speed of light, about $9.0\times10^{16}$ in m²/s².
Multiply the mass by that value.
questions.onCorrect: The energy is about $2.7\times10^{14}$ J, three times that of a gram and equivalent to about 64 kilotons of TNT.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the 3.0 as kilograms. The mass is 3.0 grams, which is 0.0030 kg.
That uses $c$ without squaring it. The energy is the mass times $c^2$.

questions.prompt: A student says that fission works because $E = mc^2$ turns matter into energy, so it could not be understood without relativity. Which reply fits the evidence?
hints: Which came first for fission: a measurement of its energy or a calculation from the mass difference?
Does the equation explain where the energy comes from, or does it convert between mass and energy?

acceptedIdeas: The energy of fission was measured directly, about 200 MeV; $E = mc^2$ only links it to the mass lost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The energy of fission was measured directly, about 200 MeV; $E = mc^2$ only links it to the mass lost

choices.label: Relativity is essential, because nuclei move so fast that Newtonian mechanics cannot describe fission
The energy of fission was measured directly, about 200 MeV; $E = mc^2$ only links it to the mass lost
The equation applies only to chemical reactions, so it says nothing about fission

questions.onCorrect: Fission's energy was measured directly, and $E = mc^2$ relates that energy to the mass difference without being needed to explain how fission works.

misconceptions.feedback: The theory of fission is non-relativistic, because relativistic effects are too small to change the dynamics of the process significantly, as the physicist Robert Serber noted.
The equation applies to every change in energy, nuclear or chemical. What differs is the size of the mass change.

questions.prompt: A sealed flask of hot tea stands on a balance in a room, and heat leaks through its walls until the tea is at room temperature. Compared with the start, the balance reading is:
hints: Has any energy crossed the boundary of the flask, and in which direction?
Energy that leaves a system takes its mass with it.

acceptedIdeas: Lower by the heat that left divided by c², an amount far too small to measure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lower by the heat that left divided by c², an amount far too small to measure

choices.label: Lower by the heat that left divided by c², an amount far too small to measure
Unchanged, since only nuclear changes alter mass, and cooling is not a nuclear change
Higher, since the heat that the room absorbs from the flask makes the flask heavier

questions.onCorrect: The flask loses the heat's mass, the heat divided by $c^2$, and the room gains it, a change far too small for any balance.

misconceptions.feedback: Every change in energy alters mass. Here heat has left the flask, so the flask is a little lighter, though by far too little to show.
The room absorbs the heat, so it is the room that gains the mass. The flask, which lost the energy, loses mass.

questions.prompt: A beam of ultraviolet light frees electrons from a metal plate. According to the wave picture of light, what should happen to the kinetic energy of the freed electrons when the beam is made four times as intense?
hints: In the wave picture, how much energy reaches the surface each second when the intensity is four times as great?
What would more energy delivered to each electron do to its kinetic energy?

acceptedIdeas: It should rise, since more energy arrives at the surface each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It should rise, since more energy arrives at the surface each second

choices.label: It should rise, since more energy arrives at the surface each second
It should stay the same, because only the colour of the light matters
It should fall, because the energy is shared among more electrons

questions.onCorrect: The wave picture predicts that a brighter beam gives faster electrons. The next screens show that the observations disagree.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what is observed, but it is not what the wave picture predicts. A wave delivers energy continuously, so a stronger wave should deliver more to each electron.
A wave's energy is not divided among the electrons like a fixed supply. A stronger wave delivers more energy to every electron at the surface.

questions.prompt: A clean metal plate ejects electrons under dim ultraviolet light and none under a very bright red lamp. Which explanation fits the photon account?
hints: What does the energy of one photon depend on?
Compare the energy of one ultraviolet photon with that of one red photon, and with the work function.

acceptedIdeas: Each ultraviolet photon has enough energy to free an electron, and each red photon falls short
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each ultraviolet photon has enough energy to free an electron, and each red photon falls short

choices.label: Ultraviolet light carries more power than red light, so it pushes harder on the electrons
A bright red lamp is still too dim at the surface, so the electrons need longer to gather energy
Each ultraviolet photon has enough energy to free an electron, and each red photon falls short

questions.onCorrect: Each photon's energy is $hf$, so an ultraviolet photon can free an electron and a red photon cannot, however many red photons arrive.

misconceptions.feedback: A very bright red lamp has more power than a dim ultraviolet one, so power cannot be the reason. What differs is the energy of each photon.
That is the wave picture again. Below the threshold no electrons are emitted however long the exposure, because no single photon has enough energy.

questions.prompt: Why does a brighter lamp of 700 nm not free electrons from this metal?
hints: What is the energy of one photon of 700 nm light, compared with the 2.3 eV work function?
Can an electron collect the energy of two photons at once?

acceptedIdeas: Each photon carries only 1.77 eV, and an electron takes one photon's energy or none
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each photon carries only 1.77 eV, and an electron takes one photon's energy or none

choices.label: A brighter lamp delivers more energy, which is spread too thinly to free an electron
Each photon carries only 1.77 eV, and an electron takes one photon's energy or none
The extra photons from a brighter lamp cancel one another, so the net energy is unchanged

questions.onCorrect: More photons arrive from a brighter lamp, but each is below the work function, and no electron can use the energy of two at once.

misconceptions.feedback: In the photon picture the energy is not spread out. It arrives in packets, and an electron takes a whole packet or none of it.
Photons do not cancel. Their energies do not pool either, so more photons of 1.77 eV still leave each electron with 1.77 eV to work with.

questions.prompt: A tube is lit with blue light and a stopping voltage is measured. The lamp's intensity is then doubled. What happens to the stopping voltage and to the photocurrent?
hints: The stopping voltage measures the greatest kinetic energy of an electron. Does doubling the number of photons change the energy of each?
The photocurrent counts electrons per second. What does doubling the photons do to that count?

acceptedIdeas: The stopping voltage stays the same and the photocurrent doubles
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stopping voltage stays the same and the photocurrent doubles

choices.label: The stopping voltage doubles and the photocurrent stays the same
Both the stopping voltage and the photocurrent double
The stopping voltage stays the same and the photocurrent doubles

questions.onCorrect: Intensity sets the number of photons, so the current doubles, while the energy of each photon, and so the stopping voltage, is fixed by the frequency.

misconceptions.feedback: That gives the intensity to the energy of each electron, as the wave picture would. The stopping voltage measures electron energy, which intensity does not change.
Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and so of electrons, but not the energy of each photon, so the stopping voltage stays the same.

questions.prompt: A made-up metal has a work function of 2.0 eV, and it is lit with light of wavelength 500 nm. What is the energy of one photon, in electron-volts?
hints: Use $E = hc/\lambda$, with $hc = 1239.84$ eV nm.
Divide 1239.84 by the wavelength in nanometres.
The answer comes out in electron-volts, and it should be a little above the 2.0 eV work function.
questions.onCorrect: The photon energy is 2.48 eV, which is above the work function of 2.0 eV, so electrons are freed.

questions.prompt: With photons of 2.48 eV and a work function of 2.0 eV, what is the greatest kinetic energy of the freed electrons, in electron-volts?
hints: The greatest kinetic energy is what is left of the photon energy after the work function is paid.
Subtract the work function from the photon energy.
Check that the result is smaller than the photon energy, since part of that energy went into freeing the electron.
questions.onCorrect: The freed electrons have at most 0.48 eV, so the stopping potential is 0.48 V.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the work function to the photon energy. The work function is energy spent freeing the electron, so it is subtracted.

questions.prompt: A photomultiplier is to detect very dim red light at 700 nm, whose photons each carry 1.77 eV. Which photocathode would respond, and why? The work functions are made up.
hints: Compare each work function with the energy of a 700 nm photon, 1.77 eV.
Which work function is below the photon energy?

acceptedIdeas: One of work function 1.4 eV, since each 700 nm photon carries more than that
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One of work function 1.4 eV, since each 700 nm photon carries more than that

choices.label: One of work function 1.4 eV, since each 700 nm photon carries more than that
One of work function 2.3 eV, since a long enough exposure makes up the shortfall
One of work function 4.3 eV, since a high work function holds more electrons ready

questions.onCorrect: The work function must be below 1.77 eV, which is why photocathodes use materials chosen for a low work function.

misconceptions.feedback: Each photon carries 1.77 eV, below 2.3 eV, and the energies of separate photons do not add for one electron. No electrons come out however long the exposure.
A higher work function means more energy is needed to free each electron, so fewer photons qualify. The work function has to be below the photon energy.

questions.prompt: A metal has a work function of 1.9 eV (a made-up value). Light of wavelength 450 nm falls on it. What is the greatest kinetic energy of the ejected electrons, in electron-volts?
hints: Find the energy of one photon from $E = hc/\lambda$, with $hc = 1239.84$ eV nm.
Subtract the work function from the photon energy.
A photon energy below the work function would give no electrons. Check that this is not the case here.
questions.onCorrect: The photon carries 2.755 eV and 1.9 eV of it frees the electron, leaving 0.855 eV, about 0.86 eV.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the photon energy. The work function has to be taken from it.
That adds the work function. It is energy spent freeing the electron, so it is subtracted.

questions.prompt: A lamp's light has a frequency just below a metal's threshold. The lamp is made far brighter and left on for a long time. What should be observed?
hints: What decides whether a single electron can be freed: the number of photons or the energy of one?
What does a brighter lamp change, the number of photons or the energy of each?

acceptedIdeas: No electrons, because no single photon has enough energy and photon energies do not add up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No electrons, because no single photon has enough energy and photon energies do not add up

choices.label: A few electrons after a delay, as energy builds up in the metal
No electrons, because no single photon has enough energy and photon energies do not add up
Electrons with very little kinetic energy, since the photons are almost energetic enough

questions.onCorrect: Brightness changes the number of photons and not their energy, so below the threshold nothing is freed however bright or long.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wave picture. Below the threshold no electrons are emitted however long the exposure, because no single photon has enough energy.
An electron either takes a photon's whole energy and is freed with the surplus, or none, and below the threshold no photon has enough, so no electron is freed at all.

questions.prompt: The stopping voltage was measured at three frequencies for a made-up metal: 4.84 × 10¹⁴ Hz gave 0 V, 6.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz gave 0.48 V and 7.50 × 10¹⁴ Hz gave 1.10 V, and the points lie on a straight line. The slope of that line, in V s, is a fundamental constant divided by the electron's charge. Which constant is it?
hints: Write the stopping voltage as a straight-line function of frequency, starting from $eV_0 = hf - W$. What multiplies the frequency once you divide by $e$?
Find the slope from two of the points: the change in voltage divided by the change in frequency.

acceptedIdeas: Planck constant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Planck constant, h. The slope is (1.10 − 0.48) V divided by 1.50 × 10¹⁴ Hz, which is 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s, and that is h/e.

questions.onCorrect: The slope is $4.1\times10^{-15}$ V s, which is $h/e$, and multiplying by the electron's charge gives $h = 6.6\times10^{-34}$ J s.

misconceptions.feedback: The work function sets where the line crosses the frequency axis, which is the threshold, and not how steep the line is.
The speed of light connects frequency and wavelength, but the slope of $V_0$ against $f$ is $h/e$.

questions.prompt: Two lamps each radiate 2.0 mW of light of a single wavelength. One lamp is red, at 650 nm, and the other is green, at 520 nm. Which lamp sends more photons each second?
hints: Power is energy delivered each second, and each photon delivers a share of that energy.
Suppose every photon in a beam carried more energy. How many of them would the lamp need each second to deliver 2.0 mW?

acceptedIdeas: The red lamp, because each red photon carries less energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The red lamp, because each red photon carries less energy

choices.label: The red lamp, because each red photon carries less energy
The green lamp, because each green photon carries more energy
Neither, because the two lamps radiate the same power

questions.onCorrect: The red photons carry about 1.91 eV and the green ones about 2.38 eV, so the red lamp needs 1.25 times as many photons each second for the same power.

misconceptions.feedback: Photons that carry more energy are needed in smaller numbers to make up the same 2.0 mW, so a larger energy per photon means fewer photons each second, not more.
Equal power means equal energy each second. The number of photons also depends on how much energy each one carries, and that differs between the two colours.

questions.prompt: Orange light has a wavelength of 620 nm. What is the energy of one photon of it, in eV?
hints: Use $E = hc/\lambda$ with $hc = 1239.84$ eV nm.
The wavelength is already in nanometres, so it can go straight into the formula.
Divide, and check that the result lies between the 3.10 eV of 400 nm light and the 1.77 eV of 700 nm light.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: E = hc / wavelength = 1239.84 eV nm / 620 nm = 2.00 eV.

questions.onCorrect: A 620 nm photon carries 2.00 eV, which sits between the violet and red ends of the visible range, as it should.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wavelength divided by $hc$, the wrong way up. The wavelength belongs in the denominator, so a longer wavelength gives a smaller energy.
That is the energy in units of $10^{-19}$ J. The question asks for electron-volts, so leave the electron-volt conversion out.

questions.prompt: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV (a made-up value). Four lamps each radiate 1.0 mW at a single wavelength. Which lamp can eject electrons from the metal?
hints: An electron is ejected only when a single photon carries more energy than the work function.
Find each lamp's photon energy from $1239.84 / \lambda$ and compare it with 2.3 eV.

acceptedIdeas: The 500 nm lamp, since only its photons carry more than 2.3 eV
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 500 nm lamp, since only its photons carry more than 2.3 eV

choices.label: The 700 nm lamp, since light of longer wavelength has more energy
The 600 nm lamp, since all four lamps radiate the same power
The 500 nm lamp, since only its photons carry more than 2.3 eV
The 1000 nm lamp, since it sends the most photons each second

questions.onCorrect: A 500 nm photon carries 2.48 eV. The 600 nm photons carry 2.07 eV, so every other lamp falls short however bright it is.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the relation. Photon energy is $hc$ divided by the wavelength, so a 700 nm photon carries only 1.77 eV.
Equal power does not give equal photon energy. A 600 nm photon carries 2.07 eV, below the work function, and no number of such photons can eject an electron.
That counts the photons and ignores their energy. Each 1000 nm photon carries 1.24 eV, far below 2.3 eV.

questions.prompt: Why does dividing a beam's power by the energy of one photon give the number of photons arriving each second?
hints: What does a watt measure in terms of joules?
If a beam delivers a certain energy each second, and each photon carries a known share, how many shares make up the total?

acceptedIdeas: Power is the energy delivered each second, so the quotient is photons each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power is the energy delivered each second, so the quotient is photons each second

choices.label: The division turns the power into the light's frequency, which counts photons each second
Power is the energy delivered each second, so the quotient is photons each second
All photons carry the same energy, so the power alone fixes how many there are

questions.onCorrect: Power is energy each second and one photon carries a fixed energy, so the division counts photons each second, and the count changes whenever the photon energy does.

misconceptions.feedback: The frequency counts wave cycles each second, not photons. A 2.0 mW beam at 620 nm has a frequency of $4.8 \times 10^{14}$ Hz but sends $6.2 \times 10^{15}$ photons each second.
Photon energy depends on the wavelength, so the same power gives different counts at different wavelengths.

questions.prompt: The 550 nm beam of 1.0 mW sent $2.77 \times 10^{15}$ photons each second. A 1000 nm photon carries less energy than a 550 nm photon. How does the number of photons each second compare for a 1.0 mW beam at 1000 nm?
hints: The beam delivers the same energy each second in both cases.
Smaller packets of energy mean more packets are needed to make up the same total.

acceptedIdeas: More, because each photon carries less energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More, because each photon carries less energy

choices.label: Fewer, because each photon is less energetic
More, because each photon carries less energy
The same, because the power is the same

questions.onCorrect: Each 1000 nm photon carries 1.24 eV against 2.25 eV at 550 nm, so the 1000 nm beam needs about 1.8 times as many.

misconceptions.feedback: Less energy per photon means more photons are needed to deliver the same energy each second.
The power fixes the energy delivered each second, but the number of photons also depends on the energy of each one.

questions.prompt: How many photons does the 1000 nm beam of 1.0 mW send each second, in units of $10^{15}$?
hints: Divide the power by the energy of one photon, with both in SI units.
The energy of one photon at 1000 nm is $1.99 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
$1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ divided by $1.99 \times 10^{-19}$ is a number of order $10^{15}$.
questions.onCorrect: The beam sends $5.03 \times 10^{15}$ photons each second, which is 1.8 times the figure for 550 nm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for 550 nm. At 1000 nm each photon carries less energy, so the count is larger.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 mW beam has a wavelength of 620 nm. How many photons does it deliver each second, in units of $10^{15}$?
hints: First find the energy of one photon, then convert it to joules.
A 620 nm photon carries 2.00 eV, which is $3.20 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
Divide the power, $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ W, by that energy.
questions.onCorrect: The beam delivers $6.2 \times 10^{15}$ photons each second, twice the figure that a 1.0 mW beam of the same colour would give.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for 1.0 mW. The beam here has twice the power, so it needs twice as many photons.

questions.prompt: A beam carries a power of 0.50 mW, and a detector reports that $2.5 \times 10^{15}$ photons arrive each second. What is the wavelength of the light, in nm, to the nearest 10 nm?
hints: The energy of one photon is the power divided by the number of photons each second.
Convert that energy from joules to electron-volts by dividing by $1.602 \times 10^{-19}$.
Then use wavelength $= 1239.84 / E$, with $E$ in electron-volts.
questions.onCorrect: The photons carry 1.25 eV each, so the light is infrared, just beyond the red end of the visible range.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats $2.0 \times 10^{-19}$ as if it were 2.0 eV. In electron-volts the energy of one photon is 1.25 eV.

questions.prompt: Four lamps each radiate 1.0 mW at a single wavelength: 450 nm, 520 nm, 650 nm and 950 nm. Put them in order of the number of photons they send each second, the most first.
hints: At equal power, the lamp whose photons carry the least energy needs the most of them.
Photon energy falls as wavelength rises.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 950 nm lamp sends the most photons each second, then the 650 nm, 520 nm and 450 nm lamps, because at equal power the photon count is proportional to the wavelength.

questions.onCorrect: At equal power the photon rate is proportional to the wavelength, so the longest wavelength comes first. The 950 nm lamp sends about 2.1 times as many photons as the 450 nm lamp.

questions.prompt: A lamp radiates light of a single wavelength, 600 nm. Its power is then doubled with the wavelength unchanged. What happens to the photons?
hints: Photon energy is $hc/\lambda$. Has anything in that expression changed?
Power is the number of photons each second times the energy of one.

acceptedIdeas: Each photon keeps its energy, and twice as many arrive each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each photon keeps its energy, and twice as many arrive each second

choices.label: Each photon now carries twice the energy, and the number is unchanged
Each photon now carries twice the energy, and twice as many arrive
Each photon keeps its energy, and twice as many arrive each second

questions.onCorrect: The energy of each photon, 2.07 eV at 600 nm, is set by the wavelength alone, so a brighter beam of the same colour is simply a larger stream of identical photons.

misconceptions.feedback: Photon energy depends only on the frequency, which has not changed, so brightening a lamp cannot make its photons more energetic.
That would multiply the power by four. A beam of the same colour carries the same energy per photon, and only the number changes.

questions.prompt: A light sensor responds only when each photon carries at least 1.50 eV (a made-up value). What is the longest wavelength of light it can detect, in nm?
hints: A longer wavelength means a smaller photon energy, so the limit is set by the smallest energy the sensor accepts.
Rearrange $E = hc/\lambda$ to give the wavelength in terms of the energy.
Divide 1239.84 eV nm by the smallest energy the sensor accepts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: wavelength = hc / E = 1239.84 / 1.50 = 826.6 nm, about 827 nm.

questions.onCorrect: Any photon with a wavelength above about 827 nm carries less than 1.50 eV, so the sensor is blind to it however intense the beam.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies $hc$ by the energy. The wavelength is $hc$ divided by the energy.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen atom gives out light when it loses energy. Suppose the atom could lose any amount of energy, with nothing restricting the amounts. What would the lamp's spectrum look like?
hints: A photon's colour is set by its energy, and the photon carries away the energy the atom loses.
If the atom could lose every possible amount, how many different photon energies would appear?

acceptedIdeas: A smooth band of colours, since any photon energy is allowed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A smooth band of colours, since any photon energy is allowed

choices.label: A few sharp lines, which is what a hydrogen lamp actually shows
A smooth band of colours, since any photon energy is allowed
A single sharp line, since every hydrogen atom is the same

questions.onCorrect: A spread of energies gives a spread of colours. The sharp lines of the real lamp mean that the atom can only lose certain amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the observed spectrum, and it is the evidence that the energies are restricted. If any amount could be lost, the photons' colours would run through the whole range.
Identical atoms can still lose different amounts of energy if all amounts are allowed, and then the photons would not share one colour.

questions.prompt: An electron in a hydrogen atom drops from $n = 7$ to $n = 2$. Use $1/\lambda = R(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2)$ with $R = 1.0974 \times 10^7$ per metre. What is the wavelength of the photon, in nm to three significant figures?
hints: Here $n_f = 2$ is the level the electron lands on and $n_i = 7$ the level it leaves.
Work out $1/4 - 1/49$ first, then multiply by $R$ to get $1/\lambda$.
Invert $1/\lambda$ to get the wavelength in metres, then convert to nanometres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1/wavelength = 1.0974e7 × (1/4 − 1/49) = 1.0974e7 × 0.2296 = 2.520e6 per metre, so the wavelength is 3.969e-7 m, or 397 nm.

questions.onCorrect: The photon has a wavelength of 397 nm, at the violet edge of the visible range, and NIST measures the line at 397.0 nm.

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the levels the wrong way round. The larger number, $n_i = 7$, belongs with the level the electron leaves, which makes $1/\lambda$ positive.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen lamp's spectrum shows a line at 300 nm, in the ultraviolet. Which of hydrogen's series could it belong to?
hints: Find the longest wavelength of the Lyman series and the shortest of the Balmer series.
Does 300 nm fall inside the range of either series?

acceptedIdeas: None, since 300 nm falls in the gap between the Lyman and Balmer series
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None, since 300 nm falls in the gap between the Lyman and Balmer series

choices.label: The Balmer series, since its lines crowd towards ever shorter wavelengths
The Lyman series, since the Lyman lines are the ultraviolet ones
None, since 300 nm falls in the gap between the Lyman and Balmer series

questions.onCorrect: The Balmer lines stop at 364.5 nm and the Lyman lines begin at 121.5 nm and go shorter, so a line at 300 nm needs some other source than hydrogen.

misconceptions.feedback: The Balmer lines crowd towards a limit at 364.5 nm, and none lies below it, so a line at 300 nm cannot be one of them.
The Lyman lines are ultraviolet, but the longest of them, 2 to 1, is at 121.5 nm, and all the others are shorter.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen atom drops from $n = 4$, at $-0.85$ eV, to $n = 2$, at $-3.40$ eV. What is the energy of the photon it gives out?
hints: The atom loses the difference between its energy before and its energy after.
Both levels are negative, so subtract carefully: the energy after is lower than the energy before.

acceptedIdeas: 2.55 eV, the gap between the two levels
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2.55 eV, the gap between the two levels

choices.label: 2.55 eV, the gap between the two levels
0.85 eV, the energy of the starting level
4.25 eV, the sum of the two level energies
3.40 eV, the energy of the final level

questions.onCorrect: The atom drops by $-0.85 - (-3.40) = 2.55$ eV, and that is the energy of the photon, a wavelength of 486 nm.

misconceptions.feedback: The photon carries away the energy the atom loses, which is the gap between the levels and not the energy of the level the electron leaves.
The energy lost is a difference, so the two level energies are subtracted and not added.
The photon's energy is the gap between the two levels, and the final level's energy alone says nothing about the jump.

questions.prompt: The working gives $n_i = 7.98$. Why can the answer be taken as 8?
hints: What kind of numbers do $n_f$ and $n_i$ stand for?
A measured wavelength and a rounded constant leave a small gap from the exact whole number.

acceptedIdeas: Levels are whole numbers, and 7.98 is within rounding of 8
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Levels are whole numbers, and 7.98 is within rounding of 8

choices.label: Levels can take any value, so 7.98 is the nearest one that fits
Levels are whole numbers, and 7.98 is within rounding of 8
An answer is always rounded up to the next whole number

questions.onCorrect: The levels are whole numbers, so a result this close to 8 can only mean $n_i = 8$.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula uses whole numbers for the levels, and the lines are evidence for that. A result near a whole number points to that whole number.
Rounding up is not the rule. The nearest whole number is chosen because levels are whole numbers, so a result of 8.02 would give 8 as well.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: what is $1/n_i^2$, to three decimal places?
hints: The level the electron lands on is $n_f = 3$, so $1/n_f^2 = 1/9$.
The bracket of the formula is $1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2$, and its value was found in the line above.
Subtract that value from $1/9 = 0.1111$.
questions.onCorrect: The difference is 0.040, and the next line turns it into a level.

questions.prompt: From which level, $n_i$, does the electron fall?
hints: Take the reciprocal of $1/n_i^2$ first, which gives $n_i^2$.
Then take the square root of that.
Check that the result is a whole number larger than 3.
questions.onCorrect: The 1281.8 nm line is the jump from $n = 5$ to $n = 3$, one of the Paschen lines.

misconceptions.feedback: That is $n_i^2$. Take the square root to get the level itself.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen lamp shows two infrared lines, at 1093.8 nm and 1005.0 nm, and both end on the same lower level. What is that level, $n_f$?
hints: Work out $1/\lambda$ for each line, in per metre.
The largest $1/\lambda$ that a series can have is $R/n_f^2$, so find which lower levels allow values as large as these.
Of the levels that pass, check which one gives whole numbers for $n_i$ for both lines.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1/wavelength is 9.14e5 and 9.95e5 per metre. For n_f = 3, 1/9 − 1/36 = 0.0833 and 1/9 − 1/49 = 0.0907 give 9.14e5 and 9.95e5. A lower level of 1 or 2 would give at least 1.5e6, and a lower level of 4 or more at most 6.9e5.

questions.onCorrect: With $n_f = 3$ the lines are the jumps from $n = 6$ and from $n = 7$, two of the Paschen lines. A lower level of 4 or more cannot reach the larger value of $1/\lambda$.

misconceptions.feedback: A lower level of 2 gives lines with $1/\lambda$ of at least $1.5 \times 10^6$ per metre, which is larger than both of these, so level 2 is ruled out.

questions.prompt: An atom in the $n = 3$ level drops to $n = 2$ and then to $n = 1$, giving out photons of 656.1 nm and 121.5 nm. What wavelength would a single photon have if the atom dropped straight from $n = 3$ to $n = 1$, in nm?
hints: The straight drop gives out the same total energy as the two steps together.
Energy is proportional to $1/\lambda$, so it is the values of $1/\lambda$ that add.
Add $1/656.1$ and $1/121.5$, then invert.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The energies add: 1/wavelength = 1/656.1 + 1/121.5 = 9.755e-3 per nm, so the wavelength is 102.5 nm.

questions.onCorrect: The photon from the direct drop has 102.5 nm, shorter than either step, because it carries the energy of both photons together.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the wavelengths. Wavelengths do not add, because it is the photon energies that do, and energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
That subtracts the wavelengths. The energies of the two steps add, and a bigger energy means a shorter wavelength.

questions.prompt: Six jumps in a hydrogen atom each give out one photon. In which part of the spectrum does each photon lie?
hints: Find which series each jump belongs to from the level it ends on.
The lowest level gives the largest energy gaps, and so the shortest wavelengths.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The jumps ending on n = 1 (2 to 1 and 6 to 1) give ultraviolet photons, those ending on n = 2 (3 to 2 and 5 to 2) give visible light, and those ending on n = 3 (4 to 3 and 6 to 3) give infrared.

items.label: From $n = 2$ to $n = 1$
items.explanation: It ends on the lowest level, in the Lyman series, and its wavelength is 121.5 nm.

items.label: From $n = 6$ to $n = 1$
items.explanation: It also ends on $n = 1$, so it is a Lyman line, at 93.7 nm.

items.label: From $n = 3$ to $n = 2$
items.explanation: It ends on $n = 2$, in the Balmer series, at 656.1 nm.

items.label: From $n = 5$ to $n = 2$
items.explanation: It is a Balmer line at 433.9 nm, within the visible range.

items.label: From $n = 4$ to $n = 3$
items.explanation: It ends on $n = 3$, in the Paschen series, at 1875 nm.

items.label: From $n = 6$ to $n = 3$
items.explanation: It is a Paschen line at 1093 nm, longer than red light.

questions.onCorrect: The lower level fixes the region: ending on $n = 1$ gives ultraviolet, on $n = 2$ visible light and on $n = 3$ infrared.

questions.prompt: A student sees a line at 420.0 nm in the light of a lamp that she thinks contains only hydrogen. The nearest Balmer lines are at 410.1 nm (6 to 2) and 433.9 nm (5 to 2). The formula matches measured lines to within about 0.2 nm. What should she conclude?
hints: How far is 420 nm from each neighbouring line, compared with the 0.2 nm accuracy of the formula?
A hydrogen line needs a pair of whole numbers $n_f$ and $n_i$, and the next one after 6 to 2 is at 433.9 nm.

acceptedIdeas: The line comes from something else, because no jump in hydrogen gives 420 nm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The line comes from something else, because no jump in hydrogen gives 420 nm

choices.label: It is hydrogen, since 420 nm lies between two lines and the formula is only approximate
It is a hydrogen line from a level between $n = 5$ and $n = 6$
The line comes from something else, because no jump in hydrogen gives 420 nm

questions.onCorrect: Every hydrogen line comes from a pair of whole numbers, and none gives 420 nm, so the line must have another source.

misconceptions.feedback: A gap of 0.2 nm is the size of the formula's error, and 420 nm is about 10 nm from both neighbouring lines, far too much to blame on the formula.
Levels are whole numbers, so no level lies between 5 and 6, and the Balmer lines come only from $n = 3$, 4, 5, 6 and so on.

questions.prompt: An electron in a hydrogen atom drops from $n = 4$ to $n = 1$. What is the wavelength of the photon, in nm to three significant figures?
hints: The electron lands on $n_f = 1$, so $1/n_f^2 = 1$.
Work out $1 - 1/16$ and multiply by $R$ to get $1/\lambda$.
Invert the result and convert from metres to nanometres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1/wavelength = 1.0974e7 × (1 − 1/16) = 1.0288e7 per metre, so the wavelength is 9.720e-8 m, or 97.2 nm.

questions.onCorrect: The photon has a wavelength of 97.2 nm, well inside the ultraviolet, as the lines that end on the lowest level always are.

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the levels the wrong way round, which makes the wavelength negative. $n_i = 4$ is the larger number.

questions.prompt: Bohr's model reproduces hydrogen's lines almost exactly. A physicist applies the same two rules to neutral helium, which has a nucleus and two electrons. What should she expect?
hints: Count the charged bodies in hydrogen and in neutral helium.
The model was built for a nucleus with a single electron going round it.

acceptedIdeas: No useful levels, since the rules describe two orbiting charges and helium has three
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No useful levels, since the rules describe two orbiting charges and helium has three

choices.label: Levels as accurate as hydrogen's, since the rules do not mention how many electrons there are
No useful levels, since the rules describe two orbiting charges and helium has three
Levels that are nearly right, since a second electron adds only a small correction

questions.onCorrect: The model is accurate only for two charged points circling each other, and it predicts no energy levels for neutral helium.

misconceptions.feedback: The model's success depends on the system. It is built for two charged points orbiting each other, and a nucleus with two electrons is a different problem.
Neutral helium has no energy levels predicted by the model at all, so there is no small correction to add to.

questions.prompt: In the $n = 1$ orbit of Bohr's model the radius is 52.9 pm and the rule $mvr = \hbar$ holds. Use $\hbar = 1.0546 \times 10^{-34}$ J s, $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg and $c = 3.00 \times 10^8$ m/s. What is the electron's speed, as a percentage of the speed of light?
hints: Solve $mvr = \hbar$ for the speed $v$.
Write the radius in metres, 52.9 pm being $5.29 \times 10^{-11}$ m.
Divide the speed by $c$ and multiply by 100 to get a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The electron moves at less than 1 per cent of the speed of light, which is slow enough for ordinary mechanics, as the model assumes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed in units of $10^6$ m/s. The question asks for the speed as a percentage of $c$.
That is 100 times too large. The speed is far below $c$, so the fraction $v/c$ is a very small number, and a percentage is that fraction times 100.

questions.prompt: Sort each case by whether Bohr's model handles it or lies beyond it.
hints: The model suits two charged bodies circling each other slowly, far below the speed of light.
Count the charged bodies in each case, and ask whether the question is about wavelengths or about something else.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hydrogen's Lyman and Paschen lines and a Rydberg state are handled, because each is two charged points orbiting slowly. Neutral lithium's levels, the brightest of hydrogen's lines and close pairs of lines lie beyond the model.

items.label: The wavelengths of hydrogen's Lyman lines
items.explanation: A nucleus and one electron, the case the model was built for, and the model agrees with the observed Lyman lines.

items.label: The wavelengths of hydrogen's Paschen lines
items.explanation: The same system again, with the electron landing on $n = 3$, and the model agrees with the observed lines.

items.label: The levels of an atom's outer electron when it is far from everything else
items.explanation: A Rydberg state: from far away the rest of the atom acts as one charged point, so two charged points orbit each other.

items.label: The energy levels of neutral lithium, which has three electrons
items.explanation: Multi-electron atoms have no energy levels predicted by the model, which also fails for neutral helium.

items.label: Which of hydrogen's lines is the brightest
items.explanation: Relative intensities of spectral lines are not given by the model, though a few simple cases came out reasonably.

items.label: Very close pairs of lines in the spectra of some atoms
items.explanation: The model cannot say why some energy levels lie so close together.

questions.onCorrect: The model suits a single electron bound to a nucleus. It has no levels for atoms with several electrons, and it does not give brightness or fine detail in spectra.

questions.prompt: A textbook says that in hydrogen's ground state the electron circles the nucleus at a radius of 52.9 pm, with orbital angular momentum $\hbar$ and a negative total energy. Experiments contradict one part of this statement. Which part?
hints: The spectral lines test the energies, and the model's energies agree with them.
Which of the three quantities in the statement is not something the lines measure?

acceptedIdeas: The angular momentum, since the true ground state has none
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The angular momentum, since the true ground state has none

choices.label: The angular momentum, since the true ground state has none
The negative energy, since the ground state has positive total energy
The lowest orbit, since real atoms have no smallest size

questions.onCorrect: The true ground state has no angular momentum, so the picture of an electron circling the nucleus is wrong, although the energies are right.

misconceptions.feedback: The energy is negative in the model and in the full theory, and the lines agree with it, so this part is not contradicted.
Both the model and the full theory have a lowest level, below which the electron cannot go.

questions.prompt: Why can no orbit hold two and a half de Broglie wavelengths around its circumference?
hints: Think of a wave going once round a circle and returning to where it started.
A standing wave on a string must fit its ends, and here the circle has no ends.

acceptedIdeas: The wave would not meet itself after one turn, so only whole numbers fit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The wave would not meet itself after one turn, so only whole numbers fit

choices.label: The wave would not meet itself after one turn, so only whole numbers fit
Half-wavelengths would give the electron too little energy to stay bound
The wave would join up, but it would radiate outside the Balmer series

questions.onCorrect: A wave that goes round the orbit has to meet itself after one turn, which only happens for a whole number of wavelengths.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no energy cutoff of that kind. The restriction comes from the wave having to meet itself after one turn.
The wave does not join up in this case, and the wavelengths of the lines are a separate matter from whether an orbit is allowed.

questions.prompt: How many de Broglie wavelengths fit around the circumference of the $n = 1$ orbit, $2\pi r / \lambda$?
hints: The circumference of a circle of radius $r$ is $2\pi r$, and here $r = 52.9$ pm.
The wavelength from the line above is 332 pm, so both lengths can be taken in picometres.
Divide the circumference by the wavelength.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2πr = 2π × 52.9 pm = 332 pm, and λ = 332 pm, so 2πr / λ = 1.00 and one wavelength fits.

questions.onCorrect: Exactly one wavelength fits, which is what the $n = 1$ orbit should hold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half the true value, which comes from using the radius as if it were the circumference. The circumference is $2\pi r$.

questions.prompt: An electron moves at $1.1 \times 10^6$ m/s on a circular path of radius 0.20 nm (made-up values). Its de Broglie wavelength is $h/mv$, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s and $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg. How many wavelengths fit around the circumference, to one decimal place?
hints: Find the wavelength first, from $\lambda = h/mv$.
The circumference is $2\pi r$, with $r = 0.20$ nm.
Divide the circumference by the wavelength.
questions.onCorrect: The result, 1.9, is not a whole number, so the wave would not join up with itself and the electron cannot orbit this way in Bohr's model.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wavelength divided by the circumference, the wrong way up. The number of wavelengths is the circumference divided by the wavelength.

questions.prompt: A student reads the passage and argues: "Bohr's model gets the ground-state angular momentum wrong, so its energy levels for hydrogen cannot be trusted either." What is the best reply?
hints: Which measurements test the energy levels, and which test the angular momentum?
Ask whether the model's energies agree with the spectral lines, as the last lesson showed.

acceptedIdeas: The error is in the orbit picture, while the lines test the energies and they agree
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The error is in the orbit picture, while the lines test the energies and they agree

choices.label: She is right, because a model that gets one quantity wrong is wrong about all of them
She is wrong, because angular momentum cannot be tested by experiment
The error is in the orbit picture, while the lines test the energies and they agree

questions.onCorrect: The lines measure the energies and the model gets them right, while the angular momentum belongs to the circling-electron picture, which modern quantum mechanics replaced.

misconceptions.feedback: A model can fit some measurements and fail others. Each quantity has to be checked against its own measurement.
The passage says the true value is known from experiment, so it can be tested, and the model's value fails the test.

extracts.text: The Bohr model gives an incorrect value L=ħ for the ground state orbital angular momentum: The angular momentum in the true ground state is known to be zero from experiment.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by many contributors

questions.prompt: De Broglie's idea turns Bohr's rule into a standing-wave condition. In what order do the steps of the argument come?
hints: The wave has to exist before a condition on it can be stated.
The substitution can only be made once both the wavelength and the condition are in place.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The electron has a wavelength h/mv, a whole number n of those wavelengths must fit round the circumference, substituting the wavelength gives nh/mv = 2πr, and rearranging gives mvr = nħ.

items: The electron is described by a wave of wavelength $\lambda = h/mv$
A whole number $n$ of wavelengths must fit around the circumference, $n\lambda = 2\pi r$
Put the wavelength into this condition, $nh/mv = 2\pi r$
Rearrange to get $mvr = n\hbar$, which is Bohr's rule

questions.onCorrect: Each step needs the one before it, and the last line is the rule that Bohr had assumed without a reason.

questions.prompt: A student says that Bohr's model is obsolete, so everything it says about atoms can be ignored. What does the lesson's evidence support?
hints: Find a case where the model succeeds and a case where it fails.
A model can be useful in one part of its domain and useless outside it.

acceptedIdeas: It is a wrong picture of the atom but reliable inside its domain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a wrong picture of the atom but reliable inside its domain

choices.label: It is useless, since a model that fails for helium cannot be used for hydrogen
It is a wrong picture of the atom but reliable inside its domain
It is fully correct, since it gives hydrogen's lines almost exactly

questions.onCorrect: Bohr's model is still taught because it gives correct results for the systems in its domain and is the simplest way into energy-level diagrams.

misconceptions.feedback: The model is almost exact for hydrogen and other one-electron systems, and its failure for helium does not undo that.
It gives the lines, but it is wrong about the ground state's angular momentum and silent on many-electron atoms.

questions.prompt: An electron source is turned down until one electron crosses a double slit every few seconds, and each arrival is recorded on the screen as a dot. After many hours, what does the screen show?
hints: Each electron is recorded as a single dot, so the question is where the dots end up as they accumulate.
The bands were seen with a dense beam. Does the beam's density change where one electron can land?

acceptedIdeas: Single dots at scattered places that gradually form bright and dark bands
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Single dots at scattered places that gradually form bright and dark bands

choices.label: Single dots at scattered places that gradually form bright and dark bands
A smooth, even glow, because one electron at a time cannot make a pattern
Two bright stripes, one behind each slit, because each electron passes through one slit

questions.onCorrect: The dots look random at first, and the bands appear as they accumulate. The bands do not need electrons to interfere with one another.

misconceptions.feedback: A pattern can be built from separate arrivals, because each electron lands at one point and the points add up. The screen does not stay smooth.
Particles passing through two slits would make that, and the screen shows bands instead. The dots build up bands, which are the signature of a wave.

questions.prompt: Detectors are now placed at both slits, and they record which slit each electron crosses. What happens to the bands on the screen?
hints: Think about what knowing the slit means for a wave that goes through both slits.
The bands depend on the electron wave passing through both slits. What does a record of the path say about that?

acceptedIdeas: They disappear, because recording the path removes the interference
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They disappear, because recording the path removes the interference

choices.label: They grow brighter, because every electron is now counted
They stay the same, because a detector does not change where electrons land
They disappear, because recording the path removes the interference

questions.onCorrect: As soon as the path is detected, the interference disappears, and the screen shows no bands.

misconceptions.feedback: Counting an electron at a slit does not make the bands brighter. It changes the experiment, and the bands that appear without a record of the path are lost.
A detector that records the path does change where the electrons land in total. Every experiment of this kind has shown the bands disappear.

questions.prompt: In $\lambda = h/mv$ the speed is in the denominator. What does that say about an electron that moves faster?
hints: The product $mv$ is the electron's momentum.
If the bottom of a fraction grows, what happens to the fraction?

acceptedIdeas: It has more momentum, so its wavelength is shorter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has more momentum, so its wavelength is shorter

choices.label: It has more energy, so its wavelength is longer
It has more momentum, so its wavelength is shorter
Its wavelength is unchanged, since the wavelength depends only on its mass

questions.onCorrect: The wavelength is $h$ divided by the momentum, so a faster electron, with more momentum, has a shorter wavelength.

misconceptions.feedback: The wavelength is $h$ divided by the momentum, so more momentum makes the wavelength smaller and not larger.
The speed appears in the formula, so the wavelength depends on it as well as on the mass.

questions.prompt: An electron moves at $3.0 \times 10^6$ m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in nm? Use $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s and $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg.
hints: Use $\lambda = h/mv$, with the mass and speed multiplied in the denominator.
The denominator is $9.109 \times 10^{-31} \times 3.0 \times 10^6$, which is of order $10^{-24}$.
Convert the result from metres to nanometres by multiplying by $10^9$.
