questions.onCorrect: The wavelength is 0.242 nm, one third of the 0.727 nm of an electron at $1.0 \times 10^6$ m/s, because the speed is three times as large.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wavelength in units of $10^{-10}$ m. The question asks for nanometres, and 1 nm is $10^{-9}$ m.
That is the wavelength at $1.0 \times 10^6$ m/s. This electron is three times faster, so its wavelength is shorter.

questions.prompt: The electron at $1.0 \times 10^6$ m/s had a wavelength of 0.727 nm. The 0.145 kg ball (a made-up value) has far more momentum than that electron. How does the ball's wavelength compare?
hints: The wavelength is $h$ divided by the momentum $mv$.
Compare the ball's momentum with the electron's: is it far larger or far smaller?

acceptedIdeas: It is much shorter, because the momentum is far larger
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is much shorter, because the momentum is far larger

choices.label: It is much shorter, because the momentum is far larger
It is much longer, because the ball is far bigger
It is about the same, since every object has the same wavelength

questions.onCorrect: The ball's momentum is about $6 \times 10^{24}$ times the electron's, so its wavelength is smaller by about the same factor.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger object has more momentum for the same speed, and the wavelength is $h$ divided by the momentum, so it is shorter.
The wavelength depends on the momentum, and the ball's momentum is a very different number from the electron's.

questions.prompt: What is the ball's de Broglie wavelength, in units of $10^{-34}$ m?
hints: The ball's momentum is $0.145 \times 40$ in kg m/s.
Divide $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s by that momentum.
The answer is of order $10^{-34}$ m, so a result near 1 in these units is expected.
questions.onCorrect: The wavelength is $1.14 \times 10^{-34}$ m, a number far too small to matter in any apparatus.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wavelength of the electron. The ball has a much larger momentum, so its wavelength is far smaller.

questions.prompt: A made-up 0.145 kg ball thrown at 40 m/s has a de Broglie wavelength of about $1.1 \times 10^{-34}$ m. Why does a thrown ball never show diffraction?
hints: Fringe spacing grows with the wavelength, so ask how the ball's wavelength compares with any gap it could pass through.
Interference patterns have been seen with atoms and large molecules.

acceptedIdeas: The wavelength is far smaller than any gap it meets, so the fringes are too fine to see
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The wavelength is far smaller than any gap it meets, so the fringes are too fine to see

choices.label: Large objects have no wave nature at all, so only tiny particles can diffract
The wavelength is far smaller than any gap it meets, so the fringes are too fine to see
Heavy objects collapse into a single path as soon as they leave the thrower's hand

questions.onCorrect: The wave is present, but a wavelength of $10^{-34}$ m is smaller than any slit or spacing a ball could meet, so the pattern is far too fine to see.

misconceptions.feedback: Every object has a wavelength, and interference has been shown with atoms and even large molecules, so size alone does not remove the wave.
Nothing in the evidence makes heavy objects collapse into one path. The wave is still there, but its wavelength is far too small to notice.

questions.prompt: An electron is to have a de Broglie wavelength of 0.10 nm, about the width of a hydrogen atom, so that atoms can diffract it. How fast must it move, in units of $10^6$ m/s?
hints: Rearrange $\lambda = h/mv$ to give the speed.
The wavelength in metres is $1.0 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
Divide $h$ by the product of the mass and the wavelength.
questions.onCorrect: The electron must move at $7.3 \times 10^6$ m/s, about 2.4 per cent of the speed of light, which is fast but easily reached.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ten times too large, which comes from taking 0.10 nm as $10^{-11}$ m. Check that 0.10 nm is $1.0 \times 10^{-10}$ m.

questions.prompt: Electrons are sent through a double slit in five set-ups. Which of them show interference bands on the screen?
hints: Two things decide the screen: whether the path is recorded, and whether enough electrons have arrived.
A slow rate of arrival delays the pattern without removing it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The dense beam and the long one-at-a-time run show bands. The two runs with detectors at the slits show none, and neither do the first ten dots, which have not yet built a pattern.

items.label: A dense beam of electrons, with nothing recording which slit they use
items.explanation: A dense beam without a record of the path shows the bands, as a wave would.

items.label: Electrons sent one at a time for many hours, with nothing recording the path
items.explanation: The dots build up bands as they accumulate, although each electron arrives alone.

items.label: A detector at each slit records which slit every electron crosses
items.explanation: Recording the path removes the interference, so the screen shows no bands.

items.label: Electrons sent one at a time, with a detector at each slit
items.explanation: A record of the path removes the bands however slowly the electrons arrive.

items.label: Only the first ten dots of a one-at-a-time run with no detectors
items.explanation: Ten dots look random. The bands appear only after many arrivals have built up.

questions.onCorrect: The bands need a wave that goes through both slits and enough arrivals to show it, and a record of the path ends the wave behaviour.

questions.prompt: An electron is slowed to $5.0 \times 10^5$ m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in nm? Use $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s and $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg.
hints: A slower electron has less momentum, so ask whether its wavelength should be longer or shorter than 0.727 nm, the value at $1.0 \times 10^6$ m/s.
Use $\lambda = h/mv$ with $v = 5.0 \times 10^5$ m/s.
Convert from metres to nanometres at the end.
questions.onCorrect: At half the speed of the electron with a wavelength of 0.727 nm, the wavelength is twice as long, 1.45 nm, and that is several times the width of an atom.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wavelength at $2.0 \times 10^6$ m/s. This electron is slower than $1.0 \times 10^6$ m/s, so its wavelength is longer, not shorter.

questions.prompt: A beam of large molecules is sent through a double slit one molecule at a time, and each arrival is recorded as a dot. After a long run, what does the record show?
hints: Recall what was found for atoms and large molecules.
Does a molecule arriving alone change the way the pattern builds up?

acceptedIdeas: Single dots that gradually build up bands of interference, as electrons do
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Single dots that gradually build up bands of interference, as electrons do

choices.label: A smooth scatter of dots, since molecules are too heavy to behave as waves
Two stripes of dots, one behind each slit, since each goes through one slit
Single dots that gradually build up bands of interference, as electrons do

questions.onCorrect: The same dot-by-dot build-up of bands has been found with atoms and with large molecules, so the wave behaviour is not limited to electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: Interference has been shown with atoms and even large molecules, so a molecule's wave nature does not disappear because it is heavy.
The pattern is built up in the same way as for electrons, with bands rather than two stripes, when nothing records which slit each molecule used.

questions.prompt: A steady musical note is a wave of a single frequency, and a click lasts only a few milliseconds. How does the range of frequencies in the click compare with the note's?
hints: A wave of one frequency has no start and no end.
How many different waves must be added to cancel the sound everywhere except in one short interval?

acceptedIdeas: It is much wider, since a short sound is made by adding many frequencies
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is much wider, since a short sound is made by adding many frequencies

choices.label: It is much wider, since a short sound is made by adding many frequencies
It is narrower, since a short sound has less in it
It is the same, since frequencies do not depend on how long a sound lasts

questions.onCorrect: A narrow burst needs many frequencies added together. A wave packet that is narrow in position likewise needs many momenta.

misconceptions.feedback: A short sound has more frequencies in it, not fewer. Waves of one frequency go on for ever, and cancelling them everywhere except in one short moment takes many of them.
A single frequency means a wave that never stops, so a sound that stops needs other frequencies as well.

questions.prompt: The working gives $\Delta v \ge 2.9 \times 10^5$ m/s. Why is the result a least possible spread and not an exact one?
hints: Look at the sign between $\sigma_x \sigma_p$ and $\hbar/2$.
A spread larger than the least is allowed. Is a spread smaller than the least allowed?

acceptedIdeas: The relation is an inequality, so a real state can spread more but not less
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The relation is an inequality, so a real state can spread more but not less

choices.label: The numbers are rounded, so the true spread could be a little below this value
The relation is an inequality, so a real state can spread more but not less
The walls of the region add an extra spread to whatever the electron already has

questions.onCorrect: The relation $\sigma_x \sigma_p \ge \hbar/2$ sets a floor, so the speed spread of a real state is at least this value and can be more.

misconceptions.feedback: Rounding is not the reason. The relation says the product of the spreads can never fall below $\hbar/2$, however accurately the numbers are worked out.
The limit does not come from walls or other disturbances. It follows from the wave nature of the electron, and it holds even when nothing disturbs it.

questions.prompt: An electron is confined to a region 0.30 nm wide, about the size of an atom. Use $\Delta v \ge \hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$ with $\hbar = 1.0546 \times 10^{-34}$ J s and $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg. What is the least possible spread in its speed, in units of $10^5$ m/s?
hints: Write 0.30 nm in metres, $3.0 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
Multiply $2$, the electron's mass and $\Delta x$ to get the denominator, of order $10^{-40}$.
Divide $\hbar$ by it, and give the result in units of $10^5$ m/s.
questions.onCorrect: The speed of this electron is uncertain by at least $1.9 \times 10^5$ m/s, which is smaller than for the 0.20 nm case because the region is wider.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for 0.20 nm, the worked example's region. This region is wider, so the least spread in speed is smaller.

questions.prompt: What is the least spread in the electron's speed, in units of $10^6$ m/s?
hints: Use $\Delta v \ge \hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$ with $\Delta x = 5.29 \times 10^{-11}$ m.
The denominator $2m\,\Delta x$ is of order $10^{-40}$ in SI units.
Divide $\hbar = 1.0546 \times 10^{-34}$ J s by it.
questions.onCorrect: The least spread is $1.09 \times 10^6$ m/s, which is about 0.37 per cent of the speed of light.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for 0.20 nm in units of $10^6$ m/s. Here the region is much smaller, so the spread is larger.

questions.prompt: In Bohr's picture the electron in the smallest orbit moves at $2.19 \times 10^6$ m/s. How does the least spread in its speed compare with that speed?
hints: Divide the least spread by the speed in Bohr's picture.
A spread comparable to the speed itself means the speed is poorly defined.

acceptedIdeas: It is about half of it, so the speed is not sharply defined
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is about half of it, so the speed is not sharply defined

choices.label: It is far smaller, so the electron's speed is sharply defined
It is far larger, so the electron would fly out of the atom
It is about half of it, so the speed is not sharply defined

questions.onCorrect: A spread of half the speed itself means that an electron confined to the size of an atom has no sharply defined speed, and the picture of a definite orbit fails.

misconceptions.feedback: The least spread is $1.09 \times 10^6$ m/s, which is half of $2.19 \times 10^6$ m/s and nowhere near far smaller.
The least spread is half the speed, not far larger, and a spread in speed is not a motion away from the atom.

questions.prompt: A student says: "Position and momentum cannot both be sharp because measuring one kicks the other, and gentler instruments would remove the limit." What is the best correction?
hints: Recall what a narrow wave packet in position requires in momentum.
Would a better instrument change the wave nature of the particle?

acceptedIdeas: The limit follows from the particle's wave nature, so no gentler instrument beats it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The limit follows from the particle's wave nature, so no gentler instrument beats it

choices.label: The limit follows from the particle's wave nature, so no gentler instrument beats it
She is right about the kick, but the limit applies only to electrons and atoms
She is right, since with gentler instruments the kick could be made as small as wished

questions.onCorrect: A narrow packet is a sum of many wavelengths, so a sharp position means a wide spread of momentum whatever instrument is used.

misconceptions.feedback: Every object has a matter wave, so the limit applies to all of them. For large objects it is negligible, which is different from absent.
That is Heisenberg's first picture, and it is now understood to be misleading. The limit belongs to the wave nature of the particle and would remain with any instrument.

questions.prompt: A baseball of mass 0.145 kg (a made-up value) is located to within 1 mm. The relation gives a least speed spread of about $4 \times 10^{-31}$ m/s. What does that mean for a pitcher?
hints: Compare $4 \times 10^{-31}$ m/s with the speed of a pitched ball.
The relation limits pairs of properties together, and does not say that either is unknowable.

acceptedIdeas: The limit is there but far too small to matter for a baseball
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The limit is there but far too small to matter for a baseball

choices.label: Baseballs are not subject to the limit, because they are not quantum objects
The limit is there but far too small to matter for a baseball
The ball cannot be aimed, because its position cannot be known

questions.onCorrect: A speed spread of $10^{-31}$ m/s is smaller than anything that any instrument could detect, so the baseball behaves as an ordinary object.

misconceptions.feedback: Every object has a matter wave, so the limit applies to the baseball as well. It is negligible for it, which is different from absent.
The relation limits the product of the two spreads, and each can be known well alone. This spread in speed is far below anything that could matter.

questions.prompt: Two excited states of an atom emit photons of nearly the same energy. State A lasts about 1 ns before it decays and state B about 1 microsecond. Which emission line is broader, and why?
hints: A state with a short lifetime exists for few cycles of its own frequency.
Fast-decaying states and slow-decaying states have lines of different widths. Which are broad?

acceptedIdeas: A's line, because a state that exists only briefly cannot have a definite energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A's line, because a state that exists only briefly cannot have a definite energy

choices.label: A's line, because a state that exists only briefly cannot have a definite energy
B's line, because a longer-lived state suffers more collisions and so broadens
The two lines are equally broad, because the photon energy is set by the levels alone

questions.onCorrect: The width of the line is inversely proportional to the lifetime, so A's line is about a thousand times broader than B's.

misconceptions.feedback: The natural width comes from the finite lifetime and not from collisions. The longer-lived state has the better defined energy and the narrower line.
A state's energy is not exactly fixed when its lifetime is finite, so the photon energies are spread, and the spread grows as the lifetime shrinks.

questions.prompt: An electron's speed is known to within $1.0 \times 10^4$ m/s. What is the smallest region that it can be confined to, in nm to one decimal place? Use $\hbar = 1.0546 \times 10^{-34}$ J s and $m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg.
hints: Rearrange $\Delta v \ge \hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$ to give $\Delta x$ in terms of $\Delta v$.
A speed known very well means a very small $\Delta v$. Should that give a larger or a smaller least region?
Convert the result from metres to nanometres at the end.
questions.onCorrect: A speed known this well forces the electron into a region at least 5.8 nm wide, much larger than an atom, because sharp momentum means a spread-out wave.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result in micrometres. Check the conversion: 1 nm is $10^{-9}$ m.

questions.prompt: Four cases have their position fixed as described. Put them in order of the least spread in speed that the uncertainty relation allows, the largest first.
hints: The least speed spread is $\hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$, so it falls as either the mass or the region grows.
Compare the products of mass and region size, the smaller product giving the larger spread.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The electron in 52.9 pm has the largest spread, about 1.1e6 m/s, then the electron in 0.30 nm, about 1.9e5 m/s, then the dust grain, about 5e-20 m/s, and the baseball last, about 4e-31 m/s.

items: A dust grain of 1.0 microgram located to 1 micrometre (made up)
A baseball of 0.145 kg located to 1 mm (made up)

questions.onCorrect: The speed spread varies inversely with the product of mass and region size, and that product is smallest for the electron in 52.9 pm and largest for the baseball.

questions.prompt: The extract gives the quantum limit on the position of one mirror in a gravitational-wave interferometer. For a mirror of mass $m$ watched for a time $\tau$ the limit is $\sqrt{2\hbar\tau/m}$. A second mirror is four times as heavy and is watched for the same time. How does its limit compare?
hints: In $\sqrt{2\hbar\tau/m}$ the mass is in the denominator, under a square root.
What is the square root of one quarter?

acceptedIdeas: It is half as large, since the limit varies as the inverse square root of the mass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is half as large, since the limit varies as the inverse square root of the mass

choices.label: It is a quarter as large, since the limit varies in inverse proportion to the mass
It is the same, since a mirror this heavy is too massive to have a quantum limit
It is half as large, since the limit varies as the inverse square root of the mass

questions.onCorrect: The limit goes as $1/\sqrt{m}$, so four times the mass gives half the limit. Heavier mirrors are easier to measure, but the limit never reaches zero.

misconceptions.feedback: The mass sits under a square root, so multiplying it by 4 divides the limit by 2 and not by 4.
Every object has a limit, and the formula depends on the mass, so a heavier mirror has a smaller one. It does not disappear.

extracts.text: For a mirror of mass 1×10⁵ gm measured over 2×10⁻³ s will be limited in accuracy to 6×10⁻¹⁸ cm.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by many contributors

questions.prompt: An electron travelling through a vacuum meets a thin insulating barrier and has less energy than it would need to climb over it. Classical mechanics says that every such electron is turned back. Many identical electrons are fired at the barrier. What does a detector on the far side record, according to quantum theory?
hints: Think about how the wave that describes a particle behaves when it meets a barrier. Does it stop dead at the edge?
If part of the wave gets through, what does that say about how often the particle is found on the far side?

acceptedIdeas: A few of them, because each has a small chance of being found beyond it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A few of them, because each has a small chance of being found beyond it

choices.label: None of them, because every electron lacks the energy to climb the barrier
A few of them, because each has a small chance of being found beyond it
All of them, because a wave is not stopped by a barrier

questions.onCorrect: A wave does not end at the edge of a barrier, so part of it reaches the far side, and the size of that part gives the chance of finding the electron there.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the classical prediction, and measurements contradict it: electrons do cross barriers like this one, and the current in a scanning tunnelling microscope is the evidence. Quantum theory gives each electron a small chance of being found on the far side.
Most of the wave is reflected, so most electrons are turned back. Only a small part of the wave gets through, and the chance of crossing is correspondingly small.

questions.prompt: A wave packet meets a barrier, and the transmitted part is much smaller than the reflected part. Identical electrons are then fired at the barrier one at a time, with a detector beyond it. What does the detector record?
hints: The square of the wave's size gives the probability of finding the particle at a place, and the probabilities add up to one.
A detector either finds an electron or does not. How often would it find one if the transmitted part of the packet is small?

acceptedIdeas: Whole electrons, but only in a small fraction of the individual runs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whole electrons, but only in a small fraction of the individual runs

choices.label: A weak signal from every electron, each carrying a fraction of it
Nothing at all, because a small part of the packet cannot trigger a detector
Whole electrons, but only in a small fraction of the individual runs

questions.onCorrect: The transmitted part is a probability and not a share of the electron, so each electron is found whole on one side, and only a small fraction of them are found beyond the barrier.

misconceptions.feedback: The packet gives the probability of finding the electron somewhere, and the total probability stays equal to one. Each electron is found on one side or the other, so the transmitted part sets how often it is found beyond the barrier.
A small transmitted part means a small probability, and a small probability is still a probability. In a long series of runs some electrons are found beyond the barrier.

questions.prompt: An electron beam meets an insulating barrier 1 nm thick, and a small fraction of the electrons tunnel through. The barrier is replaced by one 2 nm thick, of the same height, and the electrons are unchanged. How does the tunnelling probability change?
hints: Does each extra nanometre of barrier subtract a fixed amount from the probability, or multiply it by a fixed factor?
If the chance is already small and is multiplied by a factor smaller than one a second time, how does the fall compare with halving?

acceptedIdeas: It falls by far more than half, as the decrease with width is exponential
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls by far more than half, as the decrease with width is exponential

choices.label: It halves, because the probability is inversely proportional to the width
It falls to zero, because nothing tunnels through a barrier that thick
It falls by far more than half, as the decrease with width is exponential

questions.onCorrect: Doubling the width multiplies the probability by the same factor again, so a chance that was already small becomes much smaller, though it never reaches zero.

misconceptions.feedback: An inverse proportion would give only half as much. The probability decreases exponentially with width, so each extra step of width multiplies it by the same factor, and the fall is far steeper than that.
There is no thickness at which tunnelling switches off. The probability falls smoothly and steeply, and the thicker barrier still lets a very small fraction through.

questions.prompt: Three experiments send particles of the same energy at barriers of the same height. In the first, electrons meet a barrier 1 nm wide. In the second, electrons meet a barrier 3 nm wide. In the third, protons meet a barrier 1 nm wide. In which is tunnelling most likely?
hints: Change one thing at a time: compare the first and second experiments, then the first and third.
Width and mass both lower the probability. Which experiment is better than the others on both counts?

acceptedIdeas: The first, with electrons at the 1 nm barrier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first, with electrons at the 1 nm barrier

choices.label: The first, with electrons at the 1 nm barrier
The second, with electrons at the 3 nm barrier
The third, with protons at the 1 nm barrier

questions.onCorrect: The first experiment has the narrowest barrier and the lightest particle, so it beats each of the others on a factor that lowers the probability.

misconceptions.feedback: A wider barrier lowers the probability exponentially, and the electrons are no lighter than in the first experiment, so the second cannot be the most likely.
A proton is heavier than an electron, and the probability falls exponentially as the particle gets heavier, so the third is less likely than the first.

questions.prompt: A scanning tunnelling microscope holds its tunnelling current constant as the tip scans across a surface. The tip passes over a single atom that sits on top of the surface. What does the instrument do to the tip?
hints: The tunnelling current depends steeply on the width of the gap, and the feedback holds the current constant.
When the tip is over a bump, does the gap grow or shrink, and what must the tip do to put it back?

acceptedIdeas: It raises the tip, so that the gap and the current stay the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It raises the tip, so that the gap and the current stay the same

choices.label: It raises the tip, so that the gap and the current stay the same
It lowers the tip, so that the current rises to follow the atom
It leaves the tip alone, because 0.001 nm is too small to change the current

questions.onCorrect: The narrower gap would raise the current, so the feedback lifts the tip, and the recorded voltages on the piezoelectric rods follow the height of the surface.

misconceptions.feedback: Over the atom the gap narrows, which would raise the current. Holding the current constant means widening the gap again, so the tip must rise and not fall.
The current depends so steeply on the gap that a change of 0.001 nm is easy to detect. That steepness is what lets the instrument follow single atoms.

questions.prompt: A metal tip at room temperature gives off a current of electrons when a very strong electric field is applied to it, and the current grows roughly exponentially as the field is raised further. Which explanation fits?
hints: Ask whether the electrons go over the barrier or through it, and what a strong field does to the barrier's thickness.
The explanation has to work for a tip that is not heated, and for a current that rises roughly exponentially with the field.

acceptedIdeas: The field thins the barrier until electrons are able to tunnel through it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The field thins the barrier until electrons are able to tunnel through it

choices.label: The field heats the tip until electrons gain enough energy to climb the barrier
The field thins the barrier until electrons are able to tunnel through it
Electrons borrow energy from the field for long enough to climb the barrier

questions.onCorrect: A strong field makes the barrier thin enough for electrons to tunnel out, which is why the current grows roughly exponentially with the field.

misconceptions.feedback: That describes thermionic emission, in which electrons that happen to have more energy than the barrier go over it. The tip here is at room temperature, and the exponential growth with the field points to a different mechanism.
Tunnelling does not work by climbing. The wave of the electron passes through a barrier that has become thin, and the electron does not need the energy to get over the top.

questions.prompt: An experiment is reported to show particles tunnelling at apparent speeds faster than light. The extract summarises how other physicists replied. What does the evidence support?
hints: Read what the extract says the group velocity measures. Is it the speed of the particle?
The extract also mentions mathematical theorems about tunnelling in relativistic theory. What do they conclude?

acceptedIdeas: Group velocity is not speed, and theory forbids faster-than-light tunnelling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Group velocity is not speed, and theory forbids faster-than-light tunnelling

choices.label: Group velocity is not speed, and theory forbids faster-than-light tunnelling
Tunnelling is faster than light, so relativity fails for tunnelling particles
Tunnelling takes no time, because the particle is on both sides at once

questions.onCorrect: Group velocity does not measure speed, and relativistic theory implies that tunnelling is subluminal, so the claim is disputed and the theory does not support it.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says the opposite: theorems from relativistic theory imply the process is completely subluminal. An apparent speed does not show that anything travelled faster than light.

The wave is spread over both sides, but the extract ties the group velocity to the time the packet is stored in the barrier. That time is not zero, and a probability on both sides does not mean zero time.

extracts.text: In particular, the group velocity of a wave packet does not measure its speed, but is related to the amount of time the wave packet is stored in the barrier. Moreover, if quantum tunnelling is modelled with the relativistic Dirac equation, well established mathematical theorems imply that the process is completely subluminal.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article for general readers, here reporting a physicist's reply to the faster-than-light claims

questions.prompt: Six processes are listed. Which of them depend on quantum tunnelling, and which do not?
hints: For each process, ask whether the particles have enough energy to go over the barrier or whether they must go through it.
Heating gives particles more energy to climb with. Tunnelling needs no extra energy at all.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Alpha decay, stellar fusion, emission in a strong field and leakage depend on tunnelling, while a hot cathode and a ball that can climb the hill do not.

questions.onCorrect: Alpha decay, stellar fusion, strong-field emission and leakage all send particles through a barrier. Hot-cathode emission and the ball both go over it.

items.label: Alpha decay of a heavy nucleus
items.explanation: The alpha particle leaks out through the barrier that holds it in the nucleus, as Gamow, Gurney and Condon showed in 1928.

items.label: Electrons leaving a hot cathode with more energy than the barrier
items.explanation: These electrons have more energy than the barrier needs, so they go over it, which is thermionic emission.

items.label: Fusion of hydrogen in a star's core
items.explanation: A core is generally too cool for nuclei to climb the Coulomb barrier, and tunnelling lets enough of them through.

items.label: A ball rolling over a hill it has enough energy to climb
items.explanation: With enough energy the ball goes over the top, and no tunnelling is needed.

items.label: Electrons pulled out of a metal tip by a very strong electric field
items.explanation: The strong field thins the barrier until electrons can tunnel out, which is cold emission.

items.label: Leakage current through a 1 nm insulating layer in a chip
items.explanation: Electrons tunnel readily through insulating layers thinner than about 1 nm.

questions.prompt: In an invented reaction, hydrogen nuclei must tunnel through an energy barrier for the reaction to proceed. The reaction is repeated with deuterium, whose nucleus has a neutron added and so about twice the mass, and the barrier is the same. What do you expect?
hints: The probability falls exponentially as the barrier gets higher, as it gets wider and as the particle gets heavier.
Deuterium differs from hydrogen by one neutron. What does that do to the mass, with the barrier unchanged?

acceptedIdeas: Tunnelling becomes less likely, because the particle is heavier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tunnelling becomes less likely, because the particle is heavier

choices.label: Tunnelling becomes more likely, because a heavier particle carries more energy
Tunnelling becomes less likely, because the particle is heavier
Nothing changes, because the barrier is the same

questions.onCorrect: The barrier is unchanged but the mass has doubled, and the probability decreases exponentially with mass, so deuterium tunnels less readily.

misconceptions.feedback: The probability decreases exponentially as the tunnelling particle gets heavier. A heavier particle does not gain energy with its mass, and it is the mass that matters for the barrier.
The barrier is one of three things that set the probability. The particle's mass is another, and doubling it lowers the probability.

questions.prompt: A student argues that tunnelling is a rare curiosity that never matters outside a physics laboratory. Which evidence best answers her?
hints: Her claim is about where tunnelling matters, so look for evidence that names devices, nuclei or stars.
A true fact that does not bear on whether tunnelling matters outside a laboratory is not an answer to her.

acceptedIdeas: Leakage in chips, alpha decay and fusion in stars all depend on it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leakage in chips, alpha decay and fusion in stars all depend on it

choices.label: It has been observed with protons and even with whole atoms
It was predicted in the early twentieth century, before anyone saw it
Leakage in chips, alpha decay and fusion in stars all depend on it

questions.onCorrect: Chips leak by it, nuclei decay by it and the Sun's core fuses by it, so it shapes devices and stars, and it is not confined to a laboratory.

misconceptions.feedback: That is true, but it says nothing about whether tunnelling matters outside a laboratory. Observations with heavier particles do not answer her claim.
When it was predicted has no bearing on whether it matters in everyday devices, nuclei and stars, which is what her claim is about.

questions.prompt: The activity of a sample of one radioactive isotope falls from 800 Bq to 400 Bq in 3.0 hours. What is its activity after a further 3.0 hours?
hints: Ask whether the sample loses a fixed amount of activity in each interval, or a fixed fraction of what it has.
Each remaining atom has the same chance of decaying as any other. What does that say about the fraction of the sample that decays in the second 3.0 hours?

acceptedIdeas: 200 Bq, because half of the atoms that remain decay in each 3.0 hours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 200 Bq, because half of the atoms that remain decay in each 3.0 hours

choices.label: 0 Bq, because it loses the same amount of activity in each 3.0 hours
200 Bq, because half of the atoms that remain decay in each 3.0 hours
Below 200 Bq, because the atoms that remain are older and decay sooner

questions.onCorrect: The activity halves again, to 200 Bq, because each atom that remains has the same chance of decaying as before.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the fall as a fixed amount for each interval. A decaying sample has fewer atoms left to decay, so its activity falls by a fixed fraction, and a fixed fraction of what is left is never all of it.
An atom does not become likelier to decay as it ages. Its chance of decaying in any interval stays the same however long it has existed, so the older atoms are no likelier to go.

questions.prompt: A source with a half-life of 3.0 hours has an activity of 800 Bq at the start. What is its activity after 7.5 hours, in becquerels?
hints: First find how many half-lives 7.5 hours is.
The activity is 800 Bq multiplied by 2 raised to minus that number of half-lives.
After two half-lives the activity would be 200 Bq and after three it would be 100 Bq, so the answer lies between those.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7.5 h is 7.5 ÷ 3.0 = 2.5 half-lives, so $A = 800 \times 2^{-2.5} = 800 \times 0.1768 = 141$ Bq, between the 200 Bq of two half-lives and the 100 Bq of three.

questions.onCorrect: A non-integer number of half-lives works in the same formula as a whole one, and the answer falls between the values for two and for three half-lives.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the activity after exactly two half-lives, which is 6.0 hours. 7.5 hours is longer than that, so the activity is lower.
That divides 800 by 2.5. The number 2.5 counts half-lives, so it belongs in the exponent: the activity is 800 multiplied by 2 to the power of minus 2.5.

questions.prompt: A single radioactive atom has survived for exactly one half-life. What is the chance that it decays during the next half-life?
hints: Ask whether an atom that has lasted a long time is any more likely to decay than a new one.
A half-life is the time in which half of a large number of atoms decay. What chance does that give each one?

acceptedIdeas: 50%, since an atom has no memory of how long it has lasted
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 50%, since an atom has no memory of how long it has lasted

choices.label: More than 50%, because an older atom is due to decay
Nothing can be said, because the decay of one atom is random
50%, since an atom has no memory of how long it has lasted

questions.onCorrect: Every atom has a 50% chance of decaying in each half-life, whatever its age, and it is the large number of atoms that turns this fixed chance into a smooth curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the atom as wearing out. A nucleus has no memory of its age, so the chance of decaying in the next half-life is the same as it was in the first.
The moment of one atom's decay is random, but the chance of it decaying in a given time is fixed and known. Random timing does not mean an unknown probability.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 2,000 atoms of bismuth-212. About how many of them are expected to decay by beta emission to polonium-212? Give your answer to the nearest ten.
hints: Look for the percentage that decays by beta emission.
Multiply the number of atoms by that percentage, written as a fraction.
Check that your answer and the number taking the alpha route add up to 2,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 64.06% of 2,000 is 0.6406 × 2,000 = 1,281, which is 1,280 to the nearest ten. The other 719 or so decay by alpha emission to thallium-208.

questions.onCorrect: About 64 atoms in every 100 take the beta route, whatever the size of the sample, and each single atom takes one route or the other at random.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number expected to decay by alpha emission, which is 35.94% of 2,000. The question asks about beta emission.
That assumes the two routes are equally likely. The branching ratios are 35.94% for alpha and 64.06% for beta.

questions.prompt: A student works out that the artefact giving 4 decays per minute per gram is 10,302 years old, and writes down that figure. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5700 years with an uncertainty of 30 years. What is the best comment on "10,302 years"?
hints: Work out what an uncertainty of 30 years is as a fraction of 5700 years.
A result cannot be more certain than the numbers it was calculated from.

acceptedIdeas: It has too many digits, since the half-life alone leaves about 50 years of doubt
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has too many digits, since the half-life alone leaves about 50 years of doubt

choices.label: It is exact, because the decay law gives an exact age for any measured activity
It has too many digits, since the half-life alone leaves about 50 years of doubt
It is too imprecise, because the calculation could be carried to more decimal places

questions.onCorrect: An uncertainty of 30 in 5700 is about 0.5%, which is about 50 years in an age of 10,300, so only the first three or four figures mean anything.

misconceptions.feedback: The law is exact in form, but the age is calculated from a measured half-life and measured activities, and none of them is exact. The half-life alone carries 30 years in 5700, about 0.5%, into the age.
More decimal places would claim even more precision than the numbers behind the result can support. A result cannot be more certain than the data it was calculated from.

questions.prompt: Two samples contain the same number of atoms. The atoms of sample A have a half-life of 10 minutes and those of sample B a half-life of 10 years, and both isotopes are invented. Which sample has the greater activity at the start?
hints: Activity counts decays per second. Which atoms are likelier to decay in any given second?
A short half-life means a sample is quickly spent. What does that say about how often its atoms decay?

acceptedIdeas: Sample A, because each of its atoms is likelier to decay in any second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sample A, because each of its atoms is likelier to decay in any second

choices.label: Sample A, because each of its atoms is likelier to decay in any second
Sample B, because its long-lived atoms go on decaying for years and years on end
Neither, because the two samples have the same number of atoms

questions.onCorrect: A short half-life means a high chance of decay in each second, so the same number of atoms gives a higher activity and the sample is used up sooner.

misconceptions.feedback: A long half-life means each atom is unlikely to decay in any given second, so the decays come far less often. Lasting longer is the same as decaying more slowly.
Activity is the number of decays per second, and it depends on the chance each atom has of decaying as well as on how many atoms there are.

questions.prompt: Six predictions are listed about atoms of one radioactive isotope. Which of them can a physicist make, and which can nobody make?
hints: Ask whether each prediction is about one atom or about a large number of atoms.
A fixed chance can be stated exactly. The outcome of a single chance event cannot.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Predictions about a single atom's moment or route cannot be made, while predictions about fractions, chances and activities of many atoms can.

questions.onCorrect: The moment of one decay, which atom goes next and one atom's route cannot be predicted. The fraction left, the chance in a half-life and the activity after four half-lives can.

items.label: The moment at which one chosen atom will decay
items.explanation: Decay is random for a single atom, and quantum theory makes its moment impossible to predict.

items.label: About what fraction of a large sample is left after three half-lives
items.explanation: Each half-life halves what is left, so about an eighth remains.

items.label: Which atom in the sample will be the next to decay
items.explanation: Every atom has the same chance, so no atom can be singled out in advance.

items.label: The chance that an old atom decays in the next half-life
items.explanation: It is 50%, the same as for a new atom, because an atom has no memory of its age.

items.label: The activity of a source after four half-lives, given its starting activity
items.explanation: It is the starting activity divided by 2 four times over, which is 16.

items.label: Whether one bismuth-212 atom will decay by alpha or by beta emission
items.explanation: Only the percentages, 35.94% and 64.06%, can be stated. Which route one atom takes is chance.

questions.prompt: A source has an activity of 640 Bq, and 2.0 hours later its activity is 40 Bq (an invented source). What is its half-life, in minutes?
hints: Halve 640 Bq repeatedly until you reach 40 Bq, and count the halvings.
The time divided by the number of halvings is the half-life.
The time is given in hours and the answer is wanted in minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 → 40 is four halvings, so 2.0 h is four half-lives, and 120 min ÷ 4 = 30 min.

questions.onCorrect: Four halvings fit in 120 minutes, so each half-life is 30 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 120 minutes by 16, the ratio of the two activities. The ratio is 2 raised to the number of halvings, so count the halvings instead.
That is the half-life in hours. The question asks for minutes.

questions.prompt: Living carbon gives 14 decays per minute per gram, and the carbon in a bone gives 5. Taking the half-life of carbon-14 as 5700 years, how old is the bone, to the nearest hundred years?
hints: Find the fraction of the carbon-14 that is left, and the number of half-lives that fraction represents.
The number of half-lives is ln(14/5) divided by ln 2, and the age is that number multiplied by 5700 years.
Check the size: an activity of 7 would be one half-life and 3.5 would be two, so 5 lies between them and the age lies between 5700 and 11,400 years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 ÷ 14 is 0.357, and $\ln(14/5) \div \ln 2 = 1.0296 \div 0.6931 = 1.485$ half-lives, so $t = 1.485 \times 5700$ y $= 8{,}467$ y, which is 8,500 y to the nearest hundred.

questions.onCorrect: The activity is between the values for one and two half-lives, so the age is between 5700 and 11,400 years, and the logarithm gives 1.485 half-lives, or about 8,500 years.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of half-lives. Multiply it by the half-life of 5700 years to get the age.
That is one half-life, which would give an activity of 7. The bone's activity is lower than that, so it is older.

questions.prompt: Why does the 9.0 hours in the example count as three half-lives?
hints: Halve the activity, starting from 800 Bq, and see how many halvings it takes to reach 100 Bq.
A half-life halves what is left. It does not remove a fixed amount.

acceptedIdeas: The activity halved three times on the way from 800 Bq to 100 Bq
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The activity halved three times on the way from 800 Bq to 100 Bq

choices.label: The activity halved three times on the way from 800 Bq to 100 Bq
The activity fell to an eighth, so that is eight half-lives
The activity fell by 700 Bq, and each half-life removes 100 Bq of that

questions.onCorrect: Each halving takes one half-life, and three halvings take the activity from 800 Bq to 100 Bq.

misconceptions.feedback: A fall to one eighth takes three halvings, since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. The number of half-lives is the number of halvings, which is the power of 2 that gives the ratio of the activities.
A half-life removes half of what is left, and not a fixed amount. The first removes 400 Bq, the next 200 Bq and the last 100 Bq, which is three halvings in all.

questions.prompt: Why does an activity of 4 decays per minute mean that the age is a little under 11,400 years?
hints: Halve 14 once and then again, and see where 4 falls among the values.
Each halving is one half-life, which is 5700 years.

acceptedIdeas: Two half-lives would leave 3.5, and 4 is slightly more than that
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two half-lives would leave 3.5, and 4 is slightly more than that

choices.label: Four is nearly half of 14, so it is a little under one half-life
Two half-lives would leave 3.5, and 4 is slightly more than that
The age cannot be estimated until the logarithm has been worked out

questions.onCorrect: Two half-lives would leave 3.5, and the artefact has slightly more than that, so it has lasted slightly less than two half-lives.

misconceptions.feedback: Half of 14 is 7, and 4 is well below that, so more than one half-life has passed. Two half-lives would leave 3.5, and 4 is a little above it.
A rough estimate comes first from halving: 14 goes to 7 and then to 3.5. The logarithm then gives the exact figure, and the estimate gives a check on it.

questions.prompt: A helium atom contains four nucleons, and each of four hydrogen atoms contains one. How does the mass of the helium atom compare with the combined mass of the four hydrogen atoms?
hints: Think about what happens to energy when nucleons bind together, and what E = mc² says about energy and mass.
If energy leaves the atom as the nucleus forms, what must have happened to the mass that goes with that energy?

acceptedIdeas: It is smaller, because energy left when the nucleus formed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is smaller, because energy left when the nucleus formed

choices.label: It is smaller, because energy left when the nucleus formed
It is the same, because the number of nucleons is the same
It is greater, because binding the nucleons together adds mass

questions.onCorrect: Energy left when the nucleons bound together, and mass left with it, so the helium atom has about 0.8% less mass than four hydrogen atoms.

misconceptions.feedback: Masses do not simply add up with the particle count. The helium atom is lighter, because energy left when its nucleons bound together, and the energy took mass with it.
Binding releases energy, and removing energy removes mass, so a bound nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons. It does not have more.

questions.prompt: Splitting uranium loses about 0.1% of the starting mass of each atom. How much energy is released when 1.0 kg of uranium fissions completely, in units of 10¹³ J?
hints: Find the mass that is lost: 0.1% of 1.0 kg.
Multiply the lost mass by c², which is 8.99 × 10¹⁶ J for every kilogram.
Uranium loses one eighth as much of its mass as hydrogen does, so check that your answer is about one eighth of the hydrogen case.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mass lost is 0.001 × 1.0 kg = 0.0010 kg, and E = 0.0010 kg × 8.99 × 10¹⁶ J/kg = 8.99 × 10¹³ J.

questions.onCorrect: The 0.0010 kg that is lost corresponds to 8.99 × 10¹³ J, about one eighth of what a kilogram of hydrogen gives.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 1% of the mass, 0.010 kg. The loss in fission is 0.1%, which is 0.0010 kg of each kilogram.
That uses 0.01% of the mass. The loss is 0.1% of 1.0 kg, which is 0.0010 kg.

questions.prompt: A nucleus with about 120 nucleons lies on the slowly falling part of the binding energy curve, beyond mass 90. Which change would release energy?
hints: Which way along the curve does each change move the nuclei, towards the peak or away from it?
Energy is released when the average binding energy per nucleon goes up.

acceptedIdeas: It splits into two nuclei with about 60 nucleons apiece
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It splits into two nuclei with about 60 nucleons apiece

choices.label: It fuses with a second nucleus of about 120 nucleons
Neither, because only changes that destroy nucleons release energy
It splits into two nuclei with about 60 nucleons apiece

questions.onCorrect: Two nuclei of about 60 nucleons sit at the top of the curve, so the split climbs it, and the gain in binding energy per nucleon leaves as energy.

misconceptions.feedback: Fusing two nuclei of this size moves the product further down the falling side of the curve, so the binding energy per nucleon drops and energy has to be put in.
No nucleon is destroyed in fission or fusion. Energy is released when the nucleons end up more tightly bound, and the mass lost is the binding energy released.

questions.prompt: The binding energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV, and the binding energy of a tritium nucleus is 8.4820 MeV. How many times larger is the nuclear binding energy? Give your answer in units of 10⁵.
hints: Convert both energies to the same unit first: 1 MeV is 10⁶ eV.
Divide the tritium binding energy in eV by 13.6 eV.
The ratio is several hundred thousand, so in units of 10⁵ it is a single-digit number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8.4820 MeV is 8.4820 × 10⁶ eV, and 8.4820 × 10⁶ ÷ 13.6 = 6.24 × 10⁵, so the nuclear binding energy is about 6.2 × 10⁵ times larger.

questions.onCorrect: The tritium nucleus is bound about 620,000 times as strongly as the electron in hydrogen, and that is why a nuclear change releases so much more energy than a chemical one.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 8.4820 by 13.6 without converting MeV to eV, so it compares MeV with eV directly. One MeV is a million eV.
That is the ratio itself. The question asks for it in units of 10⁵, so divide by 100,000.

questions.prompt: A reactor fissions 1.0 kg of uranium, releasing 9.0 × 10¹³ J. What mass of hydrogen, fusing into helium with a loss of about 0.8% of its mass, would release the same energy, in kilograms?
hints: Find the energy that 1.0 kg of fusing hydrogen releases, using 0.8% of its mass and 8.99 × 10¹⁶ J for each kilogram of mass.
Divide the energy wanted by the energy from one kilogram.
Uranium loses a smaller fraction of its mass than hydrogen does, so the answer should be less than one kilogram.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1.0 kg of fusing hydrogen releases 0.008 × 8.99 × 10¹⁶ = 7.19 × 10¹⁴ J, so the mass needed is 9.0 × 10¹³ ÷ 7.19 × 10¹⁴ = 0.125 kg.

questions.onCorrect: About an eighth of a kilogram of hydrogen does the work of a kilogram of uranium, because fusion turns a larger fraction of the fuel's mass into energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many times more energy a kilogram of hydrogen gives. The mass needed is the inverse of that, one eighth of a kilogram.

questions.prompt: Five nuclear changes are listed. Which of them release energy, and which need energy to be put in?
hints: For each change, ask whether the products lie nearer the peak of the curve than the starting nuclei do.
Moving towards the peak releases energy, and moving away from it needs energy.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Solar fusion, uranium fission and deuterium fusion release energy, and fusing two nuclei heavier than iron or splitting iron-56 need energy put in.

questions.onCorrect: Fusing four protons into helium, splitting uranium and fusing deuterium release energy, while fusing two nuclei heavier than iron and splitting iron need it.

items.label: Four protons fuse into a helium nucleus in the Sun
items.explanation: Light nuclei fusing climb the rising side of the curve, so the products are more tightly bound and the difference leaves as energy.

items.label: A uranium nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei
items.explanation: Uranium lies on the falling side of the curve, and its pieces sit nearer the peak.

items.label: Two similar nuclei, each heavier than iron, fuse together
items.explanation: Fusing similar nuclei beyond iron moves further down the falling side, so energy is consumed.

items.label: An iron-56 nucleus is split into two lighter nuclei
items.explanation: Iron sits at the peak of the curve, so its pieces are less tightly bound and energy has to be supplied.

items.label: Deuterium nuclei fuse into helium
items.explanation: Energy-producing interactions between hydrogen isotopes are fusion, and the helium product is more tightly bound.

questions.prompt: In the Sun, hydrogen becomes helium and loses about 0.8% of its mass. What mass of hydrogen must fuse to release 1.0 × 10¹⁵ J, in kilograms?
hints: Find the energy that 1.0 kg of hydrogen releases: 0.008 of its mass times 8.99 × 10¹⁶ J for each kilogram.
Divide the energy wanted by the energy from one kilogram.
One kilogram gives a little under 10¹⁵ J, so the mass needed is a little over one kilogram.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each kilogram releases 0.008 × 8.99 × 10¹⁶ = 7.19 × 10¹⁴ J, so 1.0 × 10¹⁵ J ÷ 7.19 × 10¹⁴ J/kg = 1.39 kg.

questions.onCorrect: A little under 10¹⁵ J comes from each kilogram of fusing hydrogen, so 1.0 × 10¹⁵ J takes about 1.4 kg.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy from 1 kg in units of 10¹⁵ J. Divide the energy wanted by it to find the mass.

questions.prompt: A student says that fission could not release any energy without relativity, because E = mc² is what makes the energy possible. The extract comes from an article on mass-energy equivalence. What reply does it support?
hints: Read what the extract says the equation is useful for, and what it says was not strictly necessary.
The extract says the energy was measured at 200 MeV with a Geiger counter. What does that say about whether the energy had to be worked out from relativity?

acceptedIdeas: E = mc² helps with the size of the energy, which was also measured directly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: E = mc² helps with the size of the energy, which was also measured directly

choices.label: E = mc² does not apply to fission, because the nucleons keep their masses
E = mc² helps with the size of the energy, which was also measured directly
The student is right, because without the equation the lost mass could not appear as energy

questions.onCorrect: The equation turns a mass difference into the energy, and fission's energy was also measured directly, so the equation reports the amount and does not make fission possible.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says the equation is useful for understanding the energy released in fission, so it does apply. What it adds is that the equation was not strictly necessary once the energy had been measured.
The extract does not make the equation the cause of the energy. It calls the equation useful for the amount, and it says the energy could be measured directly without it.

extracts.text: While E = mc² is useful for understanding the amount of energy potentially released in a fission reaction, it was not strictly necessary to develop the weapon, once the fission process was known, and its energy measured at 200 MeV (which was directly possible, using a quantitative Geiger counter, at that time).
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article on mass-energy equivalence (text under CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article for general readers

questions.prompt: Why is the mass lost in the example 0.0080 kg and not the whole 1.0 kg?
hints: Ask what has happened to the nucleons when helium forms from hydrogen.
The helium has less mass than the hydrogen it came from. How much less?

acceptedIdeas: Only the small mass difference, about 0.8%, becomes energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the small mass difference, about 0.8%, becomes energy

choices.label: All 1.0 kg is lost, because the hydrogen turns into pure energy
Only the small mass difference, about 0.8%, becomes energy
Only 0.8% of the hydrogen fuses, so the rest takes no part

questions.onCorrect: The nucleons all survive in the helium, and only the small drop in mass, about 0.8%, leaves as energy.

misconceptions.feedback: No nucleon is destroyed. The nucleons end up in helium, and only the small difference in mass, about 0.8%, leaves as energy.
All of the hydrogen can fuse. What differs is the mass: the helium that forms has about 0.8% less mass than the hydrogen it came from, and that difference is the mass lost.

questions.prompt: The Parker Solar Probe moves at 68,600 m/s, and the relativistic correction to its kinetic energy is about 3.9 × 10⁻⁸ of the energy. The gravitational constant, which also enters the orbit calculation, is known to a relative uncertainty of about 2.2 × 10⁻⁵. Should the mission team use the relativistic expression for the probe's kinetic energy?
hints: Compare the size of the correction with the uncertainty that is already in the other numbers of the calculation.
A correction that is smaller than the uncertainty of the calculation could never show up in its result.

acceptedIdeas: No, since the correction is far below the uncertainty already in the calculation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since the correction is far below the uncertainty already in the calculation

choices.label: Yes, because no spacecraft before it had ever moved at such a speed
No, since the correction is far below the uncertainty already in the calculation
Yes, since relativity is the true theory and the classical formula is wrong at any speed

questions.onCorrect: The correction is much smaller than the uncertainty already present, so the classical formula is as accurate as the calculation can be.

misconceptions.feedback: A record speed is still a very small fraction of the speed of light, and the size of the correction depends on that fraction. At 68,600 m/s the correction is a few parts in a hundred million.

The classical formula is what relativity gives at low speed, so it is wrong by some amount at every speed. At this speed the amount is about 4 parts in 100 million, far below the uncertainty already in the calculation.

questions.prompt: Seven situations are listed. Which physics does each one need, taking the simplest theory that is accurate enough?
hints: For each case, estimate how large the relativistic or quantum correction would be and compare it with the precision that matters.
A speed far below one tenth of the speed of light, on a scale far larger than an atom, usually needs neither.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Classical physics is enough for the Parker probe's energy and the baseball, relativity is needed for the muons and the GPS clock, and quantum theory for hydrogen's lines, the leakage current and the mirror.

questions.onCorrect: The probe and the baseball need only classical physics, the muons and the GPS clock need relativity, and the hydrogen lines, the leakage and the mirror need quantum theory.

items.label: The kinetic energy of the Parker Solar Probe at 68,600 m/s, for mission planning
items.explanation: The relativistic correction is about 4 parts in 100 million, far below the uncertainty already in the calculation.

items.label: The flight time of a thrown baseball
items.explanation: A baseball's speed is a tiny fraction of the speed of light, and the uncertainty principle is negligible at its scale.

items.label: The lifetime of cosmic-ray muons that reach the ground at 98% of c
items.explanation: At 98% of the speed of light the lifetime is about five times the rest value, which is time dilation.

items.label: The rate of a GPS satellite's atomic clock compared with one on the ground
items.explanation: Satellite clocks have to be adjusted for both special and general relativistic effects to keep ground time.

items.label: The wavelengths of hydrogen's visible emission lines
items.explanation: The lines needed the quantum model that Bohr introduced, and quantum mechanics later replaced that model.

items.label: Leakage current across a 1 nm insulating layer in a chip
items.explanation: Electrons tunnel readily through insulating layers thinner than about 1 nm.

items.label: Position noise of a 100 kg gravitational-wave mirror at its limit
items.explanation: The uncertainty principle limits such a mirror's position, and the limit matters because the instrument measures so precisely.

questions.prompt: What is the combined uncertainty of the westward prediction (21 ns) and the westward measurement (7 ns), in nanoseconds?
hints: Square each uncertainty: 21 × 21 and 7 × 7.
Add the two squares.
Take the square root of the sum. The result is a little more than the larger uncertainty.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The squares are 21² = 441 and 7² = 49, their sum is 490, and the square root of 490 is 22.1 ns.

questions.onCorrect: Independent uncertainties combine by adding their squares and taking the square root, which gives 22 ns, a little more than the larger of the two.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two uncertainties directly. Independent uncertainties combine by adding their squares and taking the square root, which gives a smaller result.

questions.prompt: Two identical atomic clocks are set to agree at sea level. One is then carried to the top of a mountain and left at rest there, while the other stays at sea level. According to theory, what do the clocks show after a long time?
hints: Besides speed, what else changes the rate of a clock, and how does it differ between sea level and a mountain top?
For an orbiting clock, what does the weaker gravity at its height do to its rate?

acceptedIdeas: The mountain clock has gained a little, since gravity is weaker up there
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mountain clock has gained a little, since gravity is weaker up there

choices.label: The two still agree, since neither clock is moving relative to the other
The mountain clock has lost a little, since it is higher above the ground
The mountain clock has gained a little, since gravity is weaker up there

questions.onCorrect: Weaker gravity makes a clock run faster, so the mountain clock gains slightly, and it is the same effect that GPS clocks need corrected.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed is not the only thing that changes the rate of a clock. Gravity does too, and the gravity is slightly different at the two places.
The sign is the wrong way round. Weaker gravity makes a clock run faster, as with the orbiting clock whose speed slows it and whose weaker gravity speeds it up, so the clock at the top gains.

questions.prompt: An astronaut on the International Space Station moves at about 7,700 m/s, and the speed alone would put the astronaut's clock about 5 ms behind a clock on the ground after six months. The weaker gravity at that height speeds the clock up, by a smaller amount. After six months, which statement is correct?
hints: Both effects act on the same clock, in opposite directions. Which of them is larger?
A smaller effect in the opposite direction takes away part of the larger one. Does it take away all of it?

acceptedIdeas: The clock is still behind Earth's, by somewhat less than 5 ms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The clock is still behind Earth's, by somewhat less than 5 ms

choices.label: The clock is still behind Earth's, by somewhat less than 5 ms
The two effects cancel, so the astronaut's clock keeps Earth time
The clock is ahead of Earth's, because gravity speeds it up

questions.onCorrect: The speed effect is larger, so the clock stays behind, and the weaker gravity takes a little off the 5 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: Cancelling would need two effects of equal size. The gravitational effect is the smaller one, so part of the slowing from speed remains.
The gravitational effect is the smaller of the two, so it cannot outweigh the slowing from speed. The clock ends up behind and not ahead.

questions.prompt: A repeat of a clock flight predicts a shift of +120 ± 15 ns and measures +140 ± 20 ns (invented numbers). By how many combined uncertainties do the prediction and the measurement differ? Give your answer to one decimal place.
hints: Find the gap between the two values.
Combine the two uncertainties by adding their squares and taking the square root.
Divide the gap by the combined uncertainty. A value below 1 means that the gap is smaller than the combined uncertainty.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The gap is 140 − 120 = 20 ns, and the combined uncertainty is √(15² + 20²) = √625 = 25 ns, so the gap is 20 ÷ 25 = 0.8 combined uncertainties.

questions.onCorrect: The gap is 0.8 of the combined uncertainty, which is smaller than one, so the measurement is consistent with the prediction.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the gap by the prediction's uncertainty alone. The test uses the two uncertainties combined.
That divides the gap by the measurement's uncertainty alone. The test uses the two uncertainties combined.
That adds the two uncertainties directly. Independent uncertainties combine by adding their squares and taking the square root.

questions.prompt: In 2010 optical atomic clocks linked by 75 m of optical fibre were used to observe time dilation at speeds of less than 10 m/s. What does this show about choosing between classical and relativistic physics?
hints: The correction at 10 m/s is extremely small. What would an instrument need in order to show it?
The choice of theory depends on the size of the correction compared with the precision you need or can measure.

acceptedIdeas: Precision matters as well as speed, so a very good clock can show a tiny correction
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Precision matters as well as speed, so a very good clock can show a tiny correction

choices.label: Classical physics fails at every speed, so every everyday case needs relativity
Precision matters as well as speed, so a very good clock can show a tiny correction
The result must be an error, since time dilation needs speeds close to the speed of light

questions.onCorrect: A correction of about 6 parts in 10¹⁶ is invisible to most instruments, but a clock good enough to resolve it shows time dilation even at 10 m/s.

misconceptions.feedback: At 10 m/s the correction is only about 6 parts in 10¹⁶. Classical physics stays accurate for almost every purpose, and only an instrument good enough to see so small a correction needs relativity.
Time dilation is small at low speed but never absent. At 10 m/s it is about 6 parts in 10¹⁶, which only extremely good clocks can detect.

questions.prompt: Why is the gap of 19 ns compared with 25 ns, and not with the uncertainty of only one of the two numbers?
hints: Each of the two numbers has an uncertainty of its own. Which of them affects the gap between them?
A test that used only one uncertainty would ignore the other number's doubt.

acceptedIdeas: Both numbers are uncertain, so the gap is uncertain by both of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both numbers are uncertain, so the gap is uncertain by both of them

choices.label: The larger figure is chosen because it makes the test easier to pass
The measurement is more reliable, so only its 10 ns should count
Both numbers are uncertain, so the gap is uncertain by both of them

questions.onCorrect: The gap is the difference of two uncertain numbers, so both uncertainties matter, and they combine into 25 ns.

misconceptions.feedback: The test is not chosen to be easy to pass. Each number is uncertain, so the gap between them is uncertain by an amount that depends on both, and 25 ns is the fair value.
The prediction's 23 ns is just as real, and ignoring it would make the test too strict. Both numbers are uncertain, so both uncertainties enter the gap.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the time between two events shown by a clock that is present at both?
flashcards.back: The proper time. Every observer agrees on its reading, and it is the shortest interval any observer measures between the two events.

acceptedIdeas: proper time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: proper time

flashcards.front: What is the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ for a speed of 0.6 c?
flashcards.back: $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 1/0.8 = 1.25$, so each tick lasts 1.25 times as long.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 1/0.8 = 1.25$, so each tick lasts 1.25 times as long.

flashcards.front: A moving clock is measured to run slow. By what factor is each tick longer than at rest?
flashcards.back: By $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$, which is 1.005 at 0.1 c and 5.025 at 0.98 c.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the idea that two events at different places can be simultaneous in one frame but not in another?
flashcards.back: The relativity of simultaneity. Time dilation and length contraction both follow from it.

acceptedIdeas: relativity of simultaneity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: relativity of simultaneity

flashcards.front: Two strikes are simultaneous on a platform and 60 m apart along the track. A train passes at 0.6 c. How many nanoseconds separate the strikes in the train's frame?
Why can two observers in steady relative motion each say that the other's clock runs slow without contradiction?
flashcards.back: Each compares the other's single clock with two of their own, set to agree by their own frame, and the other observer would not call those two clocks in step.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the length of an object measured in its own rest frame?
flashcards.back: The proper length. It is the greatest length any observer measures for the object.

acceptedIdeas: proper length
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: proper length

flashcards.front: A rod is 2.0 m long at rest. How long does an observer measure it, in metres, when it passes lengthwise at 0.6 c?
Along which direction does length contraction act, and which lengths does it leave unchanged?
flashcards.back: It acts along the direction of motion, by the factor $1/\gamma$, and lengths across the motion are unchanged.

flashcards.front: How many joules correspond to 1.0 g of mass by $E = mc^2$? Give the answer in scientific notation, such as 4.1e13.
flashcards.back: $0.001\ \text{kg} \times (299\,792\,458\ \text{m/s})^2 = 9.0\times10^{13}$ J, about 21.5 kilotons of TNT.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the energy a body has when it is at rest, given by $mc^2$?
flashcards.back: Its rest energy. A change in a system's energy changes its mass by the energy divided by $c^2$.

acceptedIdeas: rest energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: rest energy

flashcards.front: Why does a sealed, insulated chamber with an explosion inside weigh the same afterwards?
flashcards.back: The released energy stays inside the system and keeps its mass. Mass is lost only when the energy leaves.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the least energy needed to free an electron from the surface of a metal?
flashcards.back: The work function, $W$. A photon can free an electron only if $hf$ is at least $W$.

acceptedIdeas: work function
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: work function

flashcards.front: Photons of energy 3.1 eV fall on a metal with a work function of 2.0 eV. What is the greatest kinetic energy of the freed electrons, in electron-volts?
Why does doubling the intensity of light of one frequency leave the stopping potential unchanged?
flashcards.back: Intensity changes the number of photons, and so of electrons, and not the energy of each photon, which is $hf$ and depends only on frequency.

flashcards.front: A photon has a wavelength of 413 nm. What is its energy, in eV?
flashcards.back: E = hc / wavelength = 1239.84 / 413 = 3.00 eV.

flashcards.front: Two beams have equal power but different wavelengths. Which sends more photons each second, and why?
flashcards.back: The beam of longer wavelength. Its photons carry less energy, and the photon rate is the power divided by the energy of one photon, so equal power gives more photons at the smaller energy.

flashcards.front: To find a photon's energy in eV, divide a single constant by the wavelength in nm. What is the constant, to the nearest whole number?
flashcards.back: hc = 1239.84 eV nm, so about 1240 eV nm.

flashcards.front: Use $1/\lambda = R(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2)$ with $R = 1.0974 \times 10^7$ per metre for a jump from $n = 4$ to $n = 3$. What is the wavelength, in nm?
flashcards.back: 1/wavelength = 1.0974e7 × (1/9 − 1/16) = 5.335e5 per metre, so the wavelength is 1875 nm, in the infrared.

flashcards.front: A hydrogen atom drops from one level to a lower one and gives out a photon. What fixes the photon's energy?
flashcards.back: The difference between the two level energies. It is not the energy of either level alone, and it is the same for every atom making that jump.

flashcards.front: Which series of hydrogen lines consists of the jumps that end on $n = 2$?
flashcards.back: The Balmer series, whose lines lie in the visible range. The Lyman series ends on $n = 1$ and the Paschen series on $n = 3$.

acceptedIdeas: Balmer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Balmer

flashcards.front: In Bohr's model an orbit's circumference holds 3 de Broglie wavelengths. The electron's angular momentum is how many times $\hbar$?
flashcards.back: A whole number $n$ of wavelengths gives $mvr = n\hbar$, so 3 wavelengths mean an angular momentum of $3\hbar$.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: n wavelengths means mvr = nħ, so the angular momentum is 3ħ.

flashcards.front: Name two kinds of system for which Bohr's model gives almost exact results, and two kinds for which it fails.
flashcards.back: It works for one-electron systems such as hydrogen, singly ionised helium and doubly ionised lithium, and for an atom's outer electron far from the rest. It fails for neutral helium and other multi-electron atoms, for relative line brightness and for the Zeeman effect.

flashcards.front: How did de Broglie's waves explain Bohr's rule for the allowed orbits?
flashcards.back: In 1924 de Broglie read the rule as a standing-wave condition: a whole number $n$ of wavelengths, with $\lambda = h/mv$, fits around the circumference, $n\lambda = 2\pi r$, which gives $mvr = n\hbar$.

flashcards.front: An electron moves at $2.0 \times 10^6$ m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in nm?
Electrons are fired at two slits one at a time. What builds up on the screen, and what does it show?
flashcards.back: Single dots at random places that gradually form bright and dark bands. Each electron lands at one point, and the wave decides where electrons are likely to land.

flashcards.front: A thrown ball has a de Broglie wavelength. Why does it never show diffraction?
flashcards.back: Its wavelength, about $10^{-34}$ m for a 0.145 kg ball at 40 m/s, is far smaller than any gap it meets, so the fringes are far too fine to see. The wave is present at every size.

flashcards.front: An electron is confined to a region 0.10 nm wide. Using $\Delta v \ge \hbar/(2m\,\Delta x)$, what is the least spread in its speed, in units of $10^5$ m/s?
Why can no better instrument remove the position and momentum limit?
flashcards.back: It comes from the wave nature of the particle. A narrow wave packet is a sum of many wavelengths, so a sharp position means a wide spread of momentum, whatever instrument is used.

flashcards.front: Does a short-lived excited state or a long-lived one emit the broader spectral line, and why?
flashcards.back: The short-lived one. A state that exists only briefly cannot have a definite energy, and the width of the line is inversely proportional to the lifetime.

flashcards.front: How does the chance of tunnelling change as the barrier gets wider, as it gets higher and as the particle gets heavier?
flashcards.back: It decreases exponentially in each case, so tunnelling is most noticeable for light particles such as electrons and for very thin barriers.

flashcards.front: Is the emission of electrons from a metal tip in a very strong electric field an example of tunnelling or of thermionic emission?
flashcards.back: Tunnelling. The strong field thins the barrier so that electrons pass through it, and thermionic emission is the different process in which hot electrons climb over.

acceptedIdeas: tunnelling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tunnelling. The strong field thins the barrier so that electrons pass through it, and thermionic emission is the different process in which hot electrons climb over.

flashcards.front: Which quantity does a scanning tunnelling microscope hold constant while its tip scans a surface?
flashcards.back: The tunnelling current. The tip height is adjusted to hold it constant, and the adjustments record the surface.

acceptedIdeas: current
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tunnelling current. The tip height is adjusted to hold it constant, and the adjustments record the surface.

flashcards.front: Why does tunnelling set a lower limit on how small the insulating layers in transistors can be?
flashcards.back: Electrons tunnel readily through insulating layers thinner than about 1 nm, so the layer leaks current, which wastes power and heats the device.
